[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][b][size=5][color=blue]The Greatest Historical Films[/color][/size][/b][/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]In addition to being a Film buff, I am a History buff as well. In fact, I am currently a History major and I hope one day to receive a graduate degree and teach. I have combined both of these interests for this project.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Today begins my list of [color=blue][b]100 great Historical films[/b][/color]. The films are mostly historical narratives, meaning they document historical events as they happened in a way that makes them cinematically appealing. There are also some films where history is not their intent, but more they wish to tell a decent story, and doing so during a certain period in history is interesting. These are often called "period pieces", and they are often successful at drawing attention to certain periods and events in history that aren't always covered in usual films. [/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]These films will ranked in order based on a number of criteria:[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]First and foremost is the [b][color=blue]film quality[/color][/b] itself, whether it is entertaining, whether it is well produced. Acting, directing and writing are all factors here.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=blue][b]Historical accuracy[/b][/color] is also important. It is easy for a filmmaker to twist facts around to make a more interesting presentation, and taking a little license is acceptable and sometimes even necessary, but some filmmakers can bastardize history in the interest of box office receipts. For this reason, films such as Pearl Harbor will not be appearing on this list.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Another important factor is the [color=blue][b]historical significance[/b][/color] of the film. When approaching these films I had to question whether they would be able to impact the viewer, and maybe tell them something about themselves and time they live in. For this reason a film such as Chaplin will not make the list, not because it isn't historical or a good movie, but because it hasn't had a significant impact on history.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Lastly, the films are also ranked based on their [color=blue][b]originality[/b][/color]. For this reason, topics that are covered often, such as certain war films will be given less consideration, and probably only the creme de la creme will appear at the top of the list.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]These films are going to be posted randomly, but they will be rated on a 10 point scale. Once the 100 films have been covered they will be listed by rank. Again, let me reiterate that these films are being rated based on the criteria listed above.[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][/size][/font] 

[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Here is how each film will be scored:[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=blue]Film Quality[/color] (4 possible points)[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=blue]Historical Significance[/color] (2 possible points)[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=blue]Historical Accuracy[/color] (2 possible points)[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=blue]Originality[/color] (2 possible points)[/size][/font]

 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]With all that in mind, here is the beginning of [color=blue][b]Dissent's 100 greatest Historical Films[/b][/color].
[/size][/font]
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][b][size=4][color=blue]Gladiator, Ridley Scott (2000) - Score: 8[/color][/size][/b][/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][img]http://images.amazon.com/images/P/B00003CXE7.01.LZZZZZZZ.jpg[/img][/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Gladiator is the story of Maximus, a general in Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius' northern campaigns. After Aurelius's death, Maximus is sentenced to death by Commodus, whose ascendance to the throne is threatened by his late father's favor for the general. Maximus is able to escape death, but ends up in a world of servitude, killing for entertainment in order to survive.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][img]http://www.imdb.com/Photos/Ss/0172495/3[/img][/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]The story is fictional, but based in a real historic time, during the reigns of two very real Roman Emperors. There isn't a great deal to learn about Rome in this film, but Ridley Scott gives us one of the most compelling visions of the empire, and of course their favorite past-time. Marcus Aurelius' is portrayed as a gentle, noble and capable Emperor who cares for his people, while Commodus is shown as an aggressive, narrow-minded emperor who cares only for his own popularity. While these pictures might not be completely accurate, they are close to the Historical record.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][img]http://www.imdb.com/Photos/Ss/0172495/2[/img][/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Scott must also be commended for giving the audience a very brief understanding of the Roman political structure. with the Senate answering both to the Emperor and to the people, which resulted in a constant struggle for power. Scott weaves this political struggle into the plot in order to give it depth and to create suspense.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]The film is criticized for being overly violent and sentimental, however that is how Rome was. The Romans loved blood almost as much as they loved their heroes.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3]Let us not forget the opening battle scene in Germania. Few films have documented ancient military history on such a scale. While there was some license taken to make the battle a little more exciting (such as the excessive fire), the scene was a very historically accurate portrayal of the Roman campaigns in the North.[/size][/font]
 
[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][img]http://www.imdb.com/Photos/Ss/0172495/4[/img]

[font=Trebuchet MS][size=3][color=blue]Film Quality: [b]3[/b][/color][/size][/font]

[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]Gladiator[/color][/size][/b][/font]
[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]Director: Ridley Scott (Thelma and Louise)[/color][/size][/b][/font]
[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]Players: Russell Crowe, Joaquin Phoenix, Connie Nelson, Derek Jacobi, Djimon Hounsou, Richard Harris.[/color][/size][/b][/font]
[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]Historical Epic- Im a big fan of Ridley Scott. None of his movies are particularly brilliant, and they all are very Hollywood-ized, but hes a visionary director who continues to amaze me as he changes his style and approach to almost every movie he creates. His first movie was [i]The Duelists[/i], a movie which I never really liked. A costume movie with no real plot. But his breakthrough smash [i]Alien [/i]started one of my favorite series of all time, and was in itself a good, nasty shlock horror that took an old and typical sci-fi plot and revamped it into a great film, making it a classic. Then came [i]Blade Runner, Black Rain, [/i]and[i] Thelma and Louise[/i]. All are blunt, well-made movies, but ones that stick with you. His bloody Roman epic [i]Gladiator [/i]is no exception. [/color][/size][/b][/font]
[b][size=3][color=white][i][font=Verdana]Gladiator [/font][/i][font=Verdana]succeeds on many levels where Scotts previous works failed. The acting is great. Russell Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix deliver convincing performances of their layered characters. Also, Scott has learned to temper his over-the-top gore as seen in [i]Alien [/i]and [i]Blade Runner[/i]. Dont get me wrong, [i]Gladiator [/i]is a violent movie, but it leaves a bulk of it to your imagination and the rest happens so quickly you hardly even have time to register whats happening. Also, this movie features a new film style. The year before this movie came out, [i]The Matrix [/i]wowed audiences with its bullet-time filming style. Im not sure if [i]Gladiators [/i]new style had the same effect (it didnt on me), but I did think it was pretty nifty for what it was. During most of the action sequences, frames were removed from the film to give it an odd choppy look, kind of reminding me of stop-motion animation (now [i]theres [/i]something Id like to see in a modern movie). So with all of these new things, I think Ridley has made a great movie, though in my opinion its not his best. It is very hard to top [i]Blade Runner [/i]in sheer overpowering melancholy emotion that assaults you with the scenery alone. But that said, I loved [i]Gladiator[/i].[/font][/color][/size][/b]
[color=white][img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1096836/Gladiator-photo_13.jpg[/img][/color]
[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]The movies slogan pretty much sums the plot up: The general who became a slave. The slave who became a gladiator. The gladiator who defied an empire. There you have it. Not much more to it than that, other than the little plot intricacies, all of which just develop that little slogan. And thats OK in this movies case, but its kind of a blunt story (typical Ridley). The one thing that struck me about this movie is how sad it was. Yeah, the action is seat-gripping, but the real power of this movie is in the tragedy of the story. I cried when Maximus (played by Oscar-Winner Russell Crowe) died at the end. Part of me is annoyed by this, because I absolutely hate it when a movie pulls strings to get you to feel sentimental and get all weepy. I hated it when [i]A Beautiful Mind [/i]did it, and I wasnt too fond of this movie doing it either. But despite my annoyance, the performances of this movie are powerful, and you can give in and just pull out the hanky without feeling too wimpy about it. Russell Crowe is great in this movie as the Roman general (who became a slave who became a gladiator) and he makes his character so convincing, you feel like you can hear what he thinks. Very few actors can do that (among them Daniel Day-Lewis), and I think Crowe is extraordinary at his trade. But I felt the hype surrounding him outshined his co-star Phoenix, who I felt had just as complex a character and whose acting was just as good. He really creeped me out. He was so unpredictable. Shifty, like. Very good, all around the table.[/color][/size][/b][/font]
[color=white][img]http://images.rottentomatoes.com/images/movie/gallery/1096836/Gladiator-photo_09.jpg[/img][/color]
[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]This movie differs from other big smash hits Ive seen recently in that it uses its CGI and special effects to enhance, rather than make it the main attraction. I like this in some movies, and I loved it in [i]Gladiator. [/i]The CGI (at least the CGI I could notice) is used only to recreate ancient Rome. The movie puts its focus on the character, and I think its a good change in direction for Ridley. I never really cared about his characters in other movies, even [i]Alien [/i]and [i]Blade Runner[/i] (I love Ellen Ripley, but she really became my favorite movie hero because of [i]Aliens[/i], which developed her beyond the no-nonsense, utilitarian character she was in its predecessor). [/color][/size][/b][/font]
[font=Verdana][b][size=3][color=white]But for all its merits, [i]Gladiator [/i]still only scores a 9/10 (only!?). Its a hard movie to watch a lot, its depressing, its bloody, and it just doesnt have the aura of greatness that surrounds all movies I award 10/10 to. Hard to describe, but thats how it is. But its good for what it is. Cinema hasnt seen its likes since Stanley Kubricks classic [i]Spartacus.[/i] And, hopefully, we wont see anything like it again (meaning noooo more overkill! Leave a good movie alone, and dont cash in on the craze). (R)[/color][/size][/b][/font]

[size=3]Ridley Scott's epic about ancient Rome has been compared to predecessors such as [i]Ben-Hur [/i]and [i]Spartacus[/i].  While there are certainly some stylistic differences, I would agree that the films are quite similar...which perhaps partially explains why I did not enjoy it.  [i]Gladiator[/i], like those Hollywood movies that came before it, subverts historical accuracy to tell a sweeping tale of romance, heroism and bravery.  To quote Jerry Seinfeld: not that there's anything wrong with that.  The problem with the film is that it is so solemn and convinced of its own profundity (a similar fate befalls the [i]Lord of the Rings [/i]films).  The movie attempts to be a story of political betrayal and Shakespearean double-crosses, as well as a rousing action movie that features breathtaking scenes set in the Coliseum.  It fails on both levels.  The "serious" scenes are not particularly engaging, largely due to the wooden acting by Joaquin Phoenix and Russell Crowe, who are both trying their hardest to appear complex despite the emptiness of the script.  And as for the battle scenes, I found them fuzzy and indistinct, and so furiously edited by Scott and his collaborators that the sense of flow and danger is lost.  Even the film's key setpiece, a battle that involves not only men but tigers, is quite muddled (although still one of the more rousing scenes in the film).  Scott has crafted a film supposedly rich in production values (despite the fact I was unimpressed) but devoid of emotion or weight.  I don't doubt that [i]Gladiator [/i]will take its place alongside [i]Ben-Hur [/i]and [i]Spartacus [/i]as Hollywood classics.  It will also take its place alongside those films in my mind.  Suffice it to say, it's not a very big place.[/size]

Gladiator
 
 I still cant believe that of all the nominees the Academy choose this film; hell, as you can see, I even prefer Chocolat to it.  My first major problem is the film is ugly, and no I dont mean brutal or realistic; I mean ugly, ugly.   Everything has this dull, washed-out near-botched photography quality to it that just doesnt sit well with the story; through it does fit the afterlife scenes well. Take for example the introduction of Rome;  the score and the direction are trying to make it seem grand, and mysterious, but it doesnt; it looks like a botched negative.  All the colors and contours run together and become a blur.  I think it is hampered by shoddy direction, art direction, CGI, and cinematography.  The fights are hampered by this as well; the CGI really distances the viewer from the emotions of the scene. oh god, I hate the editing and direction of the fights. The fights look like a mad butcher got a hold of them.  now, I can understand the first battle being cut together the way it is, given how it would be confusing to the soldiers; but why the devil for the climax, and most of the coliseum fights?  the themes would have worked much better if the fights were shot alternating between Maximus POV, and crowd POV, and for the love of God letting the shot be longer than .5 seconds. But no instead we get too quickly cut scenes that take the viewer out of the film, and are semi-hard the follow.  The direction only makes this worse.
 
 My second biggest problem is Commodus.  He is such a non-villain. First, Phoenix simply doesnt have the screen presence to be frightening, mean, creepy, insulting or anything negative that would inspire, or suggests antagonism . the only thing his performance evokes from me is pity.  This is worsen because he simply can not keep up with the manhood of Crowe, who is just naturally gruff and rugged.  The writing is no better; Commodus is written as a pansy push over that has no chance against Maximus. I also dont like this interpretation of the Roman Emperor. Most would not be this sneaky, and be far more blunt. This undercuts the entire drama of the film because as soon as you meet Maximus, and Commodus you know whos the boss. There is no strong force of antagonism in the film because of this. Furthermore, given that the contours of the Gladiator are well traveled this makes the film unbelievably predictable.
 
 with that being said,  Gladiator is still a fun film with a very strong performance by Crowe.  It might be formulaic, but the formula works to a degree.
 
 Traffic 
 
 Traffic is wonderful in many ways.  the way it approaches the issue of the drug war with maturity, and much intelligence being the main one.  All sides of the issues are given a voice; Soderbergh manages to pull off this off by telling three stories well, but together I find them a bit unseemly.  My major problem is there are moments in the film that just scream false. For example the countless times two characters from different stories cross the same piece of land. theres no reason for this but to make the film feel more like one story.  It could have been done in a better, more narrative natural way.  The other little nitpick is, while the film generally speaking isnt preachy (blunt yeah, preachy no), there are a few times where Soderbergh becomes a little forceful.  the worst offender is the car conversation between Wakefield (Douglas) and Seth (Eric from that 70s show).  Wakefield comment of I cant believe you took her to a places like this in no way shape or form warrants the rant by Seth concerning African-American being expected to have drugs by white suburbs kids;  hello, his comment meant a poor neighborhood, not a black neighborhood.  To top it off, Wakefield, a very intelligent lawyer, has no rebuttal. please! I also like how the film makes it a point that American drug policy, while flawed, isnt the worse in the world.  The colour coding was a stroke of brilliance because it does make the three stories much easier to follow, plus it gives each its own flavor that reflects the theme, or emotions (I.E. Douglass is blue, because it is tragic.) The screenplay also did a fair job of writing exposition into the film, while turning the drama.  For example, the scene with Ruiz (Ferrer) confessing as massive exposition concerning the ineffectiveness of border patrols, yet each sentence turns the scene around both him and the detectives being more annoyed with each other. 
 
 
 the acting all around is phenomenal.  Del Toro is the one that stands out of course, but Zeta-Jones, Douglas, Guzman, Grace, and Christensen all do a good job.  This is another movie that speaks loudly for an casting or ensemble acting Oscar.
 
 I also dont buy Helena Ayalas character arch (Zeta-Jones). She goes from a pampered house wife who know nothing about the drug business to calling hits and making large drug deals.  say what?  I dont buy it from the husband end; why would he trust her to run the business now (he is in jail), even through he never told her about it before in any form? wouldnt you think he would have another plan, than to go to his ignorant wife? I also dont buy it from the her end; the threat to her child would not force her into the business first. maybe if it was more physical, or if she tried to sell to house or something first, but not right away.
 
 Chocolat
 
 Acting goes a long way with me, and Chocolat has that in spades.  Juliette Binoche gives a quite a performance as Vianne, a single mother who opens a chocolate shop in a very conservative town. she gives Vianne just the right amount of  subtle grace, worldly wisdom and innate kindness to work wonderful.  Binoche is just charismatic in this film, and her timing is very good.  Judi Dench is the perfect complement to Binoche; her Armande is a lively, quick witted, and charming.   the rest of the cast is stellar as well; Morlina is just the right amount of weasel, Moss is stern yet sensitive; OConor is just right for the priest and Depp is his normal quirky entertaining self, a few accent problems aside.  I think this is best acted of the nominees. 
 
 apart from this Chocolat is just a charming, and moving  fable. Dont be mistaken this movie is a fable, and isnt concerned with realism.  Funny, gentle, and most of all uplifting Chocolat warms the heart. I also totally love the look, and direction in the film.  It gives it such an other worldly quality to it that fits the story.  The only problem I have with it is it is so light a strong breeze will destroy it.  
 
 Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon
 
 the film is graceful;  everything about it carries a subtle grace that fills the film with a sublime mysticism that enthralls the viewer. the fights are sheer visual poetic vehicles for the story; each fight furthers the relationship and plot of the film to the tragic conclusion.   Its a great looking film too. I love the cinematography, it is simple breath taking and a few shots look like water-colour too me. The score is great; every once in a awhile a film comes along that is hard for to express why I like it as much as I do, this is one of them.
 
 I really agree with Eberts review.
 
 I have no interest of every seeing the other nominee. I can't stand Roberts.

[left]Heres a flick that Id heard nothing but good things about, yet had managed to not watch in the four years its been available. Its the tale of Spartac I mean, Maximus  a general who becomes a slave who becomes a gladiator who pisses off Joaquin Phoenix. Somewhere in those transitions, an epic supposedly unfolds  through large scale battles, hokey CGI effects, and pacing to cure even the worse case of insomnia.[/left]
 
[left]As the plot developed, I couldnt help but feel that Id watched this film a hundred times before. The story is far from a bad one, it just felt tired. Its also hard to buy into a lot of what is going on  for example, that Maximus is randomly picked up in the countryside of Rome and put into slavery. Perhaps this was because they believed him to be a deserter, but that was never really cleared up. A certain decision by the Emperor to engage in a certain battle at the end of the movie was equally mystifying.[/left]
 
[left]The highlight ends up being the acting, rather than the story. Russell Crowe got an Oscar for his turn as Maximus, which must mean the Academy doesnt mind blatantly out-of-place accents. His performance here isnt necessarily Oscar-worthy, but he certainly could have done worse. He manages to convey emotions we might expect from a hardened soldier, though it may appear as rigid acting to the naked eye. Joaquin Phoenix is becoming one of my favorite actors. His take on the twisted Commodus (the emperor of Rome) is certainly deserving of the nomination it drew him. He balances Commodus bizarre emotions and psychotic behaviors wonderfully  and has the face of an evil emperor, to boot.[/left]
 
[left]Outside of the acting, however, things get rough. This movie has now become my favorite example for the ole CGI isnt quite there yet argument. I remember the big hype about this movie bringing the Coliseum back to life, but any distant shots of it just look downright fake. In fact, landscape shots of Rome in general just look terribly amateur. I cant help but wonder how some of these terrible-looking shots make it to the final print. It boggles my mind.[/left]
 
[left]On the flipside, the closer shots of the Coliseum are gorgeous. They truly revived the beauty of the once-immaculate structure  especially the interior. One shot follows a group of gladiators as they run onto the sands of the Coliseum for the first time, and circles around them as they take it all in with awe. As a member of the audience, you cant help but join in with them.[/left]
 
[left]Other aspects of the movie are hit-and-miss. The score is decent, or at least good enough that Disney ripped it off for Pirates of the Caribbean  the main tune of both movies is almost identical. Supporting characters are, for the most part, shallow and uninteresting (and, as far as that goes, unneeded). See: almost every gladiator except Maximus and Juba. The pacing is also painfully slow in some parts, making you wonder if they took ideas for three different movies and combined them into one. At times, it would seem that is exactly what they did.[/left]
 
[left]For two and a half hours you are treated to spectacle and quality acting, all revolving around very little story  but wait, theres more. It all builds up to one of the most anti-climactic conclusions that Ive ever seen in an epic. Its not a bad ending  but it sure isnt going to knock any sandals off. Youd think for all your patience that a decent ending wouldnt be too much to ask, but youre treated to a pretty mundane and clichéd final scene, anyway. Lucky you.[/left]
 
[left]So at the end of the day, Gladiator fails to impress in the way that I had hoped it would. I can still recommend it, as its far from a bad movie  but it is certainly not the grand saga that I was expecting. Its worth it for the acting and intermittent scenes of beauty, but dont expect an epic tale worth the investment of your attention and emotions.[/left]

This is a retelling of the same story that the old movie Fall of the Roman Empire told, with its own bunch of fiction added to take the story into new areas. The story is 90% fiction; even the historical characters are fictionalized. The most accurate thing on the screen and one of the most fascinating was the computer graphics of Rome and especially the Colosseum. They did a very good job and clearly consulted experts on its construction.
 
Once you get past wondering why with 700 years worth of Western Roman history to draw from they had to recycle a fictional one, its good entertainment. The opening battle is a wonder to watch. Who cares if Romans fought exactly like that? They did fight kind of like that, with the war machines, skirmishers and heavy infantry and auxilliary archers. Cavalry flanking moves in heavy forest is pushing it, however. They had to get Russell Crowe on a horse leading a charge somehow.
 
The gladiator segments in the Colosseum are the movie's highpoints. I replayed the Carthaginian battle it was too cool. The emperor's digs are appropriately sumptuous and the screen convinces you that it goes on and on just like the computerized graphics of Imperial Rome.
 
The movie weakens a bit near the end, the so-so story getting its logic strained to the breaking point. Maximus is finally avenged and there is so much finality to the story even the most determined sequel writers would have a hell of a time. The critics didn't like Gladiator too much and probably all puked when it got Best Picture. It just shows that they follow each other's lead into Dumbassdom at least once in a while. I'd be all for a few more epics about the period, and I'd probably pass out if they did a Hollywoodized true story.

I figured for my first entry for my rotten account that I would discuss my favorite movie.
 
I think gladiator is hands down amazing.  Russell Crowe's character is superb.  I remember going to the theater expecting a gorey movie.  The movie opens in a woody area in the country side.  Maximus (Crowe's character) is setting up for a battle.  One of the emporer's scouts returns on his horse beheaded.  Shortly after the barbarian horde appears with the leader holding the head of the scout as a trophy.  The battle begins and is one of the most beautiful things to hit a big screen.  As the flaming arrows and catapault shells explode, I couldn't help but drool.  My interest was peaked.
 
The movie continued to build an amazing storyline.  The emporer chose Maximus as his successor but they emporer's son kills him before anyone else knew his wishes.  The prince asks Maximus for his loyalty.  After Maximus denies the Prince, he and his wife and child are sentenced to death.  Maximus manages to avoid being killed and escapes wounded on horseback.  He pushes himself and the horse to the limit to try and save his family.  When he reaches his farm, it's too late.  Russell Crowe's character starts crying with snot running from his nose.  It is such an incredibly emotional scene that only a veteran actor could pull off.  
 
The rest of the movie is his progression after the death of his family.  He's presented an opportunity to exact his revenge.  The final battle is magnificent.  I am unaware of another movie that executes the emotion it builds throught the movie.  So many movies fail and leave you feeling empty and wanting more when it's over.

Many people will flame someone for saying this film is emotional and that is has "insert tears here" moments; but I disagree.         [center] [left]Maximus is the general of the Roman army. We open up with a pre-battle setting. Everyone is ready and drawn. After the true caesar is murdered Maximus is sent off to slavery and then gets his vengeance later on by becoming a gladiator who defied an empire. The story is basic and to the point and it works. It's the background story of the whole Roman defiance issues that really interested me. Rome is potrayed in an ugly and murky setting. This works because it shows the dark times the city was going through. Great directing there for Mr. Scott.

It's the small tidbits and flaws that stop it from being perfect. The ending of the film is what many believe to be horrible. I enjoyed it. Ridley Scott artfully ....well let's just use the word "borrows" from some of the best epics in movie history, and cobbles together this amalgam. Don't get me wrong, I love Gladiator. I love the cast, I love the look of the film, I love the score, and I love the story. But if you've seen Ben Hur, Spartacus, and Braveheart, you've seen Gladiator. The borrowing is done so well, though, that I just don't care. Russell Crowe shines as Maximus (though it's dumb that this is the performance he won an Oscar for when he was ignored for The Insider and A Beautiful Mind), Joaquin Phoenix is hateful as Commodus, and Richard Harris delivers a wonderful performance as the dying Caesar. My only other complaint with the movie, aside from being derivative, is that it goes about 25 minutes longer than it should. It's not original, but it is extremely well-done, and that gets a thumbs up from me.

When Steven Spielberg saw Gladiator at a DreamWorks screening, he complimented Ridley Scott by saying "You've made an opera."
 
[img]http://i30.photobucket.com/albums/c330/impavido/gladiator3.jpg[/img]
 
Gladiator has been one of my favorite films since I'd first seen it in 2000. Scott and the screenwritters took what had been an old-Hollywood staple and crafted something with uncommon drama and an almost spiritual heart. It's much more than a simple revenge tale. The character Maximus did not become a movie hero because he could kill all the bad guys...but because he reminded the audience what was worth fighting and dying for.
 
I am consistently and repeatedly engrossed in the visuals of this film. The lighting of every single scene is flawless. Scott's ability to draw your eye and create emotion simply from a setting is unmatched. Every detail adds to the visual tone and theme of what is happening in the story. Whether is is the subtlety of the snow in the Germania battle (which was natural and unplanned snow Scott decided to continue filming when it began) or the dramatic power of rose-petals falling over the hero as he enters the arena.
 
[img]http://i30.photobucket.com/albums/c330/impavido/gladiator2.jpg[/img]
 
Scott also filmed Gladiator with a great eye for the architecture of Rome and the colisseum...of both the real set and CGI variety. The architecture is never a focal point of the shot but it permeates the background wonderfully.
 
The dramatic acting is spot on, at times over-dramatic as an opera should be yet entirely relatable and believable. The entire cast is wonderfully chosen and I do not believe there is a single example of bad or even mediocre acting in the entire film. (Well...maybe the German was mediocre...but at least it wasn't Dolph Lundgren) The best of which is from Oliver Reed in my opinion. Proximo was a fascinating character and it was a good note for the world to remember him by.
 
The music by Hans Zimmer is the single best work he has done in his entire career. Using Lisa Gerrards ethereal voice adds a lot of warmth and spirituality. And using a Waltz format for the score during the Germania battle is absolute brilliance. The structure of the waltz lends well to the organization and movement of the mighty Roman army.
 
The now available 3 Hour extended cut of Gladiator, much more so than my beloved Dune, is a rare example of a quality extended cut. The scenes that are included do not drag down the pacing of the film to any annoying degree. Each scene is well shot and acted. And many add depth to the plot and several characters.
 
Some of these scenes include some fantastic scenes with Proximo and his business dealings.
More detail is added to the political side of things with Lucila and the Senators.
other scenes involve some characterization of or dialogue with other minor characters such as Quintas, The German, and the Scribe (The guy who pissed himself in the first arena battle in Zuccubar.)
 
I have always been a huge fan of Ridley Scott's work, so this is perhaps a little biased...but I give Gladiator a 10 out of 10. I'd really like to point out that I rarely ever give a movie a 10, unlike a lot of RT posters who use it very liberaly.
 
The extended cut I give 9/10 due to it's being slower than the mostly exemplary pacing of the theatrical cut. However the extended cut is still very much worth the time of any Gladiator or Ridley Scott fan.

[font=Arial][color=darkred]Director Ridley Scott has given the world of cinema some of its most unforgettable visual experiences. But can Scott breath new life into a genre whose heyday was when a badly dubbed Steve Reeves oiled his chest and wrestled loincloth-clad extras in the 1950s? You bet your sweet ass.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Arial][color=darkred]The year is roughly 180 AD and Rome is just finishing up its long-standing assault on anything that moves in the European continent. General Maximus (Russell Crowe) merely wants to retire back to his loving family and get away from the doom and war that has plagued his life. This is made all the more difficult when the ailing Emperor bypasses his treacherous son Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) and decides to crown Maximus as the Defender of Rome. Because of this Commodus rises to power through bloody circumstances and has Maximus assigned to execution and his family crucified. You'd think crucifixion would be so passé by now. Maximus escapes only to be sold into slavery and bought by a dirt-run gladiator training school. As he advances up the chain and learns the tricks of the primal sport he seeks but vengeance for his fallen family.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Arial][color=darkred]'Gladiator' is an absorbing and sweeping spectacle of carnage and first-rate entertainment. The action is swift and ruthlessly visceral. The first movie in a long time to literally have me poised on the edge of my seat. The blood spills in the gallons and life and limb go flying enough your theater owner may consider setting down a tarp.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Arial][color=darkred]What 'Gladiator' doesn't sacrifice to the muscle of effects and action is storytelling. Are you listening George Lucas? 'Gladiator' may unleash the beast when the rousing action is loose, but this is coupled with compelling drama and complex characters. Phoenix may at first seem like a snotty brat with an unhealthy eye for his sister (Connie Nielsen), but the further 'Gladiator' continues the more you see in his eyes the troubled youth who just wants the love of his father that was never bestowed to him. Maximus is a devoted family man who regularly kisses clay statues of his family while away, and must ceremoniously dust himself with the earth before any battle.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Arial][color=darkred]The acting matches every sword blow and chariot race toe-for-toe. Russell Crowe marks a first-rate staple of heroism. Every calculating glare he exhibits shows the compassion and ferocity of this warrior. He becomes a rare breed - an action hero who can think and actually act. Oliver Reed, in what sadly was his last role, turns in a splendid and charismatic turn as the head of the gladiator school of Fine Arts and Carnage. Mysteriously everyone carries a British accent closer to them then a toga two sizes too small. Even Crowe who is nicknamed "The Spaniard" speaks like he walked out of 'Masterpiece Theater'.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Arial][color=darkred]The effects and visuals are a sumptuous feast. The aireal shots of Rome and the Coliseum are simply breath taking. 'Gladiator' rivals 'American Beauty' for the most rose petals used in a movie, except in this one they don't shoot out of Mena Suvari's breasts - oh well, too bad.[/color][/font]
 
[font=Arial][color=darkred]Ridley Scott's track record may be hit or miss, but 'Gladiator' is definitely one sorely not to be missed.[/color][/font]

More past Best Picture Winners. This time I examine [i]Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King[/i] (as well as the other two LOTR movies) plus [i]Gladiator[/i]. 
 
[i]Gladiator[/i], directed by Ridley Scott, won the Oscar for Best Picture for 2000. The other nominees were [i]Chocolat[/i], [i]Erin Brockovich[/i], [i]Traffic[/i], and [i]Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon[/i]. Other notable films included [i]Cast Away[/i], [i]The Quills[/i], [i]Pollock[/i], [i]Almost Famous,[/i] [i]Dancer in the Dark[/i], [i]Requiem For A Dream[/i], [i]Before Night Falls[/i], and [i]Amores Perros[/i].
 
[b]Gladiator [/b]is another Epic Adventure, set in the Roman Empire. Russell Crowe plays Maximus, a prized general in the Roman Army. When emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) dies, his deceitful son Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) takes over, and Maximus is to be put to death. Maximus escapes, but his family is killed setting up revenge as the major plotline in this film. Although the sets, costumes and cinematography are very good, the film's story is contrived and heavy handed. It usually feels like a modern day film costumed up to fit into the Roman Empire. Ridley Scott seems to be more concerned about visuals than anything else and the ill-concieved dialogue is only necessary to bridge one fight scene to the next. How this film won an Oscar for Best Picture is incomprehensible.
 
Next up is [b]Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King[/b], Best Picture Winner for 2003. I'm also including the other two LOTR films as I felt I needed to watch them first. Amazing that I had not seen any of these until a few days ago considering how popular this trilogy was. Other nominees for Best Picture in 2003 went to [i]Lost in Translation,[/i] [i]Master and Commander[/i], [i]Mystic River[/i] and [i]Seabiscuit[/i]. Other notable films of 2003 include [i]The House of Sand and Fog[/i], [i]Cold Mountain,[/i] [i]In America[/i], [i]21 Grams[/i], [i]Monster[/i], [i]The Last Samarai[/i], [i]Pieces of April[/i], [i]Thirteen[/i], [i]Finding Nemo,[/i] [i]Dirty Pretty Things[/i], [i]Barbarian Invasions[/i] and [i]American Splendor[/i]. 
 
The Lord of the Rings Trilogy is the screen adaption of JRR Tolkien's Epic Medieval Fantasy. The trilogy, all directed by Peter Jackson, follows the journey of a hobbit named Frodo (Elijah Wood) who was chosen to carry the ring on a long and dangerous journey. Fellow Hobbit and best friend Sam (Sean Austin) is along for the journey. Frodo and Sam run into many onstacles along the way, but also have a bunch of good guys and girls trying to help them complete this long journey. Okay I don't want to go into detail! The films also feature Viggo Mortensen, Ian McKellan, Orlando Bloom, Cate Blanchett, Liv Tyler, Andy Serkis and Dominic Monaghan. 
 
I'll admit I enjoyed this trilogy far more than I expected to, but it's less than perfect. Although it's visually stunning and usually exciting, one's understanding of the story would surely be helped by reading the book. Since I have no desire to do so, I can only judge the films. Although the story of the Hobbits are developed well, it can be confusing trying to understand the signficance of many of the other characters. Some are not developed at all, despite being seen in all three films. As a stand alone film, the second doesn't work well at all. However it's an exciting and visually stunning journey, even if the screen story is sometimes flawed. Overall 
[i]Lord of the Rings: Return of the King [/i]was the most cohesive film of the trilogy, and considering the immense popularity of this series I don't have much of an issue with the later being named Best Picture.

[font=Georgia][size=3]This is a review for the unrated extended version of Ridley Scotts [i]Gladiator[/i] which was released last summer, five years after it was originally released in 2000 and was nominated for 12 Academy Awards, and winning 5, including Best Actor and Best Picture. How Ridley Scott didnt win for Best Director is beyond me. The man knows how to make an epic picture, and in my opinion nobody does it any better than he does. This extended cut of [i]Gladiator[/i] includes an additional 16 minutes of new footage. I guess the big question is does it make the film any better? Well, no, not really. The film already is great. But it does add a slightly deeper plotline involving Roman politics and Lucillas (Connie Nielsen) involvement in the plot to overthrow Commodus. This really isnt that important to the story, but it does a good job of explaining, in greater detail, how people felt about Commodus and how much they disliked his leadership. The extended cut also gives Joaquin Phoenix a nice little scene showing how Commodus punishes those who lie to him.[/size][/font]
[font=Georgia][size=3] [/size][/font]
[/color][color=red][font=Georgia][size=3]For those of you who havent yet seen [i]Gladiator[/i], well there really shouldnt be that many of you, its a great epic full of intense performances, high attention to detailed sets and costumes, a heart-pounding musical score and great camera work by Ridley Scott, a man with a vision and the eye to make it a reality. The film is about a Roman General named Maximus (played with brooding intensity by Russell Crowe) who is betrayed by Rome and his family is murdered by an evil and selfish prince named Commodus (played well by Joaquin Phoenix) who lusts after power, control and glory (and even his sister, Lucilla), none of which he rightfully earns, but merely steals by assassinating his own father, Caesar Marcus Aurelius, played with great humanity by the late Richard Harris. Maximus is sentenced to death by Commodus for disobedience, and has his wife and son crucified, but Maximus escapes death and races home to try and save his family only to find them already dead by the time he gets there. Maximus is then captured by a man named Proximo (played by Oliver Reed), a man who trains gladiators to fight to the death so he can make money. Maximus is now the slave of Proximo, and he has just gained the champion gladiator of a lifetime; a former Roman General with plenty of expierence in killing. Maximus rises to fame and then travels to Rome to fight in the Colosseum when Commodus decides to bring back the old tradition of gladiator games. Thats when Commodus discovers that Maximus is not dead, but very much alive, and he has come back to get his revenge.[/size][/font]
[font=Georgia][size=3] [/size][/font]
[/color][color=red][font=Georgia][size=3]The performances are great. The three main leads; Russell Crowe, Joaquin Phoenix and Connie Nielsen are especially good. The visuals in [i]Gladiator[/i] are pretty astounding; the Roman Colosseum hasnt look this good in ages, and the action is intense, exciting and at times quite gruesome. Can you say [i]evisceration by means of runaway chariot[/i]? God, dont you just love history! Russell Crowes great performance in this movie put his Maximus on my all-time favorite action heroes list, which also includes Bruce Willis John McClane, Mel Gibsons Martin Riggs and William Wallace, Harrison Fords Han Solo and Indiana Jones and Hugh Jackmans Wolverine and Kurt Russells Snake Plisskin. All in all [i]Gladiator[/i] delivers exactly what youd hope and expect from a Ridley Scott epic; exciting action, great cinematography, a wonderfully sweeping score and intense performances. Big scale excitement doesnt get any better than this![/size][/font]

Some scenes of the film seemed boring but were made up for in a big way by the battle scenes. They are brilliantly executed, with a perfect balance of gore and excessiveness. Ridley Scott proves again that he really knows how to direct and Epic, as he has created the best example I have seen so far. All in all a brilliant movie, a little on the long side but that didn't matter too much here, there was enough going on to make up for it.

I just can´t believe how any one dares to compare it with classic epics like "Ben Hur", "Spartacus" or even "Quo Vadis?". OK it could be pretty good entertainment to the average audience but it´s a torture to viewers with knowledge of ancient Rome. The fifties and sixties epics weren´t completely authentic either, Ustinov was an outstanding Nero, but Nero didn´t burn Rome. But they managed to recreate the atmosphere of the Roman Empire. "Gladiator" doesn´t! This movie is located in some historic ´fantasyland. Take the cinematographic style of "1492" add battlescenes from both "Braveheart" and "Saving Private Ryan", a plot from "The Fall of the Roman Empire" and a gladiator school and fight scenes from "The Gladiators" and "Spartacus" even a little bit of "Star Wars" and you get "Gladiator". Sometimes such mixtures of well-known elements and images work out see "Star Wars". But although this movie lacks innovative ideas it features nearly every known cliché and is absolutely unrealistic concerning historic accuracy. Of course nearly no historic movie (see above) is completely accurate, but none of the epics of the past (leave out the trash from Italy or Spain) ignored history like "Gladiator" does. It starts right in the beginning. The roman legions fight a germanic tribe to conquer it´s land. Completely wrong! During the reign of Marc Aurel the Romans fought desperately though still successfully to keep the germanic tribes away from their borders. They did NOT fight to conquer Germania, they didn´t conquer any new german territories after their defeat in the Teutoburg Forest battle more than a century ago. The germanic warriors shown are pure fiction, nothing is correct, not their appearance or their weapons or the tactics they use (in the movie they have none!) The battle is completely unrealistic beginning with the battlefield in the midst of a forest, the romans avoided forest battles. The roman forces used ballistas at sea or at sieges but not in field battles. Instead of arrows they threw their pilums and then fought with their swords. The roman army was infantry since the late days of the republic and had no own cavalry, they only hired cavalry from allied tribes. A roman general who was respected by his soldiers that strong could never have been arrested this easily without the risk of revolting troops. Maximus would have cremated his dead family (romans didn´t bury their dead) and why on earth was Maximus captured and enslaved at his burned homestead and brought to what, Morocco? He was a roman citizen and at least when he was identified in the collisseum he would have had to be released from his illegal slavery.
It lacks atmosphere, good cinematography (not ONE good shot of Rome!) and a convincing plot. It has some good actors, but Russell Crowe is no Charlton Heston, Joaquin Phoenix is no Ustinov and Harris is no Alec Guiness. Maybe i would have enjoyed this film if i didn't have more knowledge of  Roman history than the screenwriter.

Connie Nielsen plays one of strongest female character that I've seen. Choreographer of the action sequences was brilliant.  [b][size=3]
 Walk the Line
 [/size][/b][size=3][size=2]I guess everybody had heard that Jaoquin Phoenix and Reese Witherspoon did there own playing and singing in the movie, except for me. I had no idea watching this movie for the first time that it was not Johnny Cash and June Carter singing. They were that good. Their musical ability alone makes me feel good giving this a high score. Add to that a really good story about a great musician that is handled with much love and care by the director and actors, and this has quickly become one of my favorite biopics ever made. I have watched it several more times since the first and bought the special edition of the movie. I don't usually buy movies like this, but [b]Walk the Line[/b] was different somehow. It does depend quite a bit on musical taste however. If you don't like Johnny Cash's music, you probably wont like the movie a lot because the majority of the movie is made up of music. If you do like Cash however, there is almost no way you will dislike this movie. I highly recommend it to Cash fans. Because I don't know which of my friends like Johnny Cash or not, I'm going to skip the thumbs up thumbs down on this one.

Spectacle and human drama interweave beautifully in this epic recreation of the spirit of ancient Rome in all its pomp, splendor, and horror.
Russell Crowe proves his mastery as an extremely versatile actor with both broad and deep expressive range as well as physical presence in the role of Maximus, whose silence speaks volumes. Crowe uses his expressions, especially his eyes, to convey a wide range of emotions. Here he is solid, square-jawed, standing like a Roman god. With a quiet dignity, he commands the screen and your attention.
The fighting is fast-paced, intense and gory. But Gladiator's violent action in no way interferes with its compelling story. Justice is always a grabber, and all Maximus wants is to avenge his family. 
Not since Sparticus and Ben Hur has there been an epic like this, and Gladiator makes it official that the Roman Empire is Hip once again...("Are you not entertained?!" - Maximus)

It was released at the time when Russell Crowe was still and actor's actor; before he became a caricature of himself. The CGI backgrounds were astonishingly beautiful and despite its similarities in theme and plot to Brave Heart the film, rightfully stood on its own two feet and was amazing. Scott's direction was astonishing and truly captured the glory of battle while mixing in more than enough full out gore to keep the folks happy. What's most intriguing about Gladiator, however, is its subversiveness: an action-packed warrior movie that not only references the golden-era's gladiator epics but points out just how fucked up it is that humanity is so entertained by violence. El fin de semana pasado me puse a ver la Edición Extendida de esta película del año 2000, que tenía desde navidades pero que todavía no había podido ponerme a verla. 

Gladiator cuenta la historia de un general de la legión llamado Máximo (interpretado por Russell Crowe) que está a las órdenes del Emperador Marco Aurelio luchando contra los germanos en el año 180 d.C. Tras la batalla, el emperador quiere que Máximo sea su sucesor tras su muerte y restaure la República en Roma, a lo que su hijo Cómodo (un desquiciado Joaquin Phoenix), que es el heredero al trono, se negará liquidando a su padre antes de que nadie se entere y mandando ejecutar al fiel soldado y a su familia en Emerita Augustea (es decir, Mérida en Hispania). 

Como Máximo es un general curtido, logra desembarazarse de sus ejecutores y huye, herido, a su hogar, solo para llegar y contemplar que todo ha sido arrasado y que ha perdido la esperanza por vivir. Desfallecido, lo recogen un grupo de esclavistas que lo llevan hasta una región asolada (parece Marruecos más que cualquier punto de la península) y le obligan a luchar por su vida, convirtiéndole en un gladiador. Allí le acompañará un nubio que será su fiel amigo, interpretado por Djimon Hounson y cuando deba viajar a Roma, verá la posibilidad de ver cumplida su venganza, si sobrevive a las luchas en el Coliseo. 

Al mismo tiempo, la hermana de Cómodo, Lucila, intenta levantar a los senadores que están en contra del emperador para quitar a éste del poder y salvaguardar Roma, intentando valerse del reaparecido Máximo y su influencia con las legiones. 

Salvando los fallos e inexactitudes históricas, Gladiator es una tremenda história épica, ambientada en una de las épocas de mayor esplendor del Imperio Romano, con acción y un protagonista entero, decidido, con unas enormes ansias de venganza muy bien interpretado por Russell Crowe (aunque no sé si tanto como para darle un Oscar), al igual que el malo de la película, un Cómodo loco, paranoico y desmedido, excelentemente plasmado por Phoenix. 

Ridley Scott hizo bien su trabajo y esta película, salvando su escaso rigor histórico, es una excelente cinta, con una buena histórica y mucha acción. 

Por supuesto que se ven las claras influencias americanas, de intentar llevar el Imperio a la mejor forma de gobierno, la democrática República (algo increible en aquella época), al igual que el tipo de héroe o el final mítico, pero como entretenimiento, es una gran película que devolvió al género de los romanos la dignidad perdida muchos años atrás.

The cinematography might have been its greatest strength. Unlike most modern films, where cinematography takes a back seat to action, special effects, and overly-dramtic acting, Gladiator is a fresh reminder that visually-pleasing cinema still exists. I haven't seen this movie in over a year and I can still remember certain shots as if I had watched it last night.[/color][/size][/font]

This was an amazing film the first time, boring the second time and then I didn't watch the film for about 7 years. I caught it on Film Four and didn't want to watch it because the beginning though undeniably contains some spectacular action the use of the Zulu chant by the barbarian German Hordes is really annoying. However I did sit and watch the film and I liked it again an incredibly engaging film beautifully shot with some fantastic performances, Crowe is very good in the lead he's hard and noble and despite being an Australian accented, Spaniard in the Roman army he is an exceptionally strong presence on screen but what makes the film successful with the exception of the stylish direction from Ridley Scott is the diverse supporting turns. Both Richard Harris and Djimon Hounsou are quietly excellent in their underplayed roles as friends to Maximus; Connie Neilson is suitably brittle and lovely as Lucilla trying very hard to protect her son and maintain the mask of complacency and the late Oliver Reed as Proximo is a joy to watch all grandeur and class. The wonderful Joaquin Phoenix hamming it up gleefully as the psychotic Commodus is a lot of fun and could have easily walked away with the film if his characters wasn't such a tit. The rest of the cast (David Hemmings and Derek Jacobi) is made up of old British stars of stage and screen each enjoying their moments, it is not the best film but I feel a deserved winner at the Academy Awards (Traffic would have been good too) but I might wait another 7 years to watch it again. ;)

[font=Arial Black][color=sienna]Gladiator tells the story of Maximus the General who became a slave after the murder of the emperor of Rome. Said emperors son killed him and has Maximuss family killed and tried to have Maximus killed but being the fact he is the star of the movie he of course survives. I love this film. I dont really review films that I dont like because why waste your time watching crap. I have been watching a lot of action movies lately Hong Kong and American and this is defiantly among the best action movies I have seen. I love historical epics like this or The Last Samurai but I hated Troy and think Braveheart is overrated. [/color][/font]

[font=Arial Black][color=sienna]Anyways this could have been cookie cutter material if it werent for Ridely Scott. Scott brings a great visual sense and a wonderful actors direction to the film.  He uses CGI Rome to show it as it once was. Some people criticize CGI but its a tool like the camera. However the nice thing about both is you can show off with them.  Scott does but never to the offense of the story.  I think any kind of film work should support the story.  The story should give you justification to do the kind of things you need to do. Here Scotts direction is frantic yet subdued during the quiet scenes.[/color][/font]

[font=Arial Black][color=sienna]During the action scenes he uses a lot of quick cuts, slow motion, different camera speeds all to capture the odd reality that is battle.   However unlike a Michael Bay picture this film allows you to see what is actually happening. You can tell guys heads gets chopped off and you can tell that a guy was stabbed or a woman cut in half. Good stuff. The actors bring there best work to the table. Joaquin Phoenix is wonderful as the villain. Essentially a roman little piss ant I despised his character instead of him being one of those likable villains like in Die Hard. I wanted Maximus to kill him. The supporting cast is great. Oliver Reed and Richard Harris bring a gritty and dignified presence to the proceedings. [/color][/font]

[font=Arial Black][color=sienna]However lets get are facts straight this is Russell Crowes show.  He brings in intensity to Maximus that only somebody like Mel Gibson could in his younger years.  Sometimes he can be Mad Maximus. Crowe goes through the range of emotions in this film.  He is sad. Laughs, the character are a man of action. You rarely see Maximus giving long winded speeches. He just does what he has to do and that is it. [/color][/font]

[font=Arial Black][color=sienna]This being a Scott production you can bet the visuals are outstanding.  He seems to use a lot of muted colors.  The film is almost brown and gray with some blue thrown in.   There are no bright happy people in this film because its a tough world and thats just the way they are. Again visuals for the service of the story. [/color][/font]

[font=Arial Black][color=sienna]Now on to the controversy as to rather it should have one best picture or not.  I dont think it should have.  Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon was the superior film as was Traffic. I personally would have given it to Crouching Tiger but thats me.   However that does not change the fact that as a summer action film Gladiator is one of the best of the new Millennium. Before I finish I want to say that Hans Zimmers score is a personal favorite. They really as far as composers go dont get much better then Zimmer.  The same can be said for directors in Scott and actors in Crowe and Phoenix. Thats it later. [/color][/font]

[size=3]I had very high expectations for [i]Gladiator[/i] before I was going to watch it, loads of people I know said it was one of the best movies they had ever seen. Well, I finally brought myself to actually watch it, and I certainly enjoyed it. [i]Gladiator [/i]had plenty of great exciting battle sequences, and some truly excellent performances, as well as one of the best soundtracks I've ever heard in a movie. Overall it was a very solid and entertaining film, but I was slightly disappointed. I wasn't as emotionally involved in the film as I was with films like [i]Braveheart [/i]and [i]The Last Samurai[/i]. Don't get me wrong though, this was still a very good movie. Joaquin Phoenix was pitch perfect as the selfish Emperor, he made him a very despicable character. Russell Crowe also gave an incredible performance as Maximus, the slave who was once a great general. [/size]

Ridley Scott's modern classic may take a lot of cues from the likes of Spartacus and Ben Hur, but in many ways it surpasses them. The thrilling combat sequences are as good as any committed to celluloid, and as impressive the CGI recreation of ancient Rome is, it's the wonderful dialogue, characters and design that breathes life into it. Russel Crowe charismatically heads a magnificent cast, featuring Richard Harris as the ageing Marcus Aurelius Caesar tired of conquest and wishing to leave a legacy after his death, veteran Shakespearean Derek Jacobi providing the political intrigue behind the scenes, scheming to replace the Emperor with a democratic republic, Oliver Reed as Maximus' new mentor dreaming of recreating past glories, and Connie Nielsen as the conniving Lucilla whose true motive is only to keep her son safe. But it is Joaquin Phoenix's Commodus who is the show stopper, brilliantly portraying a spoilt child whose ambition combined with weakness of character and desire for a father's love twists him into a malicious tyrant; the scene in which he assassinates his father is superb. It even takes time out to take sideswipes at modern politics and the media "Rome is the mob. You can take away their freedom, but show them a little magic to distract them and they will still love you for it." This is what brings the film to life, and this level of sophistication makes it's contemporaries such as Alexander, Braveheart or even Scott's own Kingdom Of Heaven look like school pantomimes in comparison. Proof that the Hollywood system in the hands of true artists can produce something genuinely beautiful.

Although I feel that Ridley has let his standards slip in these past years, this does not apply for 'Gladiator'. In a setting that can only be described as epic and a collection of actors that is prodigious to say the least, Gladiator set the bar for all historical dramas that have since surfaced.
Starting out with an intense battle in the misty woods of Germania and then moving on into the Colosseum of Rome itself, this film does not lack grand landscapes - being a Scott film, it certainly doesn't lack detail or fail to portray a certain amount of authenticity. The script is pretty tight, uniquely adjusted for each social cast as well as character background, it furthers the impression of authenticity in this historical galor.
The performances themselves are impressive - featuring heavyweights Richard Harris and Oliver Reed (God rest their souls) as well as Joaquin Phoenix and Derek Jacobi (and obviously Russell Crowe), this film does certainly not lack any memorable performances. 
To add the final cherry on the proverbial cake, we also have the Oscar awarded score by Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrard - their soft melodies and superb talents bring emotion to tragedy, glory to combat and soul to an already soulless city.
Despite the fact that Rome itself has received additional attention from the TV arena (in the form of 'Rome' and 'Spartakus'), I still firmly believe that this film is still the definitive view to date of what the world was like back in the days when the Roman empire spanned the globe and stood unchallenged - held together by the few influential holders of power and by the Roman 'mob' whose fickle whims where easily swayed.

[center][i][size=4]GLADIATOR[/size][/i]
 [/center]
 [center][i]PROFILE OF AN EPIC
 [/i]
 [/center]
 [i]    Gladiator [/i]is one of the finest movie epics of all time.  Directed by the masterful Ridley Scott, it is a film that commands from its audiences a total awe and utmost admiration.  Opening in May of 2000, the film became a high grossing blockbuster.  It received five Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Actor.
 
         The script was inspired by art and culture.  Writer David Franzoni envisioned the early form of [i]Gladiators [/i]breathtaking story after reading Daniel P. Mannixs Those About to Die. Ridley Scott was pitched the film with the aid of a painting, entitled Thumbs Down by Jean-Léon Gérôme.
 
         At first glance, this story seems like a typical revenge plot, a fierce vendetta, basically of someone who wants to kill somebody.  But this is incorrect.  It is a story about someone who loves somebody.  Yes, the main character is a soldier who fights and kills, and has a talent for doing so but his true passion lies with unparalleled love for his family.  He fights not only for Rome, but for the chance to see his wife and son again.  [i]Gladiators [/i]story is about a man struggling to find his way home; it is a story about finding inner strength through fierce loyalty and love for that which is right and good.  This amazing storyline is defined and strengthened by its wonderfully intricate ensemble of characters.
 
     [b]MARCUS AURELIUS[/b]
 
         The late Richard Harris plays the aged ruler of an expanding empire, nearing the end of life and searching for the meaning of his.  According to him, his rule has been defined by bloodshed, war, and the absence of peace.  Four years of peace in twenty.  His rule has been marred by political corruption and greed, as only a raging, pulsing empire can produce.  Marcus is deeply saddened by these developments; he is dying, there is little time left to make any difference or to ever see the redemption of Rome.  There was a dream that was Rome and I fear it will not survive the winter.  The emperors allusion to the empire he commands and his own mortality is striking and poignant.
 
     [b]COMMODUS[/b]
 
     The starved-for-affection, power hungry and pompous young emperor is played by Joaquin Phoenix.  Even without his deep purple and golden armor, his spoiled demeanor suggests royalty.  Commodus is characterized by a twisted insecurity with a repugnant dash of incestuous lust.  He is a jealous son, and he desires his father, the emperors love above all things.  When Marcus Aurelius declares to his son that he will not be the next emperor, Commodus claims he would butcher the whole world if he would only love him. 

Ultimately and maliciously, he becomes the ruler of Rome, finalizing his transformation into total evil, delivering dramatic and creative methods of administering death, which is his ticket to winning the hearts and minds of the Roman mob.  Commodus wrestles with the politics and the Senate which in his opinion, merely get in the way of what Rome truly is: a grand idea, a thriving empire that mustnt be restrained or constricted.  As one senator puts it, I think he (Commodus) knows what Rome is. Rome is the mob the beating heart of Rome is not the marble of the Senate; it's the sand of the Collosseum.  He'll bring them death - and they will love him for it.  It is his goal to seduce the entire populace with entertainment, thereby distracting them from serious national issues.  His morbid fascination with blood and the sport thereof is shown with the slithering out of his tongue at the observation of yet another gladiators throat being opened in the arena.  Commodus hates the entire world, primarily because not a single thing in the world loves him. 
 
     [b]LUCILLA[/b]
 
         Lucilla is the sister of Commodus and daughter of Marcus Aurelius, and is played by Connie Nielson.  She is beautiful in both character and appearance.  She loves passionately, for her son Lucius, for her father, and though she would hesitantly admit it, for Maximus, a fire that burned long ago that perhaps has a chance of rekindling.  She fears and worries almost as hard as she loves; she is mortified of her brother and his growing power and incestuous love interest towards her.  She fears the fate of Rome, primarily because her son is heir to its throne.  As the only woman character in [i]Gladiator[/i], Lucillas lightest touch commands obedience which is stronger than any soldier with a sharp sword or senator with a sharp tongue.  
 
     [b]PROXIMO[/b]
 
         The details of the old gladiator trainer Proximos backstory goes unmentioned in [i]Gladiator[/i], but it leads us to imagine a vivid story regarding this man who used to fight in the arena and who now trains others to do thus.  Played by the late Oliver Reed, Proximo is eloquent and theatrical, delivering splendid monologues of honorable battle in the glorious arena.  Picking up a sword by its hilt and looking at it nostalgically, Proximo promises his trainees: Thrust this into another mans flesh, and they will applaud and love you for that. You may even begin to love them for that.  He worships the crowd, the bloodthirsty mob that begs for the clash of swords and the opening of mortal wounds.  He lives in the moment, is almost fearful of the past, which to him is nothing but shadows and dust.
 
     [b]MAXIMUS[/b]
 
             At the center of [i]Gladiators[/i] amazing story is one man, Maximus Decimus Meridius (Russell Crowe), the commander of the armies of the North and general of the Felix legions, and who will of course, have his vengeance in this life or the next.  Maximus is a battle-hardened warrior with a keen eye for combat and a steady sword hand.  His loyalty to his emperor and his country is only surpassed by the unparalleled love for his wife and son.  He fights not only for Rome, but for the chance to see his family again.  There are so many movies about great fighters that are only watched by young men.  By including Maximus family in the story, [i]Gladiator[/i] became appealing to women.  When broken down as a character, much like literary interpretation can do, Maximus can be viewed as the [i]ideal[/i] man.  He is strong and honorable, passionate, intelligent, and loyal.  Maximus prays to his ancestors, blessed Father, watch over my wife and son with a ready sword, whisper to them: I live only to hold them again.  Maximus character is intricate and unique, and he is an extraordinary man with a fierce heart, taking on incredible odds, and carrying the weight of an empire on his shoulders. 

As a military leader, Maximus is a man of the people.  He seems to possess the pulse of the soldiers he commands; as he passes along their ranks he receives crisp salutes and warm smiles.  In the heat of combat, Maximus nearly cuts down one of his own men, offering a sly little grin to the scared soldier upon realizing the close call.  He fights only when there is a point.  Whether its for the glory of Rome, the chance to return home, or simply to make a statement in protest, Maximus sword has a purpose.   

In [i]Gladiator[/i], Maximus life is torn to pieces.  Marcus Aurelius, as his last wish, decides to make Maximus his heir to the throne, in order to restore Rome as a republic and to end the corruption that has crippled it.  Maximus is totally stunned by the offer, for he would rather ignore the messy world of politics in favor of the warmth of familial love. Maximus hesitates to respond, and in the interim Commodus murderously seizes the throne and orders Maximus and his familys deaths.  Escaping his executioners but failing to save his family, he transitions from a respectable military commander and a loyal servant of Rome to a slave living in squalor whose only purpose is to amuse a mob in gladiatorial spectacles.  From down below in the catacombs of the Collosseum, Maximus rises up to challenge an entire empire, to defy its ruler and to make an impact worthy of Marcus Aurelius dying wish.
 

          Cinematically, [i]Gladiator [/i]is a ground-breaking achievement.  With the combined efforts of screenwriters David Franzoni and John Logan, and playwright William Nicholson, the perfect blend of spectacular action and classical playwriting was developed.  This is apparent from the very start of the film, where a general, unshaven and adorned in frosted armor observes a solitary songbird, a beautiful point punctuating a war-ravaged landscape.  And then, following at my signal, unleash hell, we see the awe-inspiring opening battle sequence, an amazing display of cinematic brilliance and visual effects; the sweeping vistas of a Germanian forest set ablaze by Roman siege engines preceding the clash of armies and swords.  Following this action are scenes of intimate drama and characterization; a father quips to his daughter: Enough of politics.  Let us pretend that you are a loving daughter, and I am a good father.  She responds humorously, taking her fathers arm: This is a pleasant fiction, isnt it? 
 
         Another example of this interesting hybrid of action and theater is Maximus single-handed victory in the desert.  Entering the arena to the roar of the crowd, Maximus wastes no time in dispatching the six gladiators with incredible skill.  As the dust settles and the blood settles into the dust, Maximus hurls one of his swords into the luxury box, spewing hatred to the audience.  Are you not [i]entertained[/i]? Spitting onto the sand and flinging his remaining gladius away, Maximus departs the arena, his point firmly made.
 
         It is this rare combination of blockbuster action and dramatic, theater style dialogue that makes [i]Gladiator[/i] a film critics delight.
 
         [i]Gladiator [/i]is also a stunning visual achievement.  Director Ridley Scott, known for his talent of creating fantastic worlds in [i]Alien [/i]and [i]Blade Runner[/i], goes to great heights to portray ancient Rome in a real and rugged way.  The soldiers are filthy and war-torn, much unlike the glittering armored and plumed-helmeted legionnaires of previous sword-and-sandal movies.  Rome itself is splendid and majestic, the Collosseum stretching wide and tall, the crown of 50,000 Romans within watching every movement of the sword.  The Academy Award for Best Visual Effects was granted to the film.  From the grittiest of gladiators to the most lavish members of royalty, the characters in [i]Gladiator [/i]are dressed in imaginative yet authentic costumes, including richly detailed jewelry and deadly accurate weapons.  Talented designer Janty Yates took home the Academy Award for Best Costume Design.  [i]Gladiator [/i]takes the audiences to places like Zucchabar, an African province of Rome, and the battlegrounds of northern Europe.   It is a genuine spectacle, mastered by the vision of director Ridley Scott. 
 
    
 
         [i]Gladiator[/i] stands alone as an intelligent epic, not merely a sword swinging kill-fest.  Though not without its blood, the film additionally inspires thought.  In the political arena, rather than the gladiatorial one, we see a fantastic and accurate depiction of history.  As Ridley Scott put it, politics today are essentially the same as in Roman times, although backstabbing nowadays is a lot more metaphorical.  Observing the raging spectators in the Collosseum, we see a whole population seduced by entertainment and distracted from more serious issues.  The themes are very contemporary in nature, and encourage us as a people to question our own morality.  Can we seriously sit in an arena, fifty-thousand strong, and watch a man kill another man?  Standing in the Collosseum, we can observe a frozen cultural phenomenon.  Through [i]Gladiator, [/i]this fantastic and marvelous film, we can observe yet another phenomenon: A stunning story with deep characters and one hero named Maximus.

[font=Andy][size=3][color=white]The critical consensus on [u]A Good Year[/u] is a disturbing 26%. This is because they went into the picture without an open mind. I'll admit the thought of a romantic comedy from screen legends Ridley Scott and Russell Crowe is strange. However, both have proven their versatility before. Scott with films ranging from [u]Alien[/u] to [u]Thelma & Louise[/u]. Crowe with such varied performances in movies like [u]A Beautiful Mind[/u] and [u]The Insider[/u].[/color][/size][/font]

[font=Andy][size=3][color=white][font=Andy][size=3][color=white]It reminds me of Ridley's film [u]Matchstick Men[/u]. Before it was released, I thought the same thing that critics were thinking about this picture. Ridley directing a comedy? I was surprised to find out that he still was able to create a memorable cinematic world in present day. You always believe in the authenticity of a Ridley Scott film. The same goes for [u]A Good Year[/u], the French countryside has never looked so appealing, or been shot so well.[/color][/size][/font]

The fact is this that film embodies a relaxing trip to the movies. The pacing is smooth, with flowing camera work and a soothing French soundtrack. The story may be a standard one, but it feels fresh in the hands of its director and actors. Everyone looks like they are having a great time, especially Crowe. He infuses the character of Max Skinner with the energy of a younger actor.[/color][/size][/font]

[font=Andy][size=3][color=white]I'd been waiting for Scott and Crowe to reteam since [u]Gladiator[/u]. This flick my not be in that vain, but their next film together [u]American Gangster[/u] is due out next year. I'm sure the critics will be more open to that type of Scott/Crowe collaboration. For now though don't trust the critics, the user's rating is much higher. [/color][/size][/font]

Gladiator! A thrilling tale of a Roman general who must battle against all thinkable odds to avenge the death of his family and restore justice to the empire. The plot is simple, legendary general Maximus Decimus Meridius, after many victorious campaigns and battles wants to return to his peaceful home in Spain, However the kind, fair and dying Emperor Marcus Aurelius wishes to bestow his title on him over his cruel son, Commodus. Commodus is understandably annoyed and kills his father calming the title of Emperor. Maximus is sentenced to death along with the rest of his family back at his home in Spain. Maximus escapes but is unable to save his wife and son. His loss of will to live makes him an east target for slavers and he is soon sold as a gladiator. He fights his way into the coliseum in Rome were he wins over the crowd and uses his celebrity status to defy the Emperor, to whom he swears his vengeance for the death of his family, after many battles and political backstabbing he gets his chance to fight the Emperor in the Arena.

This is just such an amazing film, it captures every emotion possible in only the way an expert director can achieve, we can go on for whole scenes without the need for speaking, everything is told through the genuine body language and expressions. And when there is conversing we get such emotion and wonderfully powerful quotes ? "What we do in life, echoes in eternity" Wow.

The opening scene is spellbinding, showing the true gore of battle, the fight scenes are marvellously realistic, discarding the popular "pretty" sword fighting for brutal aggressive force. The audience in the arena express every emotion, surprise, anger, and enjoyment. The cast is brilliantly chosen; we can really see Russell Crowe as a gladiator, in Commodus, Joaquin Phoenix gives us a man we can really hate, Connie Nielson shows real emotion and passion in the role of Lucilla. So apart from the spellbinding acting, scarily realistic fight scenes and the amazing script, what else can we look for? The music is just stunning, its exactly what we need brought in at exactly the right time, truly wonderful directing. And then we have the stunning special effects, we can really visualise the greatness that is Rome, the fight scenes really make you believe. Some critics have condemned the lack of historical fact, for instance an emperor would never fight a gladiator, and these comments cannot be denied, its true.

But I think we can forgive them that one fault for such an amazing movie. Without hesitation I give this movie a truly deserved 10/10!..Bottom line: magnificent. Visually and emotionally satisfying.
