Beautiful is an understatement. It is a truly remarkable film. It doesn't diminish in terms of entertainment after many watches. It's a film you can watch over and over again. Its true success would have been its popularity with the ladies as well as the guys. It is after all a brutal, testosterone-filled film, yet its plot is so brilliant. Its a relatively simple plot, so brilliantly directed and beautifully shot.
Special mention of the beautiful shots should go to the introduction of Rome. It's breathtaking and the score which hums along with it is majestic. Extremely fitting for the scene. The afterlife shots were extremely well filmed and superbly integrated.
The dialogue is fantastic. There are so many memorable quotes. One quote even sums up the plot: "A general who became a slave; a slave who became a gladiator; a gladiator who defied and emperor".
The acting is outstanding. Special mentions go to Joaquin Phoenix, who is superb as the disturbingly meticulous power-hungry Commodus. He really does scare me in that chilling way. Connie Nielsen is excellent as his sister. She really has to show a range of emotions; love, hatred, remorse, anger etc.... Djimon Hounsou is great as Maximus' council and a great confidante. Russell Crowe, well, an excellent performance. One of the best acting performances I've seen for a while. His best film. You really feel for him. Masterful.
The gladiatorial sequences and the opening battle sequence were excellent. Their realism is unparalleled. Extremely well choreographed. The gratuity is not spared, which obviously adds to the realism.
The score is magnificent. The music is brilliantly used. The vocals in the closing afterife sequence really does capture the moment. The scores used during the battles capture the glorious nature of the Roman culture. They're epic.
The premise is magnificent. Superbly directed, wonderfully shot, beautifully acted. A film worthy of superlatives, though I don't like giving them.
Some of the ladies I know are deterred because the film is seemingly action-orientated. Do not let the title fool you. There is substance behind the action, which is used to further the storyline. 
"Are you not entertained?" I'm happy to report that I was extremely well entertained. Everyone should see this!! An utter masterpiece.

Most films require that the viewer identifies with the character to truly be engrossed with the film. If you can't feel something for the character, than the audience is lost.

Luckily, in Ridley Scott's case, Russel Crowe is so captivating and convincing as a general loved by his troops and as a slave loved by the people that the movie really works. Possibly one of the greatest actors today, Crowe carries this epic film on his very capable shoulders.

Not to say that he is the only reason this works. The supporting cast, most notably Connie Neilsen, buoy the film to new perspectives.

Jacquin Phoenix definitely captures the egotisitcal persona he should display, stealing every scene he's in. Phoenix will surely be put on the map with Gladiator.

But the real shining star in this film are the incredible action sequences which jolt the viewer right in with the opening sequences, as Maximus' true worth to the Roman Empire is displayed. Scott's camera work within these completed sequences takes a modern twist that really works for the gruesome scenes.

Crowe will now get the respect he deserves for this collosal performance. Gladiator makes the most of its 2 and a half hours, marking a triumphant comeback for the long forgotten epics of the classic days of film. ALL HAIL MAXIMUS!

Maximus: At my signal, unleash hell. 

While I still do find the amount of praise for this film somewhat strange, I do believe that this Ridley Scott sword and sandal epic is a damn fine film, complete with wonderful visuals, strong performances, and a fairly entertaining story.

Russell Crowe stars as Maximus, a well regarded general of Ceaser Marcus Aurelius' Roman army. At the beginning of the film, Maximus has just defeated another empire and is ready to be crowned the next emperor of Rome; that is until Marcus' whiny son Commodus, played by Joaquin Phoenix, decides that he deserves it more, murders his father and blames Maximus for the crime.

Maximus: It's the frost, it sometimes makes the blade stick.

Maximus manages to escape his execution, but upon making it home, Maximus finds his family to have been slaughtered. He is then captured and put into slavery. Years later, despite hating to serve as a gladiator in the local games, Maximus is a natural, and he and his fellow gladiators get a chance to fight in the Roman Colosseum, as Commodus' has attempted to gain popularity by having more and more gladiator fights in the arena. Of course, as the two cross paths, which means that revenge may be afoot.

Maximus: My name is Gladiator. 

Despite a little fun with history (Marcus Aurelius apparently wanted to turn Rome back into a Republic...riiigggghhhht) the story boils down to a good guy wanting to take down the bad guy (as all films like this should) and even if the film runs a little long by keeping us informed about the drama unfolding in the senate, the progression of the story through the world of a gladiator is a lot of fun.

Crowe is solid throughout. He gives it his all, showing us a born leader who is tough, smart, but capable of caring. Phoenix is very good too, making sure to capture the whiny aspects of his character to a great scene chewing degree. Of course, the respect I have for Djimon Hounsou as Crowe's only real friend is met with a cool, underplayed performance. Then you have solid work from the older cast members as well.

Being a Scott film, this whole flick is slickly made, using a lot of dark, muted tones, mixed with some pretty solid effects to help recreate Rome, along with a layer of grit to keep all the action feeling very visceral. Signature kill shots and fight scenes are a plus here. The fact is, this film is very much in Ridley Scott's wheelhouse, playing to his strengths as a director, where he can combine some great drama with large scale epics. Hans Zimmer's score is a good example of how everything gets factored in.

A strong film that has a very watchable quality to it, do in no small part to Crowe's strong lead performance and Scott's eye for well handled visuals.

Maximus: I knew a man once who said, "Death smiles at us all. All a man can do is smile back."
Commodus: I wonder, did your friend smile at his own death?
Maximus: You must know. He was your father.

]"An exhilarating, sweeping epic that begs to be seen on the largest possible screen."[/b]
 
 
I wholeheartedly agree. I bought the dvd in China when I visited there. It has turkish and chinese subtitles that I can't switch off.  This film has generated some backlash over the years as an overrated film.  Perhaps, but as a Best Picture that is going to happen.
 
But I digress..... this is the type of film that is a real cinematic experience. Like so many films like it that achieved Best Picture status, it really moves you and takes you in. If you can just get past the first 20 or so minutes when this man goes through devastating loss.... we have a picture here that details how events can turn a person inside out.
 
If you haven't seen this because you think its another robes and sandals movie... forget that. This is about survival in the Roman days when life was very cheap. By the way, this was one veteran actor's (Oliver Reed) last film. He's the one that buys the Gladiator (Crowe) from his captors and gets him trained for the arena, although he doesn't need it.  He was a general in the Roman legions and saw plenty of action.  The experience serves him well in the arena.
 
By the way, the reigning Caesar at the start of the movie gets murdered by his sick son who is seemingly married to his sister! Not sure of that but they are way to familiar with each other to be otherwise. But anyway, ambition has its cost and the Roman empire is seen in its decline.

I was lucky enough to catch a showing in the cinema tonight. Last time i saw this in the cinema was on my holiday in Orlando, I believe spring or summer of 2000.

It's been a while and after a few viewings now i definitely know how I feel about this movie. There was a time when this was an absolute classic to me. It still kind of is but I see it's faults.

To be fair, Ridley did something amazing by bringing a dead and buried genre that hasn't existed for years or even decades. When was the last 'big' epic movie before Gladiator? And who would have thought the genre would ever make it back in this century and time? So for that alone, he deserves and the film deserve a lot of respect. The movie works out well also because of it's mixture of action, story and character development. It's a long movie but you don't feel it.

I personally don't have a problem with the film itself but I do have a problem with some of the directing or editing of the movie. There was a few shots and edits that made me feel like it took away from the final product. Maybe that's a bit fussy but it's being honest.

Phoenix was definitely the key character in the movie for me and he plays his character with such menace that you love to hate.

This movie has become amongst many peoples favoruite of all time lists and I could see why. It might not be as high on my list anymore but i still think it's a brilliant modern epic take on a genre that was mind blowing a few decades ago.

Gladiator is basically 300, only not so much digital and having a more thought-out plot. Gladiator was always a guy's movie... I remember a time when Maximus was the baddest mother fucker around, who shows confidence, and girls drooled over him (and the other gladiators), Commodus was the epitome of movie villian, and Connie Nielson was the miscasted and unnecessary beauty who still looks good at her age. If I were to compare the action... obviously 300 has loads of it, but I thought the fancy visuals and slow speeds that fast-forward ruined some of it (can't deny the violence looks beautiful at times). Gladiator is perfectly staged Hollywood techniques with a raw, gritty feel courtesy of classic filmmaking (where did those movies go?). I say film still looks better than blurry, saturated digital, hi-definition video... who would agree? Sofia Coppola ("Film feels more romantic"). 

The film's historical inaccuracies would drive the history major or teacher mad with the rage virus. Still a wonder why people seek 100-percent historical info from Hollywood films. In the short run, Gladiator offers an intriguing, dramatic and heartbreaking story with buckets of action. This film is just a lil' over seven years old, and it still holds up pretty good today. When I looked at Gangs of New York (from 2002), I sensed that film hasn't aged well after some praise I handed it to (still a good movie nonetheless). What helps Gladiator hold on a little bit longer is: drama on an epic scale, old school filmmaking techniques, acting from veteran actors Oliver Reed and Richard Harris, a recent 3-disc extended cut, and a beautiful score by Hans Zimmer. Oh yeah... it's the guy's movie that won the Oscar for Best Picture. Wouldest thou agree with the pick? I didn't mind, even though Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon was the better flick, and my top choices got the shaft.

This is wonderful storytelling. The opening Battle Scene simply mesmerizes, showing the brutal nature of combat for Roman conquests. I went back to see the film again. The first time I didn't hear anything Crowe said before the battle. I was just too visually caught-up. The second time I listened very closely and caught the wise yet succinct line from Maximus "what we do in life... echoes in eternity." Awesome.

A simple man v. an emperor. I just loved the resilience Maximus showed throughout the movie. I find in most movies, there is an irritatingly slow process where the character has to "find himself," not so with Gladiator. Maximus does what is needed.

I liked how there were only two or three issues within this film. One was the afterlife. Aspects of the afterlife are opened, but not overdone. Love of family is given sizable focus. I liked the theme of love of country that we see as well, although it may not be justly deserved, it is never questioned.

The visual effects were amazing. It actually had me wanting to believe that's the way Rome actually looked in all it's glory. The battle of Carthage reenactment was really great.

The ending is just hypnotic. Intentionally or unintentionally it was simply emotional. The music is wonderfully beautiful as if Maximus' family are telling him...you have arrived.

Bottom line: magnificent. Visually and emotionally satisfying.

Even though it is a fictional story, the way it is told would make you believe otherwise. The name basically says it all, after a very neat battle, Crowe is betrayed by the dead Emperor's son and rises through gladiatorial ranks to get revenge. The combat is brutal and unforgettable, which is why Gladiator is so good. When the story is not focusing on Crowe though, it focuses on Phoenix (in his best acting role). He is the new Emperor, though most don't like him, especially the Senate. The movie does well in the transitions between the battles and heavy on dialog Senate story lines. They never overdue the Senate so you don't get bored, and they don't overdue the battles so it doesn't feel like some crappy hack-and-slash flick. Though I always felt Crowe was a bit dull in his characters, he was able to nail the gladiator role. A story about a man who loses everything, in hope he will get back something isn't a unique storyline, but is executed better here then in most. With that in mind, the ending is very satisfactory and not cliche in the surprising twist to this usual type of ending.

Who would think that a film centered on a gladiator, a role founded on bloodsport and violence, could cover such varied emotions from love to revenge to honor. Russell Crowe delivers a magnificent performance for the ages as Maximus, a warrior who truly embodies the motto "strength and honor". Joaquin Phoenix's Commodus poses a brilliant counterpoint to Crowe's Maximus, his scenes matching those of Maximus blow for blow. Retracing Phoenix's filmography has been a real treat for me.

At the same time, I have finally discovered the work of Ridley Scott. Surely I have to take a deeper dive into this fine director's canon, though I have to understand Gladiator is one of his best. At times the plot struck me as strangely Shakesperean, what with Commodus's jealousy and megalomania akin to Hamlet's struggles with power.

The writing is memorable, the cinematography stunning, and the music unmatched thanks to Hans Zimmer. Gladiator is a gripping - if a bit self-indulgent at nearly 3 hours - film, and one for the ages. At the end of it all, yes, I was very much entertained.

My favourite film of all time, well, so far anyway. I'll tell you why: there aren't many historical films that move you the way Gladiator does. From watching Maximus fall from a general of the Roman army to a gladiator, it is clear he will go to any lengths to avenge family no matter the consequences. The battle scenes and gladiator fights are spectacular, the computer graphics to reconstruct the Coliseum and Rome are magnificent. I particularly liked the way Maximus Elysium was portrayed, it made the film much more emotional towards the end. I believe the world class cast also contributed to finesse of the film: Richard Harris was superb as emperor Marcus Aurelius and I would have wanted him to have a bigger part, Connie Nielson and Joaquin Phoenix were terrific as the emperor's children but their relationship was most odd, Oliver Reed was highly amusing as Proximo and it was very unfortunate that he died during filming, but above all, Russell Crowe was simply outstanding as Maximus, he deserved his Oscar for his fine performance. Another feature that I loved was the soundtrack, which is particularly odd, as I don't usually like soundtracks that much. However throughout the film I realized that the music made the film much powerful, I think it may also be the music instead of the drama that makes me tearful every time I watch Gladiator. I therefore bought the soundtrack and I thoroughly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the film. In short, due to the battle scenes/gladiator fights as well as the revenge, romance and freedom themes, I believe Gladiator is a truly magnificent film.

Directed by: Ridley Scott. Starring: Russell Crowe, Joaquin Phoenix, Connie Nielsen, Richard Harris, Oliver Reed. << "My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife...and I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next." >> The story follows Seizer Marcus Aurelius in his final days of reign over Rome. His son, Commodus, a man with lack of moral, is to take his place only by Marcus' word, but when he turns and says that Maximus, a general, is to rule to restore the power to Rome, Commodus kills his own father, orders Maximus' family to death and Maximus is captured and used as a Gladiator, where Maximus aims to seek out revenge. 'Are you not entertained?'...I still most certainly am after watching this film countless times, it is now time for me to review the film the way it should be. Now in many cases, I believe the film is terribly underrated and I go against people and agree with this film winning best picture for many reasons. I cannot judge how historically accurate this all is, a lot of it does feel stylized and modernized and people believe that the bloodshed makes the film....but that is never the case. Sure Ridley Scott shoots the film with skill and experience and his battle scenes are great and bloody, but its his distant shots of war and Rome; and the close personal conflicts of characters where he is at his most powerful. The screenplay delivers more than just memorable battle sequences, its a developed story of betrayal, honor, secrecy and the lengths we will go to to have our revenge. The dialogue is brilliantly written and strong in deliverance from its actors, there are many memorable lines that will last a long time. The cinematography is like another layer of the story, its reflects it so beautifully, from the lack of color during battle to represent life and hope lost, to the beautiful range of bright colors used to represent the hope and beauty of Rome. The acting is a major highlight of the film, with Russell Crowe delivering a commanding and powerful performance, Joaquin Phoenix tapping into the depth of his character and being quite captivating and strong supporting roles by Connie Nielsen and Oliver Reed...and the always outstanding Richard Harris. Another film I could go on and on about, many people are blinded by the violence and bloodshed that they don't see the true brilliance of this film. A masterpiece that will remain memorable for many years to come.

Gladiator is the best movie to deal with Ancient Times. Maximus is a powerful Roman general, loved by the people and the aging Emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Before his death, the Emperor chooses Maximus to be his heir over his own son, Commodus, and a power struggle leaves Maximus and his family condemned to death. The powerful general is unable to save his family, and his loss of will allows him to get captured and put into the Gladiator games until he dies. The only desire that fuels him now is the chance to rise to the top so that he will be able to look into the eyes of the man who will feel his revenge. The movie is very entertanining and the collusiem is done awesomely. The performances are some of the best you will ever see. Although some of the scenes can make you sick as the time when his son and wife are crucified. The movie is very detailed and sticks to the story which is brilliant. Russell Crowe acted awesome this is his best performance ever. While the other performances are top notch and are not over the top. For Ancient Movies they are usually good but this movie had to deal with a lot of good Ancient Movies like Ben Hur but Gladiator does not dissapoint. True that the script isn't the best ever but still is very good. [b]Overall the movie is the best movie to do with Ancient Times.[/b]

''My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife. And I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next.''

When a Roman general is betrayed and his family murdered by a corrupt prince, he comes to Rome as a gladiator to seek revenge.

Russell Crowe: Maximus

Joaquin Phoenix: Commodus

Epic, dramatic, heart-wrenching, action packed and dramatic. Ridley Scott's roman historical masterpiece, forget the still good but flawed kingdom of heaven this is the one to watch.

Russel Crowe gives his best performance of his career. The late Richard Harris and Oliver Reed give high performances and a quality that shines timeless etherality. Joaquin Phoenix is an equal cold maddened son who's hunger and thirst for power is a vision to see.

''At my signal, unleash hell.''

A tale of redemption of a man fighting for good. A cause bigger than himself and to overthrow a tyrant obstructing the birth a republic. Revel in the violence, behold it's beauty and magnificence, wasn't a doubt in my mind that Ridley Scott would reap the rewards of his efforts and win awards galore. People who criticize this film are the same people that ridiculed Blade Runner, Alien, and my message to them is to get stuffed, thats as polite as i can put it. Gladiator features some wonderful cinematography by John Mathieson. The battle scenes are very graphic. (This movie is not for the squeamish, that's for sure.) There were some scenes in particular that really struck me, such as when Crowe appears to be floating over the ground very fast. The use of colour and colour tones added a great deal to the mood of the movie. Excellent. The script was being written and re-written as the filming was going on, yet it doesn't show that the actors had no idea how the movie was going to end when they began filming. The acting is terrific. Russell Crowe is wonderfully cast as Maximus. Many reviewers agree that he is now officially a star. Joaquin Phoenix also proves his mettle as the emotionally troubled Commodus, whose behavior and emotion toward his sister could give anyone the creeps. Connie Nielsen makes you believe that, as Lucilla, she really is torn between natural loyalty to her brother and doing what she knows is right. Oliver Reed, in his last performance, is memorable in his role of Proximo, the former gladiator who is the owner of Maximus and brings him to Rome. In short, the actors were brilliant in their roles, not over-acting, but giving subtle, strong performances.

''I don't pretend to be a man of the people. But I do try to be a man for the people.''

The fights staged in Gladiator are masterful set pieces; stylized and captured gloriously. However, the fighting in Gladiator is not unrealistic; it's graphic and bloody. The warriors who battle each other are not super-men, they are normal men, real fighters, who get bashed and beat up at every turn. These soldiers combat in a truly gritty way, they are warriors who need to smell and rub their hands in the earth they battle upon. Chief amongst these mortal combatants is Russell Crowe's, a hero of mythological stance, whose raw aggression on the battlefront, coupled with his powerful expressions (combating and not combating, his silent moments from his execution to his first brawl in the arena are his best) and compelling heroics earned him a well earned Oscar. These battle-scenes of Gladiator are, of course, extremely well tended to by Ridley Scott who is the master at crafting epic war scenarios (see, I told you fanboy-praise would sneak its way in!). The patient, slow pacing of the film seems to take a sudden halt here, and then fast-forward in an amazingly rapid-fire pace with quick shots, swinging swords, vivid skies and a great score by Hans Zimmer to further emphasize the dramatic mood. The very culmination of this is not at the end, but rather early. It is the moment that Maximus removes his helmet, reveals his identity and faces the emperor, after a long and ferocious battle. It is a scene so poignant that I always wish it would have been saved until later on in the film, thereby giving it even more weight. But no matter, because rest assured that it is goosebumps-inducing enough. A gloriously entertaining, heartfelt and carefully crafted war adventure by Ridley Scott in which little feels missing or incomplete. What more could you ask for? Great acting from the cast I suppose, well, this is also present in Gladiator. Best of all, the actors have good dialogue to work with so they don't choke on the dated lines. Russell Crowe propels this film with his heroic personality, Connie Nielsen adds introspective depth, and Joaquin Phoenix is excellent as the twisted but idealist emperor Commodurus.

Gladiator is visually stunning; it is the work of a master craftsman. It is also emotionally intriguing, something some Scott films lack. Its soul-searching music (applause to Hans Zimmer) and its ambitious, gorgeous view of the after-life are beautiful. Its truly gritty-edge give it a dirty, gruesome magnificence.

So, I wrote an essay on this for school and I don't really have anywhere else to put this, so beware: this is LONG.

Quintus: People should know when theyâre conquered. 
Maximus: Would you, Quintus? Would I?

The introductory scene of Ridley Scottâs powerful epic Gladiator already provides a strong foundation for the events about to unfold. From the start, we sense the rising tensions between Maximus, a resilient, morose battle general of Rome who simply wants to get home, and the calculating, hypocritical Commodus, the forthcoming emperor. The backdrop of Romeâs internal problems serves as merely that, a backdrop, while in essence the film remains a picture of the internal and external struggles between characters. In 2001, Gladiator was nominated for twelve Academy Awards and won five, including the prestigious Best Picture and Best Actor for Russell Crowe. In a year with Stephen Soderberghâs double threat Traffic and Erin Brockovich, this was truly a remarkable feat. Thanks to Ridley Scottâs masterful directing and the help of the cast, Gladiator truly remains a film likely to withstand the annals of time, even despite problems with the overblown ending.

It is the job of the director to make sure all the elements of a film are working together. He knows when to deftly cut a scene when needed and how to pull out the best possible performances from the actors. Simply looking at the way the film is organized by contrasting colors and seasons is evidence enough for Ridley Scottâs skills as a director. The atmosphere evoked by the movie is indeed Scottâs greatest achievement â it is something that isnât shown by dialogue or even facial expressions, but rather the action of placing contrasting scenes side by side, cutting the camera from one area to another in a steady, pulsating rhythm. The focal story is told in colors of grimy yellows and dismal grays and dirty reds, capitalizing on the earthy filth of the battles and the dreary brilliance of the Roman city. Whenever green is introduced it is like a breath of fresh air, but Scott uses the color very sparingly â only occasionally in the dream sequences and in one scene where Maximus and Juba are waxing philosophical on the afterlife. Also, the shifting of the seasons is significant. Most of the film takes place in a hot, sweaty climate, a climate suited to the sultry battles of the Roman Coliseum. However, the first half hour is shown in the wintry forests of Germania, where Maximus is leading his troops to fight the barbarians. Somehow, although there is just as much blood shed in Germania as in the Coliseum, the winter environs provides for a more civilized manner of fighting than in the barbarous circle of the Coliseum, surrounded by the cheering crowds. The entwining of the colors with the changing seasons provides for a beautiful contrast that the viewers not only see but also feel to a great extent. The fact that one can connect the glittering Elysian fields more to the jaded winter battlefield scene than to the grimy Coliseum fights is no coincidence - it is as if Ridley Scott is saying, âafter we kill the so-called barbarians, look at what barbarous things we turn to for enjoymentâ.

Truly a strong point of the movie is the acting. The well-nuanced performances of each actor reveal a layer about their character that gives a genuine gravitas to the film. Although the character of Maximus himself is not incredibly interesting, Russell Crowe exudes a mix of raw desire and tenacity and brings a sense of realness to the character, which is what makes him so memorable. Maximus is the all-suffering victim, purely a man who wants to serve his country well and then go home to his humble farm. After Marcus Aurelius asks him to act as standing emperor, this sole dream is wrenched apart and never fully comes back to him until he reaches the afterlife. You never forget that scene where Maximus grasps his dead wifeâs feet dangling from a rope and cries. Croweâs character is almost never allowed to bare his vulnerability so nakedly, but that moment is truly the one that transforms him from a man of simple desires to one that seeks vengeance for the perpetrator of such a grisly crime. The viewers know, innately, that this definitive scene is what consumes and empowers Maximus up until the end. It is Crowe that makes that sense of knowing possible. 

However, although Crowe is indeed brilliant, I believe the true star of the film is the underrated Joaquin Phoenix. A well-known method actor, Phoenix rarely gets cast in leading roles, but in this film really proves his salt as the weak, vacillating emperor Commodus, who really just wants to be loved. Phoenix plays Commodus to perfection, avoiding traps less-experienced actors would make by not totally villainizing the role, instead making the viewers sympathize with his decisions even while loathing them. Truly, Phoenix makes us understand that all he does is merely an effort to make the people love him a little more. The reason that Commodus challenges Maximus so much is not so much because he hates Maximus, but because Maximus has usurped the love of his father, and goes on to usurp the love of his people. Likewise, Commodus does not kill his father because he hates his father, but because he loves his father and is frustrated beyond sanity that his father does not love him back. One could have perceived Commodus as a highly ambitious man willing to destroy everything to get to the top had he been played by a lesser actor, but Joaquin Phoenixâs subtly haunting acting gives Commodusâs character much more depth. And that defining scene between Commodus and Marcus Aurelius with the âI would butcher the whole world if you would only love meâ? Beautiful.

Of course, no movie is perfect, and a fatal error Scott makes is the directorâs-ending-syndrome. At a whopping 155 minutes, Gladiator does not have a definitive ending that makes the viewers emerge from the film and go âWow.â Scott falls too much in love with his own style and tries to stuff too much into an already stuffed-full movie. A good ending should be slightly ambiguous, with just enough information to keep the viewer thinking far past the end. Scott would do well to follow the example of auteurs Hitchcock and Kubrick, by building up to the climactic scene and boom, ending it with uncertainty. Instead, he prolongs the ending by showing the Elysian Fields and Maximus giving directions to the Senate and Maximus reuniting with his wife and Lucilla demanding Maximus a proper burial and Juba burying Maximusâ family deities. The ridiculous last words, pronounced by Juba, are not anything particularly illuminating and simply reiterate a shred of dialogue that wasnât all that interesting to begin with: âNot yet.â In the majority of the movie, Ridley Scott knows when to cut scenes at the right moment, but the ending definitely could have been shortened by five or six minutes.

Ridley Scottâs exquisitely crafted masterpiece, supported by the supreme acting talents of Russell Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix, will be a film that will be discussed and dissected in the coming years. We can even ignore the less-than-perfect ending because the rest of the two-and-a-half hour venture we embarked on was well worth the trip. It remains proof that the profit-whoring producers of Hollywood can still produce something beautiful once in a while.

Rusell Crowe became one of my favorite actors after Gladiator. Where other movies struggle to "enlighten" us according to some half truth, Gladiator effortlessly resonates directly to the deepest and best within us by getting the message straight. There are just so many messages and themes in the story, enlightening and new...it lays the foundations of movies like 300, LOTR ,TROY and more to come

This movie gives us the unvarnished truth about life and then challenges us to live by a code the ancients new well: to be true to one's best self, for nothing else will ever be of any lasting consequence. In the final analysis, lasting self-esteem and true inner peace can only come from living up to our highest ideals without flinching or compromising. This entails loss and severe hardship. Maximus is an example of how to struggle with this tough challenge we humans are saddled with.

His arrow-straight nature, uncompromising sense of duty and his ability to endure pain and suffering for the truth make him a worthy role model. A person of true character. Where are such men today? Who and what have our "gods" become?

We should all be so lucky to stand in such a man's presence so we may become dyed in his colors.

Way overrated, probably because it's easy to understand.  An excellent trial run for the more meditative "Kingdom of Heaven," but lacks subtlety.  Occasionally intimate, but often devolves into self-congratulatory sabre- (or spatha-) rattling, or invokes inarticulate values like "honor," "glory," and "duty."  Maximus isn't really a very deep character.  The "savior" motif at the end is misapplied.  Worth seeing for its few, rare moments of existential futility: Richard Harris' "whisper" monologue, and Russell Crowe's "Are you not entertained"?  For more like this, see the extended cut of "Kingdom of Heaven."  P.S. The highly-reviewed soundtrack ratchets between forced sentimentality and ludicrous bombast.

"My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife. And I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next."



The general who became a slave. The slave who became a gladiator. The movie that is a masterpiece. In 180 A.D. General Maximus Decmimus Meridius has recently led the Roman Army to a victory over the barbarians of Germania. He is Emperor Marcus Aurelius' favourite soldier of the empire and he names the general 'Keeper of Rome' and will be given temporary leadership of the Roman Empire. Aurelius' believes his son, Commodus, will understand his decision but his son has other ideas. When Commodus learns Maximus will be made temporary leader of Rome, he suffocates his father to death as an act of revenge. Commodus then orders Maximus and his family to be executed. Maximus escapes execution but he does not make it back home in time to save the lives of his wife and son. After Maximus collapses at the sight of his dead loved ones, he is captured and taken to North Africa where he is enslaved and is forced to fight in gladiatorial games. His slavemaster, Antonius Proximo, sees how Maximus is able or organize fellow slaves into fighting as a cohesive unit and destroy any challenge. Maximus himself is undefeatable and Proximo decides to take the man to Rome to fight in the Roman Coliseum. Is in this gladiatorial arena where Maximus rises in rank, wins the favor of the crowds, and defies Emperor Commodus and inches each day closer to avenging his family as the gladiator. Just as how director Ridley Scott gave us gripping vision of the future in the science fiction classic Blade Runner, Scott here gives us an incredible story of a gladiator who became more powerful than the Emperor of Rome in ancient times. Gladiator is one of the most acclaimed epics of all time and is one of the many masterpieces of cinema Ridley Scott has delivered. Scott's aim with gladiator was both to craft a spectacular film and revive the swords and sandals epic; a genre which had not proved to be a decent crowd puller since Spartacus (1960) and The Fall and the Rise of the Roman Empire (1964). Gladiator deserves every amount of critical acclaim it has received over the years. It had a budget of $103 million and grossed $457,640,427 worldwide at the box office. It also won five Academy Awards which included Best Picture, Best Actor (Russell Crowe), Best Costume Design, Best Visual Effects, and Best Sound. It also received nominations for Best Supporting Actor for Joaquin Phoenix and Best Director for Ridley Scott. Delivering one of the best, if not the best performance of 2000 is Russell Crowe as the general turned slave turned gladiator, Maximus Decimus Meridius. He is of Hispano-Roman decent who is at the beginning of the film, unleashing hell in Germania. He is favored greatly by Emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) who in a way wishes Maximus was the son he had. The son he does have is Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix), a vain and power hungry man who never proved to his father that he was fit for the throne. Commodus murders his own father, orders an assassination for Maximus and his family, and he also desires his own sister, Lucilla (Connie Nielson). Lucilla is a widow who seems to have had a desire for Maximus in the past and she has a son named Lucius Verus (Spencer Treat Clark). Maximus survives being executed and it is because of Antonius Proximo (Oliver Reed), a former gladiator himself, that Maximus joins the gladiatorial arena and makes his way to Rome to avenge his family. Each of the actors here really deliver their roles believably with each emotion. Phoenix plays his role excellently as the jealous, lazy, and sociopathic Commodus. Russell Crowe is without a doubt the highlight of the film and he completely makes a brutal gladiator a character for the audience to care for and believe in. The cinematography is excellent and you feel as if you have truly gone back in time to ancient Rome. The look of the Roman Coliseum is believable and people have finally got a true image of what the Coliseum must have looked like in its prime. The film uses both hand crafted sets and CGI for the landscape of Rome. Filming took place in four countries over a four month shoot. CGI was stealthily used to reanimate the late Oliver Reed (Proximo) who died during filming. The fight sequences are choreographed very well to deliver rousing actions scenes with a top notch score composed by Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrard. The costumes done on the gladiators are very striking and just as terrifying sometimes as the hungry tigers Maximus must defend himself against while he is battling Tigris of Gaul (Sven-Ole Thorsen), an undefeated gladiator called out of retirement. The crowds of the Coliseum are a sight to see themselves and the chants of Maximus ring through the walls of the Coliseum and in your mind once the credits have rolled. Gladiator has all of the ingredients of a classic epic masterpiece. The opening battle scene of Germania is cited as one of the best battle scenes of all time by CNN. Russell Crowe's portrayal of Maximus was named Entertainment Weekly's sixth favourite action hero and named Gladiator their third favourite revenge film. Gladiator has been responsible for an increased interest in Roman history, sometimes called the "Gladiator Effect." It assisted in the revival of the historical epic in the new millennium with films such as Tory, Kingdom of Heaven, and 300 being released. Gladiator isn't for everyone, as some may find the political jargle to drag the story down. It is still a film worth checking out if you can stand the long running time and have an interest in the story of a gladiator. "What we do in life echoes in eternity." - Maximus Decimus Meridius

"My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius. Commander of the armies of the north, general of the Felix Legions. Loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife, and I will have my vengeance. In this life or the next." And so it goes the epic tale of General Maximus. One of the best epic films ever made, it is not a film without its problems as there are a few places the story is not realistic and a few places where history gets ignored. But overall, Maximus is such a powerful, likable character and the recreation of Pax Romana Rome is so convincing that you end up watching the movie in awe at its sheer power alone. Admittedly, the ending leaves a little to be desired as it was not handled with the full energy that the rest of the movie was but it is still a beautiful story with even better cinematographic execution and truly realistic combat gore to reflect the harshness of the age. Joaquin Phoenix delivers a performance of absolute excellence that at times even manages to overshadow the General.

Most directors would kill to have one masterpiece in their body of work. Most would crawl across broken glass to have two. But with Gladiator, Ridley Scott joins the hallowed ranks of Stanley Kubrick, David Lynch and Francis Ford Coppola, with his third complete and utter triumph. After a long period in the critical wilderness, few could have believed that this prodigious talent, who peaked so early in his career, could ever recapture his past form. But disregarding his subsequent efforts, there can be no doubt from watching Gladiator that Scott is one of the greatest directors of the last twenty years.

Ten years after its release, itâs easy to blame Gladiator for any number of films which have followed close on its heels. Aside from Scottâs slightly underwhelming Kingdom of Heaven, weâve had to deal the hagiographic hyperbole of Troy and Alexander. And then there is 300, which combined the looks of Gladiator and Sin City before stripping out all the substance of both to create something truly silly. One could further argue that without Gladiator, there would be no Pirates of the Caribbean; Scottâs success, both critical and commercial, seemed to suggest that long-dead genres were not so long-dead.

If we ignore its legacy for the moment, we are left with a powerful film which, like Batman Begins, is a perfect marriage of substance and spectacle. Like Christopher Nolan, Scott is a commercially-minded auteur, someone who marries a pure artistic vision with a no-nonsense approach to filmmaking. Scott knows what will sell, but he doesnât let the box office dictate his shooting style. Gladiator is a very accessible film, but it is also emotionally intense and visually striking, containing any number of images which wouldnât look out of place in an art film. These range from the poppies falling in the arena before the final showdown, to the shadows on the bust as Marcus Aurelius is killed: one eye is seen in light, the other in shadow, representing the empire slipping into darkness.

Being a swords-and-sandals epic, the film does have to conform to some extent to the conventions of Spartacus and Ben-Hur. Despite coming from all over the Roman Empire, our main characters all speak English in vaguely British accents. We know that our main character will not die before the end of the film. Much blood will be spilt, thereâll be plenty of crowd shots, and there definitely wonât be a happy ending. On that basis, youâd think you could sketch out the plot of the film on the back of a serviette. But Scott is cleverer than that, and knows that weâre cleverer too.

What Scott manages to do in Gladiator is to inject these conventions with new life, not by subverting them so much as bending them and adding his personal touch. Scott gives us a central battle between good and evil, but he twists it by making Maximus either the most reluctant of heroes or the most enticing of anti-heroes. He is not a killing machine on a spiritual warpath; he kills because he has to, only when he has to, and he does not enjoy it. The film avoids falling into the trap of justifying his killings, either by belittling the people he kills, or by suggesting that the reward of seeing his family in Elysium was worth all the bloodshed. Itâs ultimately tragic, since the central character is essentially broken and slowly dies over the course of the film.

Russell Croweâs performance in the central role is incredible, but equally incredible is that of Joaquin Phoenix as Commodus. In the emperor Scott gives us a villain who is sinister and creepy, and yet strangely vulnerable. His incestuous love for Lucilla is writ large, but this can equally be read as his means to express an overall desire to be loved. Commodus is also a tragic figure, insofar as he causes his own downfall, craving to be loved whether by his sister or the people of Rome. In the end, both turn against him; his sister realises her love for Maximus, and the crowd look on in silence as Maximus pushes a knife slowly into his throat. We do not warm to Commodus but we completely understand his pain and anguish at being neglected by his father and lied to by his own soldiers. We feel sorry for him as he dies, rather than just cheering Maximus on.

Credit must also go to Scott, as well as the writers, for giving this story a compelling female presence, something which previous historical epics have lacked. Scott has a good track record with strong female characters; think of Ripley in Alien, Rachael in Blade Runner, or both leads in Thelma and Louise. Unlike James Cameron, however, he never feels the need to gloss over their more âfeminineâ, sensitive qualities. Where Cameron in Aliens gave Ripley a gun and called it feminist, Scott allows Connie Nielsenâs character to work to her own strengths. She is a loving mother with genuine feelings, who is also intelligent and wise in matters of the state, and exerts influence by choosing who she trusts.

At its heart, Gladiator is not really a film about revenge, redemption, or weaponry. Itâs a film about love, whether for oneâs family or the people one serves. What starts off as a film about duty and honour slowly transforms into a battle between the hardship of the mortal world and the forgiving arms of the next. After the death of his family, Maximus spends the rest of the film in a deep quandary. He knows he must fight the injustice of Commodusâ rule, but the longer he resists, the longer he stays away from his family, and the further he must go in stopping his foe.

What Scott manages is to give us all these interesting and arresting ideas within a well-told story beset with enough breathtaking spectacle to stop us losing interest. Unlike The Dark Knight, the set-pieces are kept to a minimum and make sense in the order in which they come. More impressively, the themes of the story are never put on hold as the crowd-pleasing action unfolds. Even in its most blockbuster moments, like Maximus and Commodus having a punch-up in the arena, the film still carries immense weight and depth. They are not just men in shorts hitting each other, they are symbols, locking horns for the future of Rome in a way which neither really wants.

All of Scottâs films are visually arresting, but in this one he really excels himself. John Mathiesonâs cinematography is brilliant, capturing Scottâs 2nd century through a wonderful range of metallic greys, woody browns and olive greens. By opening with a battle scene, we are thrust straight into this world. Five minutes in, before a single word has been spoken, we feel right in the centre of that battlefield, in a world with its own culture in all dimensions. The battle scenes themselves are gripping; before the arrival of The Lord of the Rings, this was one of the best on-screen battles around.

Gladiator is a monumental triumph of a film, an epic with a great sense of heart and purpose which never fails to enthral and entertain. Although on a par with Alien and Blade Runner, the film is perhaps most similar to Apocalypse Now: for all its tiny flaws and little meanderings, the film holds an intense hypnotic pull on your senses, so that in the end you just canât help but love it. If you want realism or historical accuracy, you wonât find it here. But what you will find is a powerful story which echoes through the ages, brought to us through riveting performances and helmed by a director at the top of his game. If Robin Hood even faintly resembles this, it could be the film of the year.

Russell Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix both deliver top notch performances and build incredibly strong rivaling characters. Director Ridley Scott does an excellent job; he makes excellent use of somber gold, amber, and brown colors to intensify the somber mood and emotion of the heroâ(TM)s hardships. The scenes of the various parts of the vast Roman Empire are very diverse but always lively and rich. The movie really looks stunning with the crowded streets of ancient Rome, bloody battle scenes, and the ferocious crowds of the Coliseum. It is a great movie, a joy to watch over and over again and is a true classic.

300, Braveheart, Gandhi, Malcom X, Gladiator:  these aren't just movies...these are histories and possiblities of truths that exist in this world. They are ideals that we either breathe life and honest discipline into...or we let become hollow vessels of a time when they held power unto themselves.

well, that word...

that's a word I strive to live toward each day. Arguably the best Roman epic ever made, this beautifully shot and thrilling picture single-handedly revived the swords-and-sandals epic in 2000.  Scott, as ever, is a master at creating worlds and his Ancient Rome is stunning.  His colosseum still looks fabulous, and Maximus' fight with Tigris (and the tigers), with the sun splaying in through the stonework, is just beautiful.  For me, however, the first battle in Germania, and Maximus' subsequent escape, all frost and mud, is the most visually memorable sequence.  Gorgeous and much-imitated score from Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrard; solid support from old hands Harris, Reed and Jacobi; but this film belongs to one man.  The searing, relentlessly masculine central performance from Russell Crowe deservedly won the Oscar the following year.  Despite his underrated work in LA Confidential, this rightly made him into a star and reveals him as one of the most talented mainstream actors of his generation.  Shame he turned into such a diva after this.  Bad show, Mr Crowe.

Gladiator has that epic quality about it, which makes it an enduringly popular film. Whilst Russell Crowe does his hard stares and rasping voices in the centre, it leaves many of the secondary cast to play around, such as Joaquin Phoenix as the brilliantly twisted Commodus, and Connie Nielsen as his reluctant sister. Oliver Reed also makes a good final performance. The plot is very much mimicking that of Sparticus in places, but is seperate enough not to always be confusing the two. Action sequences are quite gripping, and such bouts in the Coliseum between the poorly armed gladiators and the well armed chariot racers and dynamic and memorable. A great and moving musical score also delivers in terms of atmosphere.

Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) and Maximus (Russell Crowe) stand in the center of the coliseum surrounded by centurion guards. Maximusâ(TM) eyes are a blaze as he stares down the man who killed his wife and family, silent is the crowd. Tension is the only word that can be used to describe this scene. It is the climax of a tension that has been building from the first scene when you see Phoenix and Crowe together. There is indescribable reverse chemistry between the two actors in this best picture winning film, Gladiator. You can believe that they are mortal enemies. Croweâ(TM)s Oscar-winning performance is brilliant as a Roman General who after an attempt on his life and the death of his family is driven into slavery and eventually gladiatorial games. There is something in Croweâ(TM)s face that shows a man who has more on his mind than the audience knows. The character he conveys just makes you want to root for him the entire film and keep on rooting until after the credits have rolled.
    Gladiator is an epic sweeping film that lasts 155 minutes. It is another huge action film on the resume of British film director Ridley Scott (Alien, Blade Runner). Unlike many of Scottâ(TM)s recent films Gladiator has something more. Gladiator has character development, a beautiful score, realistic period settings and story that you care about. The film takes places in the late 2nd century at the beginning of the decline of Rome. The costumes are lavish and accurate, the weapons are spot on and the dialogue gives the essence of an ancient wisdom. During a scene where Maximus is enters Rome, he and the audience see the coliseum for the first time, completely generated by computer animation, the building is astoundingly realistic every brick of the building sits in the same place it did 2,000 years ago when the real coliseum still stood. It is truly a sight to behold.

But perhaps when you think of the roman empire you're thoughts will instantly go to...gladiators (it only figures since man's true nature is a violent one). Well to be precise, one gladiator in specific and his thirst for love, vengeance, freedom, vengeance, love, in exactly that order. This film is as great as i've heard as to be expected of course. From a respected general of legionnaires, to slave to respected gladiator to icon and martyr. Then we get some gladiator fights (typical, might've been something incredible in 2000), meh not so much now, but tends to be character driven and i like that. This is wonderful storytelling. The opening Battle Scene simply mesmerizes, showing the brutal nature of combat for Roman conquests. I went back to see the film again. The first time I didn't hear anything Crowe said before the battle. I was just too visually caught-up. The second time I listened very closely and caught the wise yet succinct line from Maximus "what we do in life... echoes in eternity." Awesome.
A simple man v. an emperor. I just loved the resilience Maximus showed throughout the movie. I find in most movies, there is an irritatingly slow process where the character has to "find himself," not so with Gladiator. Maximus does what is needed.
Aspects of the afterlife are opened, but not overdone. Love of family is given sizable focus. I liked the theme of love of country that we see as well, although it may not be justly deserved, it is never questioned.
The visual effects were amazing. It actually had me wanting to believe that's the way Rome actually looked in all it's glory. The battle of Carthage reenactment was really great.
The ending is just hypnotic. Intentionally or unintentionally it was simply emotional. The music is wonderfully beautiful as if Maximus' family are telling him...you have arrived.
Bottom line: magnificent. Visually and emotionally satisfying.

The general becomes a gladiator, rising up through the rankings focused on enacting revenge on the emperor, and thus becoming a power political piece the newly crowned Caesar can not kill due to his popularity with the people of Rome. A soaring epic that nails almost everything right, with fantastic performances from Crowe and Phoenix that helped make them the movie stars they are now. This is a special, unique movie about the Roman empire and the way Scott captures it is utterly thrilling.

Russell Crowe stars as Maximus in a general turned gladiator fighting for his life and his freedom to kill the murderer of his wife and child, consequently the new emperor of Rome (Joaquin Phoenix). The music is wonderful, most notably the Battle, which is appropriately named for the opening battle scene. Gladiator also shows the short lives of gladiators for public entertainment in the Roman empire, something that has been depicted since Spartacus or Ben Hur.

Cinematic perfection! An unforgettable and masterfully directed epic, from the brilliant mind who brought us such timeless classics as "Alien" and "Blade Runner". It's not often I use the word masterpiece for a film, but this spectacular piece of historical action deserves nothing less. The story, of a Roman general named Maximus, who goes from a soldier to a slave to a gladiator champion in the majestic Colosseum, is one of the most moving, impressive and triumphant tales ever told. Roused by the amazing battles and stirred by its emotional power, I always come out of this film with a lingering sense of awe and wonder. I wish I could erase my memory, only to experience it for the first time again. For this is epic story-telling at its finest hour and one of my favourite movies of all-time. If you haven't seen it yet, you have certainly missed something!

It has the life of one man who is forced to become a slave after the death of his family and then fight as a gladiator and work his way to the top to face off a man who has destroyed everyone in his path, even his own father. The acting is just superb, the visuals are amazing, and the story is just simply beautiful. We have true conflict. True sacrifice. So many elements that make a near perfect movie are in this very film. It's unforgettable. I am admittedly not a fan of Russel Crowe, or Joaquin Phoenix. Normally I find that Crowe is not subtle enough (with the exception of Beautiful Mind and Cinderella Man) and Phoenix is way to subtle (with the exception of Quills). Both actors have their place in film, and both do a fine job in this one in particular, but I can't help wishing for someone else in the roles. 
 
 That being said, this movie benefits from being an epic well done. It is well written and contains unparalled (at the time) production values. It also gets bonus points for not shying away from killing the main character's family (including his son, something studios would normally shy away from). Having not watched this movie all the way through until recently, I went into it knowing the end. But that's fine. It is a vengeance film at heart, and I'd be hard pressed to name a vengeance story where the main character doesn't complete his veangeful quest. The difference is that most veangence stories end with a character feeling empty and wasted. Not so here, when your character looks forward to his own death and his opponent is so despicable you want him to die. This would normally be shallow, with the characters so black and white, but this simple storytelling serves its point.
 
 The point is that you want to pick sides and root for your opponent, much like a roman senator would choose his Gladiator. You enjoy watching him thrash his way up the ranks, knowing the whole time that he will win out in the end. 
 
 Another thing that helps this movie is its ancestor, the great Spartacus. A lot of the design (costumes, arenas, weapons) take their cues from this classic. Spartacus taught us about gladiators, and this film reminds of that venerable classic. It is familiar moviegoing territory, and it feels like going home for hollywood.
 
 I would recommend this if you, like I, avoided it for so long. This is one that lives up to its hype.

''My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife. And I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next.'' When a Roman general is betrayed and his family murdered by a corrupt prince, he comes to Rome as a gladiator to seek revenge. Russell Crowe: Maximus Joaquin Phoenix: Commodus Epic, dramatic, heart-wrenching, action packed and dramatic. Ridley Scott's roman historical masterpiece, forget the still good but flawed kingdom of heaven this is the one to watch. Russel Crowe gives his best performance of his career. The late Richard Harris and Oliver Reed give high performances and a quality that shines timeless etherality. Joaquin Phoenix is an equal cold maddened son who's hunger and thirst for power is a vision to see. ''At my signal, unleash hell.'' A tale of redemption of a man fighting for good. A cause bigger than himself and to overthrow a tyrant obstructing the birth a republic. Revel in the violence, behold it's beauty and magnificence, wasn't a doubt in my mind that Ridley Scott would reap the rewards of his efforts and win awards galore. People who criticize this film are the same people that ridiculed Blade Runner, Alien, and my message to them is to get stuffed, thats as polite as i can put it. Gladiator features some wonderful cinematography by John Mathieson. The battle scenes are very graphic. (This movie is not for the squeamish, that's for sure.) There were some scenes in particular that really struck me, such as when Crowe appears to be floating over the ground very fast. The use of colour and colour tones added a great deal to the mood of the movie. Excellent. The script was being written and re-written as the filming was going on, yet it doesn't show that the actors had no idea how the movie was going to end when they began filming. The acting is terrific. Russell Crowe is wonderfully cast as Maximus. Many reviewers agree that he is now officially a star. Joaquin Phoenix also proves his mettle as the emotionally troubled Commodus, whose behavior and emotion toward his sister could give anyone the creeps. Connie Nielsen makes you believe that, as Lucilla, she really is torn between natural loyalty to her brother and doing what she knows is right. Oliver Reed, in his last performance, is memorable in his role of Proximo, the former gladiator who is the owner of Maximus and brings him to Rome. In short, the actors were brilliant in their roles, not over-acting, but giving subtle, strong performances. ''I don't pretend to be a man of the people. But I do try to be a man for the people.'' The fights staged in Gladiator are masterful set pieces; stylized and captured gloriously. However, the fighting in Gladiator is not unrealistic; it's graphic and bloody. The warriors who battle each other are not super-men, they are normal men, real fighters, who get bashed and beat up at every turn. These soldiers combat in a truly gritty way, they are warriors who need to smell and rub their hands in the earth they battle upon. Chief amongst these mortal combatants is Russell Crowe's, a hero of mythological stance, whose raw aggression on the battlefront, coupled with his powerful expressions (combating and not combating, his silent moments from his execution to his first brawl in the arena are his best) and compelling heroics earned him a well earned Oscar. These battle-scenes of Gladiator are, of course, extremely well tended to by Ridley Scott who is the master at crafting epic war scenarios (see, I told you fanboy-praise would sneak its way in!). The patient, slow pacing of the film seems to take a sudden halt here, and then fast-forward in an amazingly rapid-fire pace with quick shots, swinging swords, vivid skies and a great score by Hans Zimmer to further emphasize the dramatic mood. The very culmination of this is not at the end, but rather early. It is the moment that Maximus removes his helmet, reveals his identity and faces the emperor, after a long and ferocious battle. It is a scene so poignant that I always wish it would have been saved until later on in the film, thereby giving it even more weight. But no matter, because rest assured that it is goosebumps-inducing enough. A gloriously entertaining, heartfelt and carefully crafted war adventure by Ridley Scott in which little feels missing or incomplete. What more could you ask for? Great acting from the cast, I suppose ? well, this is also present in Gladiator. Best of all, the actors have good dialogue to work with so they don't choke on the dated lines. Russell Crowe propels this film with his heroic personality, Connie Nielsen adds introspective depth, and Joaquin Phoenix is excellent as the twisted but idealist emperor Commodurus. Gladiator is visually stunning; it is the work of a master craftsman. It is also emotionally intriguing, something some Scott films lack. Its soul-searching music (applause to Hans Zimmer) and its ambitious, gorgeous view of the after-life are beautiful. Its truly gritty-edge give it a dirty, gruesome magnificence. One of my fave films of all times, one i have watched countless times. Near the beginning in the forests was filmed near my relatives too and I've been. Simply breathtaking scope and settings and the music hits your soul. I am certainly entertained. ''What we do in life echoes in eternity.''

Epic story? Check. Brutal action? Check. Dynamic direction and editing? Check. Ridley Scott's classic has it all and does it all in this exciting movie about a fallen general fighting his way to revenge through rings and rings of gladiators. The personal revenge plot gets mixed in with a dash of political scheming (no movie about the Roman Empire would be complete without some plot-hatching senators), but our fine hero Russel Crowe does get the chance to personally kill the emperor in a hand-to-hand fight in the arena. The pase of the movie is great (I watched the Director's Extended Edition), altough some of the fightscenes are too chaotic. If I had to point to one thing that distracted me most in the movie it would be Hans Zimmer's score, which sometimes feels oddly out of place for the period piece, and is just too intrusive from time to time. Overall, a great movie, with a great supporting cast and a very silent and sulking hero chopping off limpbs and heads. What else could you want.

It's a fantastic journey of a Roman general, Maximus (Russle Crowe) who has lost everything that has mattered to him, his wife and son, who were murdered. He becomes a gladiator who is fresh on the hunt for redemption and vengance as his blood lust beckons him to kill the corrupt Roman emperor. 
 
May contain spoilers Spoilers:
 
 
Normally, I complain whenever a main character is killed in a movie, but only because when it occurs it is done in a grim way. Not so with [i]Gladiator. [/i]The ending is pitch-perfect, using dignity, sorrow, and our connection with Maximus, which, by the time the film ended, was enormous. 
 
End of spoilers:
 
If you haven't seen [i]Gladiator[/i], (which, chances are by now, you have), then, frankly, see it now.

"Father of a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife and I shall have my vengeance in this life or the next" A man robbed of his name and his dignity strives to win them back, and gain the freedom of his people, in this epic historical drama from director Ridley Scott. In the year 180, the death of emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) throws the Roman Empire into chaos. Maximus (Russell Crowe) is one of the Roman army's most capable and trusted generals and a key advisor to the emperor. As Marcus' devious son Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) ascends to the throne, Maximus is set to be executed. He escapes, but is captured by slave traders. Renamed Spaniard and forced to become a gladiator, Maximus must battle to the death with other men for the amusement of paying audiences. His battle skills serve him well, and he becomes one of the most famous and admired men to fight in the Colosseum. Determined to avenge himself against the man who took away his freedom and laid waste to his family, Maximus believes that he can use his fame and skill in the ring to avenge the loss of his family and former glory. As the gladiator begins to challenge his rule, Commodus decides to put his own fighting mettle to the test by squaring off with Maximus in a battle to the death. Gladiator also features Derek Jacobi, Connie Nielsen, Djimon Hounsou, and Oliver Reed, who died of a heart attack midway through production. Review This film is a very ingenious screenplay of a man's loyalty, suffering, courage and emotions. Gladiator is a 2000 historical action/drama film directed by Ridley Scott, starring Russell Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix. Crowe portrays the loyal General Maximus Decimus Meridius, who is betrayed when the Emperor's ambitious son Commodus (Phoenix) murders his father and seizes the throne. Reduced to slavery, Maximus rises through the ranks of the gladiatorial arena to avenge the murder of his family and his Emperor. While Gladiator was criticized by historians for its historical inaccuracies, its epic scope and intense battle scenes won praise. The film's success may have helped to revive the historical epic genre, with subsequent films such as Troy, Alexander, and Kingdom of Heaven, the last of which was also directed by Scott.

The Romans were simply the most badass civilization of the ancient world. They conquered most of the known world and ruled it for close to 1000 years, so it?s only natural that they would inspire a multitude of manly movies in the future.

The plot is a typical revenge story; the dying Marcus Aurelius chooses the general Maximus to suceed him as emperor over his own cowardly son Commodus, and Commodus kills Maximus' family and Maximus is sold into slavery. Maximus doesn't take lightly to that shit and vows revenge.

The combat scenes in Gladiator are nothing short of spectacular. The opening battle with the flaming Germans is great, but it is in the arena that Maximus truly shows his skill with the gladius (that?s ?sword? for you non Latin-speaking barbarians). He kills everything from chariot teams and tigers, to beating the crap out of this humongous Gaul.

Maximus, had he really existed, would have probably been the manliest Roman since the great general Gnaeus Manlius (he?s real, seriously!).  If you consider yourself a connoisseur of manly cinema, make it your business to see Gladiator at least once.

Ridley Scott's modern classic may take a lot of cues from the likes of Spartacus and Ben Hur, but in many ways it surpasses them. The thrilling combat sequences are as good as any committed to celluloid, and as impressive the CG recreation of ancient Rome is, it's the wonderful dialogue, characters and design that breathes life into it. Russel Crowe charismatically heads a magnificent cast, featuring Richard Harris as the ageing Marcus Aurelius Caesar tired of conquest and wishing to leave a legacy after his death, veteran Shakespearean Derek Jacobi providing the political intrigue behind the scenes, scheming to replace the Emperor with a democratic republic, Oliver Reed as Maximus' new mentor dreaming of recreating past glories, and Connie Nielsen as the conniving Lucilla whose true motive is only to keep her son safe. But it is Joaquin Phoenix's Commodus who is the show stopper, brilliantly portraying a spoilt child whose ambition combined with weakness of character and desire for a father's love twists him into a malicious tyrant; the scene in which he assassinates his father is superb. It even takes time out to take sideswipes at modern politics and the media "Rome is the mob. You can take away their freedom, but show them a little magic to distract them and they will still love you for it." This is what brings the film to life, and this level of sophistication makes it's contemporaries such as Alexander, Braveheart or even Scott's own Kingdom Of Heaven look like school pantomimes in comparison. Proof that the Hollywood system in the hands of true artists can produce something genuinely beautiful.

Historical dramas are a difficult genre to work in. There is always that balance between accuracy and entertainment and the point of harmony between them is different for each viewer. Most people just want to be entertained and so don't have a major problem with the films portrayal of past events. There are others, like myself, who think that one does not have to be sacrificed for the other, that an accurate portrayal of times passed can still be wrapped around a good yarn. Any film with a historical setting is obviously setting itself up for this sort of scrutiny, especially one that is set against known events and uses real life characters. Now don't get me wrong, I loved this Ridley Scott epic, but there are still a few points to be raised against it. Having said that it is still way above most of the other films that fall into this category. Mel Gibson, for example, has a way of rewriting the facts when he attempts this kind of thing. The Patriot took place in a clean cut, black and white version of the American War of Independence that would be unrecognisable to any historian and to say that Braveheart was a portrayal of William Wallaces life is like saying that Star Wars is a factual critique on space exploration. With Gladiator we are on slightly firmer territory.
The story is set against a factual period in Roman history. In the last year of the reign of Marcus Aurelius (AD 180) the bulk of the Roman army is campaigning in Germania. In an opening battle scene that will go down in cinema history, Maximus has just completed a stunning victory over the tribes of the region, bringing the last of the barbarians under Roman rule. As Marcus Aurelius knows that he is not long for this world and fearing that his son Commodus will not make a worthy emperor, he offers the job of Protector of Rome to Maximus, a sort of caretaker role whilst the old Republican ways can be re-established. Commodus finds out the plan assassinates his father and orders the death of Maximus, who being the hero of the piece manages to escape. Eventually he is captured and put to work as a Gladiator, and as his masters fortunes rise, he finds himself fighting in Rome before, Commodus himself. The rest of the film is about Maximus struggle to stay alive against the machinations of the evil boy emperor and to try to manoeuvre himself into a position from where he can put Marcus Aurelius dying wishes into motion. As he gets nearer his goal the powers that be are set to thwart him and it all comes to a head in a final show down between the wronged ex-General and the young Emperor. This is the plot at its most brief as there are many twists and turns along the way, but to say too much would be a give away, and this is a film that, for all my criticism should be viewed by everyone.
Marcus Aurelius and Commodus are historical realities and they are portrayed ably by Richard Harris and Joaquin Phoenix respectively. Russell Crowe is like a young DeNiro in the lead as a brooding hunk, his body language and expressions saying so much that is dialogue doesn't have to. Maximus, as far as Im aware, is thankfully a created character and Crowe comes across as everything that you think a Roman Warrior should be. Not so much a supporting cast as a lot of A list players taking on lesser roles make every scene come alive. Connie Neilsen plays the old flame and is as regal and elegant as a member of the Roman nobility should be, even if its just an image of our own making. Oliver Reed is the slaver that Maximus is set to work for, and sadly passed away during the making of this film, but he will rest assured that he went out giving one of the best performances of his life. Derek Jacobi and David Schofield as the scheming senators pay some memorable scenes and even Omid Djalili (Irans only stand up comic) is in there adding a touch of humour.
Essentially though Gladiator is an action movie, and there is plenty of that. From the opening battle scene onwards the action hardly lets up, clawing his way up through the arenas of the backwaters of Empire, Crowe gets many opportunities to play the role that he is associated with, the action hero. The fights are hard hitting and hypnotic, the choreography makes each one unique, be it man on man, lion or against an array of chariots. The cinematography is stunning, most of the backdrops, especially when the story moves to Rome are created on computer and the shots of the coliseum are breathtaking. The irony is that Ridley Scotts work is normally dark and shadowy, Blade Runner, Alien and Black Rain for example and here he makes a stunning visual feast that goes against everything that he is associated with, and that is the sign of a gifted man.
The purist will find a few bits difficult to swallow, Commodus introducing one of the political rivals as Senator Gaius for example, is like calling Mr Blair "Prime Minister Tony not a big moan I`ll grant you but something that with a bit of care could have been ironed out. The big stumbling block is this plot device of re-establishment of the Republic a political system that was not only a thing of the past but also an idea that would have been so treasonous that to talk of such things would have meant arrest and probably execution. "Rome was founded asa Republic"claims Commodus at one point, well that's not true is it, the Republic came about as a result of a backlash against the rule of a succession of tyrannical kings. This idea of having Maximus become the Protector of Rome is also an odd concept and more in keeping with Cromwell's position in Seventeenth century England that anything found in the Roman world.
In 1964 Anthony Mann made a film called, The Fall of the Roman Empire, which is set very much against the same set of events. In fact Scotts film is seen by many as a remake of the film for the modern audience. The difference is in Manns film the conclusion is drawn that this is the beginning of the end for the splendour of the Roman Empire and the film ends with the Praetorian Guard, the real power behind the throne, auctioning the job of Emperor to the highest bidder. Scotts conclusions are less cynical and leave you with the vague feeling of a happy conclusion and the emergence of a Rome that was all sweetness and light. This obviously never happened, the Republic never got its second chance, but it seems that in modern film making the idea that the hero doesn't win through is something that hollywood just cant stomach and so they don't let the facts get in the way of a good yarn.
But that aside this is still a great story set against a recognisable time and place and as such portrays the period very well. The look and feel of the story seems valid, as far as we know, and there is no shortage of action. It is a long film at two and a half hours, but that seems to be becoming the norm these days and so wont seem too exceptional. Hans Zimmers soundtrack is also a fantastic and stirring classical undertaking, worth owning in its own right. Watch it as pure entertainment, enjoy the story, soak up the ambience and if you wish to really find out about the realities of the period, hit the history books.
