Russel Crowe puts in a an oscar-worthy performance in this film. Joaquin Phoenix follows right behind Crowe, and the other actors turn in excellent performances as well. 
The music is also very well done, and is certainly some of Hans Zimmer's finest work. The cinematography, costume design, special effects, and production design were all oscar worthy efforts in this film.
 There are three elements of this film I did not like, however. First, the willingness of Maximus initially to kill other [often] innocent people in order to earn his personal freedom is most certainly selfish, even if he was grappling with grief over the murder of his wife and son. Second, the pursuit of revenge against Commodus goes against what is right, according to God's word. "Vengeance is Mine, I will repay", says the LORD. I know that the character of Maximus is not a Christian, but he still had a conscience. We should leave vengeance to God. Third, the violence is quite graphic. I think the filmakers went too far in their pursuit of realism. At times it seemed as though they were glorifying the violent spectacle that was the Roman gladiator contest.  I recommend watching the edited version on t.v., if you can.
    To end on a positive note or two, I did like the affection Maximus showed towards and earned from the men he led in battle. He earned their love, devotion and respect as a general. I was also touched by the simple yet powerful love he had for his famliy, his home, and even for his horses. I also like the fact that he was willing to fight to free Rome from the oppression of the evil Commodus. One thing I will say about Commodus: though his sinful actions were inexcusable, I can relate to his desire to be loved. I think we all can. However, we must still do right even if no one on this earth loves us, for God always loves us and wants us to live the way He designed us to live.

Ridley Scott's Roman epic, Gladiator, is considered one of the greatest movies ever made. Now, I don't argue that its a great movie, but I don't know if I would say its one of the greatest. Its epic film making, directed by Ridley Scott, and I'm not saying I don't like that style but its usually just more of the same. The usual over-the-top battles, over-acting characters, and excessive gore. Gladiator definitely falls into that category along with the other epics. For some reason, this one stands out. Now the acting is still pretty over-the-top but the actors are able to engage their characters quite well and definitely bring something great to the table. The cinematography is excellent, the storyline is creative (though again a bit derivative), and the movie is all around well made. I can't quite put my finger on what separates this from the other Hollywood epics, but I found it substantially more enjoyable than most. Its a great movie that is most definitely worth watching.

What more good can be said about Ridley Scott? I mean the man is a master craftsman of cinema. Granted over the years he has been hit or miss, and I will say a lot more miss than hit - but around this time he made Gladiator and IMO the superior Black Hawk Down. With Gladiator he shaped an experience for the ages, and crafted it down to its finest detail - from picture to performance, and design to music. This isn't altogether a bad thing, but those expecting a new Roman epic that will stand the test of time (like Spartacus and Ben-Hur) are in for some surprises.

The currently hot Russell Crowe stars as Maximus, "the general who became a slave" who begins the film as a commander so high in the echelons of the Roman army that the aging Caesar Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) hand-picks him to become the next Caesar... instead of his own son Commodus (not pronounced Commode-us, played by Joaquin Phoenix).

Joaquin Phoenix's appearance in a movie always means trouble, and sure enough, dad is soon dead, Commodus is Emperor, and Maximus is off to execution. It's a roundabout road (that lasts 150 minutes) to get from general to slave and slave to gladiator. From there, Maximus ends up in Rome at the Colosseum (you know: The Colosseum), threatening to overthrow the Emperor and return power to the Republic. And here we are, 1600 years before the American Revolution.

Gladiator's finest hour comes when the gladiating begins (though this is a good 60 minutes into the picture). And we are talking serious carnage. Bloodletting. Decapitations. People severed in two. Dirty fighting. Joey would like this movie.

Shot in an aggressive yet vaguely annoying chop-chop style, Gladiator borrows heavily from the camera style Spielberg used in Saving Private Ryan's battle scenes: Print every other frame of film twice, and run at regular speed. This casts everything in a dreamlike quality, which sometimes works in the film but gets old due to overuse and overall poor lighting.

Then there's the chit-chat of Gladiator's "plot," a threadbare bit of political intrigue, with Commodus worried sick about Maximus's rise to popularity via the mob crowds at the pit, Connie Nielsen's Lucilla (Commodus's sister), also worried sick in fear that her son will be killed... blah blah blah. I zoned out whenever one of these weepy people took the stage, waiting for the fighting to start again. You know, with the chariots! And the tigers!

There's something Jerry Springeresque about Gladiator, but Crowe lends a lot of legitimacy to the proceedings. Less effective is Phoenix, who invites you to believe he is an actual Emperor of Rome. This turns out to be impossible, as Phoenix comes across as, well, River Phoenix's little brother. There's also the little issue that Gladiator stretches the boundaries of "historical fiction" to new and impossible lengths, which almost goes without saying. Almost.

The new three-disc DVD set is exhaustive and exhausting, with a new, 17-minute-longer cut of the film anchoring the set that includes Russell Crowe's first ever commentary track. Oddly, director Ridley Scott all but disowns the cut -- saying the original theatrical cut is "the director's cut" (it's also included here). A 200-minute making-of documentary fills up one disc, and a third disc of various extras (storyboards, costume designs, more deleted scenes, and so on) round out the box set.

Fun story, fun action. The theatrical release was great itself, but the extended cut is like another three or four layers of icing on an already iced cake. 

The extended version clocks in at almost three hours and includes scenes that add more to the story and helping it make more sense. Among the removed scenes is Emperor Commodus' sister, Lucilla, meeting with senators and their discussion of the tyrannical rule of her brother, his mismanagement, arrogance and that he has to be stopped at all costs. If that wasn't enough, it's packed together beautifully. It's three discs housed in a fold out digibook with a 3D slip cover and comes with a booklet explaining how the movie got off the ground accompanied by selected scenes. The special features are massive with a seven part documentary that is as long as the film. One of the best special edition/extended cuts I've ever seen.

Gladiator is the kind of movie upon which Hollywood once built its reputation but rarely produces anymore: the spectacle. Filled with larger-than-life characters, gorgeous scenery, impressive set design, and epic storytelling, Gladiator is designed not just to entertain, but to enthrall. It draws audiences in and immerses them in a reality that is not their own. A boisterous reaction is expected every time the protagonist defies the odds and wins a conflict, or changes the tide of battle in his favor. This is filmmaking on a grand scale.For New Zealand-born, Australian-bred actor Russell Crowe, Gladiator represents an opportunity to expand his reputation.Gladiator shows that he can dominate the screen with a cold stare, a clenched jaw, and a sure gait - attributes normally reserved for the likes of action mega-stars like Arnold Schwarzenegger and Sylvester Stallone.The supporting cast is comprised primarily of European notables. Perhaps Scott's greatest achievement with Gladiator is neither keeping the pacing of a 2 1/2 hour movie tight nor choreographing a spectacular battle scene, but creating a second-century Rome that is entirely credible and stunning in its detail. Ancient Rome is one of the most romanticized civilizations in the history of humanity, and rarely has it been brought to life with the grandeur of this film. The Coliseum, for example, has been resurrected to its full glory (largely through the use of digital technology). Gladiator consistently looks good, although, during some of the fights, rapid cutting creates a sense of disorientation and confusion.Like many of the great Hollywood historical epics, Gladiator is the story of the triumph of a heroic figure over seemingly-insurmountable odds. In this case, he is a slave taking on the most powerful man in the world - the Emperor of Rome. The ending may be a unlikely, but it is as exhilarating and satisfying.

All through watching this hackneyed piece of gladiator melodrama, I couldn't get over the feeling of deja vu. Honestly, every single plot point is predictable from miles away, creating the feeling that the characters are moving along tracks instead of out of developed and believable motivations. All that's left for the viewer is an ample sense of spectacle and some decent cinematography. Still, Cecil B. DeMille provided that well enough over half-a-century ago and he didn't have the pretensions to think of his films as anything other than mass entertainment. I cringed at the campy dialogue which seemed to be spoken by statuary rather than by living characters and at the swelling, operatic music that nudged the viewer, in case we didn't get it already, that this was a serious moment: this was a moment where you should cry. This is a film that stomps, believing that something real, something surprisingly delicate or complicated, is not what the audience wants. And maybe it was right. It did, after all, win the Academy Award for Best Picture, triumphing above the far more original and brilliant Requiem for a Dream. But, in cinematic history, it can only be seen as a failure, and a dull one at that. Decades ago, films like Spartacus actually complicated our stale view of an epic and created something thought-provoking, although flawed, for an audience to contemplate. This one though serves up some facile gray dish that can only be made for a passive, lazy audience. Finally, it's hard to believe that this was directed by Ridley Scott, who a few decades ago, used to be considered a cinematic visionary. Now he seems as old-fashioned and out-of-date as the film itself.

Gladiator is an experience than many more historical epics have tried to recreate. From Troy to Alexander and including the more recent "Clash of the Titans" there has been little success and a lot of wasted potential.
   The main reason Gladiator works so well is that it rises above the standard fare. The conflict and plot are simple enough, vengeance for a wrongdoing, but the story rises above a mere revenge tale as it includes political machinations and the fate of the Roman Empire that all depend on the actions of one gladiator.
  If it all sounds quite droll and boring at this point, fear not. The combat action scenes are liberally sprinkled throughout the movie, and by themselves they make the movie worth watching. Swordplay and wild animals and chariots all make an appearance and the audience need only answer one question: Are you not entertained?
 Yes, indeed we are.

  The script doesn't bother with trying to recreate the language or manners of the times. Everyone here is speaking in modern accents with a small smattering of antediluvian phrases scattered in to indicate that the story is taking place in the past. Luckily the very, very skilled cast sells it to us with enthusiasm, led by Crowe.
  The impressive achievement is that Russell Crowe makes us forget that he is a Major movie star and full embodies the role of the general turned gladiator. Its easier to appreciate a the film when you can forget that you're watching an actor. The rest of the cast easily holds their own, especially Phoenix, who exudes the perfect mix of creepiness and foreboding that creates the perfect villainous counterpart for Maximus. You will want him to lose, you will root for Maximus, and you will stick around to the end because you care about these characters.

   All in all, there's enough here to satisfy any moviegoer. Action, suspense, and intrigue, a very understated romance and a very supportable hero. Rarely does a movie succeed on all the goals it sets for itself, and almost never is the end result this entertaining.

I think this movie definately has its place. I think it is a good one: well-formed and fast-paced. And there are definately worse movies out there to see. But I have to admit that I spent a great deal of time squirming. First there's the gore and carnage that floods the scene every couple of minutes. Now, I like my action flicks, but I like them with as little death as possible. (I apologize, I do NOT enjoy watching fake death, ESPECIALLY in hordes of innocent no-name characters.) But while I could excuse that on grounds of the action genre. I absolutely HATED the creepy sexual scenes with Joaquin Phoenix. He was a real sicko and I'm supposed to be entertained by him? Of course that statement can change if you decide that "Gladiator" isn't really entertainment, it's inspiration. But then again, it sounds silly to say that our inspiration is found within artificial blood, guts, death and incest. It actually doesn't sound too far from the colosseum. Okay, maybe that was a little too strong. I would agree that "Gladiator" has its place. But until "the mob" can begin to wake up to the comparisons between the story and the real world, "Gladiator" is of no more importance than one of its namesakes would have been in ancient times.

Gladiator ignited or rekindled a fascination with historical epics for a lot of people, and rightfully so. It hearkens back to movies like Spartacus and Ben-Hur, sweeping and grand film events that go all out in taking you back to a specific time and place.

It's a very good movie. The story of a once great man who is stripped of his family and his honor and left with nothing but his desire for revenge and the gladiatorial arena, is simple and powerful. But there are two real reasons why Gladiator works so well: Russell Crowe is the perfect Maximus, and the sets are absolutely awe-inspiring. This is the closest to seeing ancient Rome that any of us will ever get, and if you weren't impressed by Commidus's entry to Rome or the scenes in the Colisseum, I don't know what WOULD impress you. Each building and battle rings of authenticity and attention to detail. 

Crowe gives a believability to Maximus that many actors wouldn't have been able to pull off half as well. He makes Maximus seem a man who truly would inspire awe among the public and his followers, and jealousy from those who feel threatened by him. There were several notable performances from this cast, but Crowe stands above them all. It's still his finest role, in my opinion.

Gladiator is the best movie that Ridley Scott has made since Blade Runner. It's impressive in all aspects, and completely deserves the lofty reputation that it has.

"Joey, do you like movies about gladiators?" Hey, who doesn't!?

The awe-inspiring trailers for Gladiator may have you dreaming of Spartacus and Ben-Hur, but you may be surprised to find this film in reality a less palatable mélange of Braveheart and Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome. This isn't altogether a bad thing, but those expecting a new Roman epic that will stand the test of time (like Spartacus and Ben-Hur) are in for some surprises.

The currently hot Russell Crowe stars as Maximus, "the general who became a slave" who begins the film as a commander so high in the echelons of the Roman army that the aging Caesar Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) hand-picks him to become the next Caesar... instead of his own son Commodus (not pronounced Commode-us, played by Joaquin Phoenix).

Joaquin Phoenix's appearance in a movie always means trouble, and sure enough, dad is soon dead, Commodus is Emperor, and Maximus is off to execution. It's a roundabout road (that lasts 150 minutes) to get from general to slave and slave to gladiator. From there, Maximus ends up in Rome at the Colosseum (you know: The Colosseum), threatening to overthrow the Emperor and return power to the Republic. And here we are, 1600 years before the American Revolution.

Gladiator's finest hour comes when the gladiating begins (though this is a good 60 minutes into the picture). And we are talking serious carnage. Bloodletting. Decapitations. People severed in two. Dirty fighting. Joey would like this movie.

Shot in an aggressive yet vaguely annoying chop-chop style, Gladiator borrows heavily from the camera style Spielberg used in Saving Private Ryan's battle scenes: Print every other frame of film twice, and run at regular speed. This casts everything in a dreamlike quality, which sometimes works in the film but gets old due to overuse and overall poor lighting.

Then there's the chit-chat of Gladiator's "plot," a threadbare bit of political intrigue, with Commodus worried sick about Maximus's rise to popularity via the mob crowds at the pit, Connie Nielsen's Lucilla (Commodus's sister), also worried sick in fear that her son will be killed... blah blah blah. I zoned out whenever one of these weepy people took the stage, waiting for the fighting to start again. You know, with the chariots! And the tigers!

There's something Jerry Springeresque about Gladiator, but Crowe lends a lot of legitimacy to the proceedings. Less effective is Phoenix, who invites you to believe he is an actual Emperor of Rome. This turns out to be impossible, as Phoenix comes across as, well, River Phoenix's little brother. There's also the little issue that Gladiator stretches the boundaries of "historical fiction" to new and impossible lengths, which almost goes without saying. Almost.

The new three-disc DVD set is exhaustive and exhausting, with a new, 17-minute-longer cut of the film anchoring the set that includes Russell Crowe's first ever commentary track. Oddly, director Ridley Scott all but disowns the cut -- saying the original theatrical cut is "the director's cut" (it's also included here). A 200-minute making-of documentary fills up one disc, and a third disc of various extras (storyboards, costume designs, more deleted scenes, and so on) round out the box set.

Gladiator is an epic-by-numbers. Sweeping shots over cities, a few thousand digital extras wearing togas, a few seconds in a battle scene where the music turns to silence and the direct-o-matic uses a different shutter speed... Seen it all before. While everyone else was dropping their jaws, my thumbs got busy with the twiddling.

If you're going to make a movie where the audience can root for the underdog, you should at least blur the lines a little. Gladiator's heroic goodies and hissable baddies are so obvious even Spielberg would have complained. For the Autobots, we have Russell Crowe. He gets fired from his job, sentenced to death, manages to escape only to find his wife raped and his children murdered, is sold into slavery, forced to perform in front of bloodthirsty crowds as a gladiator, loses his car keys and steps on a dog poo. For the Decepticons, we have Joaquim Phoenix, who killed his own dad, ordered the deaths of Crowe and his family, forces people to fight and die for his entertainment, wants to do his sister, and kicks puppies in the teeth. It's as balanced as a see-saw with Jabba the Hutt on one end and an Olsen twin on the other.

A terrific, crowd-pleasing update of the old Hollywood swords and sandals epic.  It's a pretty simple revenge story mixed in with some Roman history (which is wildly inaccurate for dramatic purposes).  Scott is still one of my favorite visual directors, and the attention to detail here is still as impressive as the day the movie opened.  Hans Zimmer's score is fantastic, and the action is incredibly exciting.  It's also worth noting how uniformly great the cast is.  Russell Crowe makes a great hero and Joaquin Phoenix is a really nasty villain.  Plus, you've got a lot of brilliant older actors like Oliver Reed and Richard Harris.  It's not the most complex thing in the world, but the effort put into it really makes it an impressive, emotionally appealing film.

A wholly satisfying action adventure epic in the vein of Ben-Hur. After his family is killed, General Maximus finds himself a slave in gladiatorial combat. He finds a purpose with much sought after vengeance, and becomes a symbol to take back his beloved empire from the tyrannical Commodus.

The movie mixes so many elements together that it works well. even though some of the character development scenes in between the action scenes drag on,  they make sure to find a correct balance between the two to make for excellent tension.

The musical score is what makes the scope of the film feel more epic. The Arabian score when Maximus is taken to the slave trade market or the thundering final piece when Commodus rises on the platform with rose petals is like the icing that goes on top of the very delicious cake.

Although Russell Crowe is the main character, the spotlight is absolutely stolen by Joaquin Phoenix. He is able to go from calm and collected to creepy and chilling in seconds. Joaquin Phoenix is able to make a great villain, as his character is well written as a spoiled son who longs for his father's love, but is always trying to fill the void.

A fine combination of direction, acting, and music make for one of the best films of all time.

In the final days of Marcus Aurelius' reign, the aging emperor angers his son Commodus by making it known that he wants Maximus, a fearsome and respected Roman general, to be his successor. Power-hungry Commodus kills his father and orders the death of Maximus. But the latter flees, only to discover that his wife and child have been murdered by Commodus. Captured, Maximus is forced into slavery, where he is sold to Proximo, a former gladiator who serves as both mentor and slavemaster. Maximus trains as a gladiator in the arena, where his fame grows. He goes to Rome, intent on avenging the murder of his wife and son by killing the new emperor Commodus. Maximus has learned that the one power stronger than that of the emperor is the will of the people, and he knows he can only attain his revenge by becoming the greatest hero in all the empire.

I was very impressed with the opening scenes of this film, which were set on the Germanic frontier of the Roman Empire around 120AD, somewhere in the regions of either the Rhine of Danube rivers.  They conveyed the spectacular image of that ancient warfare to great effect. It is from the point of Maximus being sold in to slavery after the failed attempt of the Roman Emperor's son, Commodus, to have him executed that the film becomes a virtually pornographic spectacle of blood and gore with about as much point to it as the ancient Circus of Rome itself (The Circus of Rome, unlike those of today, was not for children's viewing, but was more so to satisfy the blood-lust of the idle citizens of Rome- kind of like WWF wrestling but with swords, tridents and javelins- and the blood, etc, was real). 

The substance of the plot here gives way to the spectacle of violence: until the development of a conspiracy that embroils Maximus.  Designed to remove the usurper Commodus from the Emperor's throne and restore the power of the Senate by facilitating Maximus' escape and subsequent return at the head of legions loyal to his memory who would over-throw Commodus in a military coup, if the plot was not first uncovered by Commodus.

In short, remove the middle third of the film if you are looking for substance and you will have it.  Otherwise I recommend doing something useful while the scenes in the Colosseum are playing, like doing the dishes or vacuuming.  All the same, the ending was beautiful and poignant, and the film had a great sense of the age.  Mostly enjoyed.

"Gladiator" is a rousing epic that stirs the soul. Between political battles and arena confrontations, director Ridley Scott knocks your socks and helmet off. Nearly everything about the film is breathtaking; the acting, the music, the sweeping cinematography, and the stunning visual effects blend almost seamlessly with each other in a way that mesmerizes. Besides straying from true history, the only other fault with the film may be its sometimes slow pacing. Some audiences may find the dramatic staredowns to be too long or over-the-top, but those sequences serve their purpose well. (By the way, I saw the extended edition, so some of those parts were probably longer than what was released in theaters.)

Nevertheless, the film is spectacular, especially for its philosophical musings about republics and caesars. Few films build their drama around politics and exchanges of philosophy, and most films that do tend to weigh themselves down with it, but "Gladiator" is a carefully balanced with thought and plot. (This is now a new term of mine: the Plot/Thought Balance.)

If you examine the 4-star Schaeffer System below (based on Francis Schaeffer's 4 methods of Biblical art critique), you will see the Content/Vehicle Integration category. The Plot/Thought Balance and Content/Vehicle Integration are very similar. Schaeffer's idea of CVI is that an artwork's vehicle (i.e. the plot of a movie, the style of a music piece, the subject of a painting, the shape of a statue) must suit its intended purpose (i.e. its message). In this sense, "Gladiator" succeeds in strides. Ancient Rome is the perfect time and place to set up a believable story about political strains and betrayals. Therefore, "Gladiator's" CVI is spot-on. The PTB, on the other hand, is an element of filmmaking that can only come into play if a film's CVI is perfect. Since "Gladiator" is perfect in its CVI, then its PTB comes into question. Essentially, the PTB is the ultimate utilization of both content and vehicle; the content must be clear and precise, and the vehicle must never stop for the content to be presented.

"Gladiator," as I mentioned before, is very carefully balanced. You can tell when a film has exquisite Plot/Thought Balance when you find yourself missing an important plot point because you're still zoned out on deep insight, or you may have missed some deep insight because you were caught up in tasteful drama. In such a case, a second viewing of the film is inevitable and vital.

I have but one qualm with "Gladiator," and it involves Ridley Scott's rather half-hearted portrayal of Rome's pagan spirituality. The characters' faith in these gods and ancestors is supposed to come across as inspiring and feasible, but we are never given any reason to believe that the gods are on anybody's side or that they even exist for that matter. The religion in the film serves very little purpose except that Maximus dreams of living with his wife and son in the afterlife in a "heaven," and that's the only part of the film's spirituality that comes across as sincere. But when Maximus or anybody else prays to a statue or dead relative, it's awkward and hollow.

Still, since Ridley Scott likely only included that part of the story for the sake of being epic, then it at least goes to show (from a Biblical standpoint) that everybody longs for that afterlife peace, and "Gladiator" paints that desire in a noble light. Therefore, for the sake of storytelling and honest representation of the human condition, the film's spirituality is still accessible. (I'm not saying you should try paganism [Please don't.]; just view the film with a grain of salt.)

Overall, "Gladiator" is epic, splendid, and gripping. There is plenty in it to enjoy and think about many times over.

Schaeffer System: 3 1/2 out of 4 stars

Technical Excellence: 1 star
Validity: 1 star
Worldview: 1/2 star
Content/Vehicle Integration: 1 star

This is sort of an interesting place to jump in--almost awkward. I count myself a Ridley Scott fan, indeed I look eagerly toward his new films as they're announced (though it should be pointed out I do not always see them, such as A Good Year)--but for all this I've been known to vehemently disparage two films in his oeuvre, one for sheer stupidity (Hannibal, which I loathed) and one for its idea theft (an issue I take very seriously). That second film is, in fact, this one. I was suckered in by a fantastic deal on the 3 disc extended DVD, and decided--as, honestly, I'd already been planning--to give the film another go. The first time I saw it was in theatres, where about forty five minutes in, I turned to my father (with a degree--which I shamefully still can't keep straight in terms of educational level in this instance--in Classical Studies) and whispered, "Is any of this historical?" when he replied, "No," I spent the rest of the film in a fog, incensed that it was stealing so blatantly from two films I had recently seen in school--The Fall of the Roman Empire and Spartacus. I enjoyed the film somewhat in spite of this, but the experience was soured instantly by my perception and the confirmation that remark gave me. I'm known for the zeal with which I pursue arguments against the quality of films which I find in some way insulting to my ethical stance on adaptations, and this film was no exception. For months I angrily ranted about how this film had stolen a major portion of its plot from the Sir Alec Guiness film The Fall of the Roman Empire, and how it was then smashed into Spartacus, and no one seemed aware of this, or, if they did, they only knew the latter. I'm greatly offended when a film chooses to lift ideas and pretends not to have done so, and it's extremely difficult for me to enjoy it--the same holds true if they claim an influence and then fly in the face of it, as applies to other films. Over the years though, while my zeal has not lessened, the degree to which it will affect my experience in and of itself has lessened somewhat, if I feel there is strength behind it. In this case, as with even Hannibal, I was always quick to note the quality of craft within the films, even without a bias towards Ridley, who I could not have named to save my life in those days. Thus, my decision to try again here. I'm debating the same with Hannibal, but that one didn't have much floating under it and I felt was actually awful in and of itself. But, I--as usual--digress. Still, what we have here is the return of the epic sword-and-sandal film, which was not quite so triumphant as to encourage legions of films to follow, but we have seen more than a handful, and certainly more than might otherwise be expected. In it we see Russell Crowe as Maximus, general of the Roman legions, here disgraced and set into exile through the machinations of Caesar Marcus Aurelius' (Richard Harris, in a nicely paternal and wise role) son Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix--I should mention this series of events bears no resemblance to history, but a strong resemblance to those in Fall, despite the writers' rather unbelievable claim that they'd never seen it) so that he, himself, can become the new Caesar. The lost Maximus is enslaved and becomes a gladiator; here we see the strains of Spartacus, as he first befriends the Numidian Juba (Djimon Honsou), which is rather similar to Spartacus' early association with Woody Strode as Draba, also under a former gladiator who was freed and began training gladiators. This is also the first appearance of the fictitious Senator Gracchus, apparently. Still, as I said, that's not the point this time--I just feel it's worth noting that these were very strong impressions and not feeble strains of similarity, but pretty strong ones. Anyway, the most direct descendant of this film was certainly Ridley's own Kingdom of Heaven, which bears a strong visual similarity to this film, though here we are clearly speaking of how one man can affect a world and change it purely by his own hand, where in Kingdom of Heaven it is at least somewhat more unified, though still centered on a single character. I think this is where Ridley has his strongest talents--he shows his background in graphic design and his education in it. He has style. Not overly slick and plastic like Michael Bay, nor as out of control and obsessive as Terry Gilliam, but controlled artistry. Colour filters--in truth, nearly every time I refer to this subject, I am thinking of this film and Kingdom of Heaven, which is odd, considering I am quite big on the style of both, I just feel that the style has been unsuccessfully mimicked by others--are put to use, especially in the hauntingly beautiful images of Maximus' home, and especially what I can only assume are the Elysian fields, set to music that apparently I'm not alone in feeling sounds like Enya, but I did know that it wasn't (apparently the name attached is one Lisa Gerard). Ridley also knows to use slow motion for underlining and emphasis (not to appear "awesome" or to overuse until neverending sluggish boredom like Zack Snyder) and strange motions like Maximus' floating a few times throughout the film. We see his affection for particulate matter as it snows in the opening battle scene and the final confrontation involves falling flower petals. This as well as the overblown version of Rome that appears, brought to my mind images of Julie Taymor's Titus, but, as with his art in general, Ridley has a more subdued form of this stylization and only achieves near-anachronism. Everything feels exactly appropriate to the period, and yet somehow seems outside of it; this, too, is something I'm known to complain about--it seems the workshops have carefully sculpted every helmet and piece of armor down to picking and choosing where to place dents, dings and scratches for the ultimate "real" effect, somehow leaving the clear impression that they are not real, without ever giving it away at the same time. This sort of surreal feeling is engaging and pleasant, despite what it may sound like, and adds to the feeling that Ridley is a master painter, and that his medium is film. He perfectly crafts things--I've heard stories of his work on his own cinematography, down to carefully positioning every single light himself--and sets them in motion and the end result is a clear work of art, without the pretension of something like a Julie Taymor or David Lynch, and allows it to remain a thoroughly entertaining cinematic work at the same time. Working within this, as mentioned, are primarily Joaquin Phoenix and Russell Crowe as opposing forces in the battle for the control and future of Rome. We hear lines like "At my signal, unleash hell," and "I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next." Russell and Ridley are both to be given credit for making lines like this completely plausible and acceptable in the universe these characters inhabit; they could easily be completely laughable and ridiculous, unacceptably over-the-top--but they work. Worst things first: Ridley Scott, a director I respect very much, does a very poor job editing near and medium fight-scene shots, making it next to impossible to view what's actually supposed to be happening. That said, the quick cuts reduce the level of gore (and I have a sneaking suspicion that the fight scenes were paired down for the DVD; the theatre version seemed far bloodier). Despite the minor shortcoming of the edits, Scott has effectively created an impressive environment and sense of scale, implementing large-scale sets to blend together the stunning and credible CGI. Much discussion has centered about the quality of the story and performances; for my money, Russell Crowe's Maximus Decimus Meridius is a interesting amalgamation of various semi-mythical Roman heroes, and Joaquin Phoenix gave an arguably better performance than Benicio Del Toro's Oscar-winning supporting role in Traffic. All that aside, the film's best quality is the old-school Shakespearean story of political intrigue, betrayal and power versus duty. Call me old fashioned, but I like this movie.

This is the one, the king of all battlefield movies, the one that so many have attempted to emulate, but like so many of General Maximus' enemies, have fallen so far short at the hands of this legend! An epic duration it may be, but well worth the wait to see how an army general goes from a potential successor to Caesar, to slave on death row in a matter of seconds, thanks to the wicked ways of his power mad 'brother'. The journey we then witness is one of revenge on how the slave wishes to fight through all of what is put in front of him on the centre stage of the colosseum, just to destroy Commodus (who executed both the emperor and his own wife and child), and install a peaceful ruling of Rome. With emotions running high both during, and at the pinnacle of the tale, there's gallons of bloodshed, numerous family betrayals, epic gladiatorial scenes and a legacy that will remain a classic in movie history for years to come. There is literally no film that will outdo this in terms of raw uninterrupted entertainment. Not only Russell Crowe as lead, but the supporting cast are all perfect and create a lasting character memory for each of their roles. Even the soundtrack is fitting as although it's merely the same melody played in a different style each time, it has a hard hitting impact to go with each of the emotional scenes. Rarely would I be prepared to subject my ass to the potential numbness of a three hour movie, but even my buttocks can gear themselves up for this beauty, as simply put, it's an outstanding cinematic spectacle!

At least it's better than "300". I'd let the director of "Alien" give me pre-medieval action drama before a man best known for his Dodge commercials. Bu What we've got here is a whole collage of Greco-Roman gloss that's been done before, and in most cases, done better. There's no greater depth or message here. It's simple, shallow, skull crushing entertainment, and there's not really anything wrong with that as long as it's done well enough. What doesn't work is the violence. It's brutal, but it's presented through the scope of a 12 year old kid on Ritalin. Not that I'm implying that Mr. Scott has been slipping something into his scotch, but I fear he's fallen victim to the Michael Bay curse of flashy, hyperkinetic cinematography and editing. Take the opening battle sequence. When Mel Gibson made "Braveheart", he put the camera in the middle of the melee, but he let it roll just long enough to catch a quick but horrifyingly certain glimpse of a soldier's head splitting like a cantalope. Scott is going for the same thing here, but he forsakes realism for style, and most of the time, it's impossible to tell what's going. It's as though the camera operator is being repeatedly gored and bludgeoned from behind. I'm all for visceral realism, but how can something be visceral if you don't know what it is? What makes the movie work relatively well are the music, and the actors. The score is nothing new, but it hits the right emotional notes. Crowe, on the otherhand, doesn't have enough of an emotional range. He kills a gladiator like no other, though, and that's his greater purpose here. Joaquin Phoenix has a few unsure moments, but he makes a very booable and hissable villain whom you can't wait to see meet the wrong edge of a sword. The man who walks off with the film, however, is the late Oliver Reed, in his last appearance. He's perfect for the part, better than the material he is given. You listen to him growl and by God, you believe him. He's the best part of the film's tepid midsection, which drags slowly, like a corpse through the coliseum. The finale is disappointing. It feels brief, after much buildup. For a movie bent on delivering spectacle, to go out on such a meek note after such giddy promise, is nothing short of a crime. The best scene in the entire film comes at the midpoint, in which the whole arena raises their fists, thumbs erect in the air. Two million thumbs up. By the Ebert and Roeper school of criticism, this is a fine movie. From a more long term perspective, it's harmless as long as it's not repeated too often. Cinema only grows from invention, not from repetition. The fact that this won Best Picture is not a good sign for interesting, challenging movies.

GLADIATOR (2000) directed by Ridley Scott starring Rusell Crowe, Joaquin Pheonix, Connie Nielsen

A great General of Rome is betrayed by the son of Marcus Aurelius after his death. The son kills his wife and son and leave him for dead. He will be taken and bought to become a slave then a gladiator. He'll go to Rome for the games of killing and will slowly prepare his revenge and take Rome back, like Marcus Aurelius wished it before his death. A woman, the man's daughter will help him trying to pull the string with the politics in the background.

When Gladiator came out it was pretty much a dead genre and even if it didnt reinvent the wheel it was pretty effective thanks to Ridley Scott and the actors performances.

After this film, Russell Crowe was big. Did he deserve his Oscar for his role as Mximus ? Or did he get the statuette cause they didnt give it to him the previous year for his obviously better performance in The Insider ? It doesnt matter. He is quite good here. Intense like he should and in good shape kicking some ass. Joaquin Pheonix is the the son. A bit insesteous on the side. He betrays his father and his people. Pheonix almost overact but he is in control of his character's madness making it memorable. Connie Nielsen is the sister, good, but not great. She plays in tone, like any Hollywood actress should, she is strong but thats it. Ricahrd Harris is quite good as Marcus Aurelius and Oliver Reed, in his final performance is pretty good too.

Gladiator isnt a short film but time goes by quite fast. Its very entertaining. Quite bloody. It has some cool fight scenes, some good speeches even if sometimes it sounds a bit cheesy but it works. The camera moves well when it should and the editing is effective for the genre. Ridley Scott proved he was back in the game. The visual effects are the greatest, but for the time they were pretty good. This is what a Hollywood blockbuster looks like when there is talent behind it. Not necessarly Best Picture material but a fun epic ride.

A number of giant, career-making performances (plus another impressive turn in the director's chair for Ridley Scott) fuel this rich, hard-hitting saga of betrayal, grief and revenge in imperial Rome. The dueling fates of Maximus (Russell Crowe) and Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) share the front and center, twin note-perfect parts that continuously clash over the spotlight, but dozens of supporting players also deserve recognition. Richard Harris as the guilt-ridden sage, Marcus Aurelius. Oliver Reed chewing scenery as a grizzled, cynical combatant-turned-slaver. Djimon Hounsou and Ralf Moeller, comrades in arms who convey an intimate, crucial sense of kinship. As an intensely emotion-driven story, Gladiator can't function without this level of acting power. In less capable hands, it might be laughed off the screen. With Crowe, Phoenix and company in command - and, again, Scott there to expertly piece it all together amid an appropriately epic score by Hans Zimmer - we're swept off our feet.

It's an enveloping film; a thick flood of sights, sounds and moods. We marvel over the bustling Roman Colosseum, tense our muscles in the raging chaos of battle, find peace in the metaphor of golden wheat fields as an afterlife. Maximus's justified outrage becomes our own, Commodus (with his barely-contained mania) our bane, and once it's got those hooks in, the script doesn't give an inch. An exceptionally powerful production, damn near perfect in all respects.

This is a work of fiction, and must be approached as such. I have seen numerous reviews that criticise the film for its lack of authenticity and historicity -- this is perhaps an unfair criticism. It is as unfair as if to say Star Wars is unhistorical, or the events portrayed on Spin City didn't really happen historically -- of course they didn't. This is what fiction is all about. Of course, there will be some grounding in reality (do we really want to divorce fiction completely from reality so that every city becomes Metropolis and every proper name must be changed?). Once I realised that this movie was intended to be a work of fiction, and not a dramatically-charged documentary, I relaxed and had an enjoyable time. The battle sequences that open the film are well done and realistic with regard to tactics and conditions of the Roman fight against the Germanic tribes. It is a great film one whihc sets the standared in what was considered a dead film genre

Most films require that the viewer identifies with the character to truly be engrossed with the film. If you can't feel something for the character, than the audience is lost.

Luckily, in Ridley Scott's case, Russel Crowe is so captivating and convincing as a general loved by his troops and as a slave loved by the people that the movie really works. Possibly one of the greatest actors today, Crowe carries this epic film on his very capable shoulders.

Not to say that he is the only reason this works. The supporting cast, most notably Connie Neilsen, buoy the film to new perspectives.

Jacquin Phoenix definitely captures the egotisitcal persona he should display, stealing every scene he's in. Phoenix will surely be put on the map with Gladiator.

But the real shining star in this film are the incredible action sequences which jolt the viewer right in with the opening sequences, as Maximus' true worth to the Roman Empire is displayed. Scott's camera work within these completed sequences takes a modern twist that really works for the gruesome scenes.

Crowe will now get the respect he deserves for this collosal performance. Gladiator makes the most of its 2 and a half hours, marking a triumphant comeback for the long forgotten epics of the classic days of film. ALL HAIL MAXIMUS!  3 Stars  6-22-2000

Ridley Scott has done to Roman Epics what Steven Spielberg did for WW II movies: destroy all the traditional cliches and bring a more realistic approach to the subject. What most impressed me was the realistic portrayal of the fights making us realize that violence is not an entertainment. The high quality of the production is reflected in every single detail: from the shining face mask of the gladiator to the giant coliseum, passing by a bird's-eye view of Rome that the Romans themselves couldn't have even seen, to the splendid illustrations of the atrocities of the arenas and the battlefields.
The plot is just like what one would expect from such movies. The message is simple: Loyalty and honor are worth fighting for.

''My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife. And I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next.''

Gladiator may not be entirely true, but its absolutely epic. It's easily one of the most epic films you'll ever see. I've never been a huge fan of Ridley Scott, because I didn't like Alien very much, but this is his masterpiece. SUMMARY:

Victorious general Maximus Decimus Meridias (Russell Crowe) has been named keeper of Rome and its empire by dying emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris), so that rule might pass from the Caesars back to the people and Senate. Marcus' neglected and power-hungry son, Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix), has other ideas, however. Escaping an ordered execution, Maximus hurries back to his home in Spain, too late to save his wife and son from the same order. Taken into slavery and trained as a gladiator by Proximo (Oliver Reed), Maximus lives only that he might someday take his revenge and fulfill the dying wish of his emperor. The time soon comes when Proximo's troupe is called to Rome to participate in a marathon of gladiator games held at the behest of the new emperor, Commodus. Once in Rome, Maximus wastes no time in making his presence known, and is soon involved in a plot to overthrow the emperor with his former-love Lucilla (Connie Nielsen), Commodus' sister, and the democratic-minded senator, Gracchus(Derek Jacobi). REVIEW:

The screenplay is ever so mighty. Written by David Frazoni, John Logan, and William Nicholson, the screenplay is absolutely perfect. The story itself has depth, substance, and epicness. Probably the strongest element of the script is the dialogue. There are so many epic lines here, that are so memorable. All the characters are superb. Maximus is a powerful hero we can all take a liking to. Commodus is the opposite. We're supposed to hate him. He's a general asshole - he's attracted to his own sister, he killed his own father - he's evil. The potrayal of Ancient Rome is quite fantastic - it gives the story real tension. In the film, the Gladiators MUST win the attention of the people of Rome. Their name from the people will become more powerful than the emperor himself, and that's what Maximus tries to do. The climax is terrific, and the way the film ends - so epic! Russell Crowe throws himself into the role of Maximus with gusto. Joaquin Phoenix is hissable as the rotten Commodus. I must say, Connie Nielsen was rather disapointing as Lucilla. Her performance wasn't that convincing. Oliver Reed brings a fantastic attitude to Proximo, and Richard Harris is also very good as the former Caesar. Djimon Hounsou has a special appearance in this, playing a Gladiator friend of Maximus - he's actually very good. One of my favourite elements of the film was Han Zimmer's score. Now We Are Free - such a beautiful and epic song. The rest of the songs fit the material well, with the most intense pieces for spectacular battle sequences, which brings us too the next topic - the action. Scott stages the battle scenes so well, and they're shot with skill, and the editing is good. The battles in the Colesium are more than enough to keep you on the edge of your seat. The climatic fight scene at the end is a wonderful creation. Visually, the film is very impressive. The production design is fantastic, and the cinematography by John Mathieson is absolutely beautiful and amazing. The film is paced quite well. No other film is more epic. This is a prime example of why I love film, and why I watch film - it has all the components I want from a masterpiece. Ridley Scott has done a superb job with this - it's no wonder it won an Oscar for Best Picture.

Popular sword and sandals epic follows the basic outline of "The Fall of the Roman Empire" with rousing, violent battles staged like WWF fights. Russell Crowe is Maximus, a Roman general who seeks revenge for the death of his family and emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris), at the hands of the new emperor Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix). Maximus, who is forced to become a slave then a gladiator, is presented as a warrior who fights only out of duty or necessity. His moral superiority feels fraudulent. Hokey dialogue abounds over the afterlife. Still, it is often enjoyable. Commodus is shown to be a vain weasel with no scruples. The muscular Crowe gives a commanding performance. Its easy to imagine soldiers following his lead and crowds cheering for him. Phoenix is enjoyably hammy. Digitally enhanced effects of large crowds often looks fake. Stirring score by Hans Zimmer. Written by David Franzoni, John Logan, William Nicholson. Directed with usual visual flair by Ridley Scott. With Connie Nielsen, Djimon Hounsou, Derek Jacobi, David Hemmings, and Oliver Reed in his final role. Won Oscars for Best Picture, Actor (Crowe), Costume Design, Sound, Visual Effects.

One of my all time favorites. An epic story of the Roman general Maximus, loyal to the emperor Marcus Aurelius. This loyalty goes both ways as the dying emperor appoints maximus as his successor instead of his own son Commodus. Commodus, deeply insulted by this, smuthers his own father and then tells everybody he has dies of natural causes and has appointed him as the new emperor. 
Maximus refuses to show his loyalty to the new false emperor and gets sentenced to death for it. He manages to escape and finds out his wife and son are murdered by the imperial guard (the Pretorians). He is then found by a slave trader, Proximo, who wants Maximus to be a gladiator. Soon, Maximus turns out to be one of the best gladiators the empire has ever seen.
Still hungry for revenge, Maximus fights his way to the center of rome: the Colloseum, to face his sworn enemy, emperor Commodus...

This will be an informal review, since we all know the film came way back in 2000.

In currently re watching Gladiator, it's a lame T.V showing in 4:3, plain stereo, and I've seen just a couple of minutes, but I'm already in awe of the entire film, everything sums up to a great masterpiece, the rebirth of the swords and sandals epic, the likes we haven't seen since Kubrick's Spartacus and Wyler's Ben-Hur.

Back in 2000, Dreamworks released this power house epic in a quite and discrete manner round May, it had very little time to build up any hype, and the trailers and campaigns were puzzling. More over, it had Ridley Scott, who had been on a self imposed hiatus after the lukewarm G.I Jane back in 1997. I remember it wasn't even advertised as Scott's big return or anything, just as an action film set in Roman times.

I, for some strange reason found the film strangely appealing, maybe cause I was a big fan of the genre, and the closest I had seen of it in a movie house was Braveheart.

I went with a friend and a cousin on opening weekend. We waited in line for almost an hour, when the manager came out and said they had set the schedule for a 1h 30min action movie, but it ran  for almost 3hrs. I was angry with the dumb manager, but even more puzzled with the film...3hrs? I said to myself, that is an epic. I had admiration for Russel Crowe, after both L.A Confidential and The Insider, but this looked like a role for a Mel Gibson, which oddly enough was offered the part but passed cause he though he was too old, and Mel was right.

Anyway, the film started, and my oh my, was I shocked, but in amazement. The opening shot, which has now become a cliche, a constantly ripped shot and narrative tool by second rate swords epics since then, but in Gladiator it's still a poignant and intriguing shot.

Then, the most ambitious battle I had seen on film, with an impossing enviroment, strong looking Cinematography, a fantastic Production Design, impressive Stunt Coordination, use of Editing, etc. The opening battle of Gladiator set a new standard for motion picture epics, it was the battle to which all battles in the future would be measured.

But it was not a big splash of action, effects and bloodshed, the audience was introduced to one of the most remarkable heroes since Spartacus, Judah Ben-Hur, and William Wallace.

Russel Crowe's performance in the film was strong, effective and impressive from the first scene onwards. He was such an imposing leading man, he was casting destiny and perfection, and despite the bad rep he got for his Aussie accent, he was perfect. And his perfection remains constant throughout the film.

The movie has a supporting cast as epic as the film itself. The then young and relatively unknown Joaquin Phoenix was another massive revelation. His portrayal of Commodus, and the numerous layers he manages on the film are certainly amazing. He is a fantastic antagonist to Maximus, which I think goes back to the classic rule of Hollywood, the more interesting the villain is, the more interesting the hero will be. The late  Richard Harris and the late Oliver Reed were both fantastic, and Connie Nielsen, although she was sort of ignored, I thought she was amazing, perfectly casted, and added an undefined malice yet a sweetness and beauty to the film.

The Screenplay by David Franzoni, John Logan and William Nicholson is the other incredible element that makes the film stand aside from all of the half ass ed wanna be epics made after Gladiator(aside from Lord of the Rings Trilogy). The film has a powerful story, all the fantastic Production Design, Cinematography and Editing would be meaningless without the touching, intensely dramatic and highly rewarding and "striking story" of Maximus, "the General who Became a Slave, the Slave who Became a Gladiator, the Gladiator who Defied an Emperor." The movie is so rich in character development and narrative, which recalls classic epic drama and narrative seen in epics from the 60s, like the great Spartacus and Ben-Hur. It was also the first time the Roman Empire was so honestly portrayed, which also spawned an interest in roman history seen in the rave Age of Empires games and the HBO series Rome.

There were some who attacked the film for historical inaccuracies, well, all I have to say is what Spielberg said about Lawrence of Arabia: "The film would not have been as romantically poetic and mythic had it just been a straight chronology". I personally think the film respected the nature of the era, and raised the interest of investigation of the period, which is all good.

I have mentioned lots of people but one, Ridley Scott, who reached a level of excellence in the film that maybe not even he imagined. As I mentioned, Scott had been on a 3 year hiatus, but he was fresh as ever with Gladiator, reviving a genre, and creating a film with sequences that will live on and will forever be remembered. He redefined his own style and the style of making movies, and despite the competition he had, I think he deserved Best Director that particular year.

Another element that set the tone for the future was the grand soundtrack by Hans Zimmer and vocal Lisa Gerrard. It was amazing, plays perfectly in the movie, and has become a classic.

It's been almost 10 years after the release of Gladiator, and it remains perfect, a grand epic, the one Hollywood forgot it could do.

The film spawned a rebirth of the epic genre, with films such as Troy, King Arthur and 300 following it. As you can tell from the list, Gladiator was copied, but never matched. And aside from Lord of the Rings, there really hasn't been any epic movie has worthy and memorable.

Gladiator will become as timeless as Spartacus and Ben-Hur, and it could not deserve the spot more. The film is an amazing experience, I have not met anyone personally who dislikes the movie or who can dismiss it. I remember the experience of seeing it on a big screen, it was magnificent. Let's hope we get the chance to see it again like that. And I'm pretty sure we will..."but not yet...not yet."

Ridley Scott blew the dust off of a forgotten genre, and unleashed Gladiator upon the world. Evoking the spirit of those old historical epics of years past, Scott uses all the tricks of a modern film-maker to bring this distinctly old fashioned tale into the 21st century. A great story, flawlessly directed by Scott, with Russell Crowe absolutely scintillating in the lead role, "the general who became a slave, the slave who became a gladiator, the gladiator who defied an emperor". The film is filled with lavish period detail, with credit going to the costume designers, production designers, and everyone else who worked to create the air of authenticity this film has. Another factor this film has working for it is some superb, and bloody, battle sequences, from the opening battleground war, to the gladiator battles inside the digitally-rebuilt Colosseum, they are brutal, brilliant and stunning set-pieces. Add to this a suitably villainous performance from Joaquin Phoenix, one of the last performances from Richard Harris and the last performance from Oliver Reed (died during production in a Maltese pub), and you have all the ingredients for a modern classic, rewarded handsomely at the box office and Oscar ceremony.

For some reason, I cannot disassociate this movie from a column, by Leah McLaren if memory serves, in the Globe & Mail where she practically climaxed in paper and ink over Russell Crowe's status as (and I'm paraphrasing now) the greatest model for traditional masculinity since the young Richard Burton graced the screen.  Seriously, my Saturday morning paper had drool marks all over it.  Hers, not mine, but I admit her op-ed piece did make me go and see the movie.  

And Leah -- if indeed it was Leah -- wasn't far wrong: Maximus wears a wolf-pelt to keep warm up in Germania, has a RADA-two-pints-over-lunch accent, and hacks his way through the other gladiators like it's recess at the Rugby School for Boys, but deep down inside he's doing it all for his dead wife and son.  It's rather touching, really.  And really, really bloody.

Apart from the mighty Maximus, I love Richard Harris in this film -- Ridley nailed the casting on that one.  My only complaint is Joaquin Phoenix: over the top, yes, crazy Roman Emperor, yes, but I never understood why, if they knew he was a nutjob since childhood, Marcus Aurelius didn't have him killed before the movie started.  But, I guess that would have ruined the plot...

A massive epic, Ridley Scott's work of art - Simply a masterpiece

"Gladiator" is, to me, one of the best films ever made, probably even in my personal Top 10 Movies of All Time -list. It's a massive epic motion picture that pleases your eyes and ears with effective visuality, drama, romance and more. The story tells about a Roman general Maximus who gets betrayed by an evil prince. By the acts of the prince, Maximus's family gets murdered and he wanders into sorrow where tears won't be spared. He then finds himself captured to become a gladiator among other slaves, but he still seeks for revenge. Maximus tries to keep himself alive in battles which he is forced into, only that he might someday take his revenge against the evil prince. The story has so much more in it, but I'll just leave the rest of it for the viewers, as I certainly do not want to give away any spoilers.

Like I already said, the story is simply fantastic. It's so deep and touching, being very original at the same time. Despite of the movie being a massive epic one it still isn't clichÃ© at all, it just maintains the level of drama in a level that doesn't go over the top. It has a nice flow too and there is no boring scene in any part of the movie, every scene matters and every scene is significant in its own way, that's just how incredible the storytelling is. The building of the main character, the whole theme from victorious to sad, from sad to anger and from anger to a satisfying ending, everything goes like it's supposed to. The creation of the world has been achieved terrificly well; The sets, the dressing, all the details, basically everything. Although there was a lot of CGI used in the creation of the world, the CGI department deserves a big plus on making everything so believable and realistic. Everything looks smooth and soothing, just the way you want it to look like. You can't complain, really.

What comes to role performances, well, in my opinion Russell Crowe does an absolutely phenomenal role performance as Maximus. The anger, the sorrow, all the expressions and body language, just great. I don't care if Crowe is an asshole in real life, because whatever they say in the press he still is an amazing actor. He has actually become one of my favourite actors because of his past role performances, he is just everything a director wants from an actor, performing every role flawlessly. He does have that sort of a rough appearance, but he can play a nice guy too. What comes to other role performances there is one more to mention; Joaquin Phoenix. To be honest, I've never liked Phoenix that much, don't know why, but I have to admit that he is too an amazing actor. As the evil prince Commodus he is that brilliant fierce himself again, a perfect actor for an evil role.

This is by far Ridley Scott's best film yet to date and when Hans Zimmer's music is put on top of the cake you just can't go wrong with that. The directing is superb and the music is magnificent. Like mentioned above the directing consists of mixtures of genres; Drama, romance, adventure and action. Every department is handled in superior way, in a way that leaves your notebook blank on the side of the faults the movie would suffer from. The music has this main theme in it, which is beautifully composed, including that beauty and also thrill and intensity. "Gladiator" is all in all a tremendous motion picture which everyone should see, a born legend some could say. Fantastic story, phenomenal role performance by the lead actor, superb directing and beautiful music; All this compile a film that I can't imagine to be a disappointment to anyone, a definite 9 out of 10.

"My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife. And I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next."

Director: Ridley Scott Starring: Russell Crowe, Joaquin Phoenix, Connie Nielsen, Oliver Reed, Richard Harris Running time: 155 minutes Country: UK, USA

Oh my God! I was totally blown away by this epic masterpiece from the extremely talented Ridley Scott. This is a historic story that is very emotional with a very powerful dialogue which is very rare not just from Ridley Scott but also of all cinema. It was a very heartfelt story that teaches us all about what both life and death can give us and what they mean. It teaches what afterlife could be like if it actually exists. This film makes a slight possibility that life after death could exist. The way this story is set up is really good because there is a lot of raw emotion, a lot of hard hitting cinematic action effects and with very powerful directing and a very good script. I think I loved pretty much everything about Gladiator. It has a lot of outstanding action with the sound effects and visual effects. It was very intense because we all knew that Maximus was somehow going to win the fight but it was really questionable of how graphic it could be and it certainly was with a lot of very graphic realistic effect to it. It was a very tragic story regarding Maximus losing his wife and son but after that there was a lot of pride that brought that really strong life force so to speak towards his character. This is a film that can make people cry because of the emotional story but it didn't make me cry. Yes, it is a very emotional story but I wouldn't call it heartbreaking and one you could cry at.

Russell Crowe delivers a performance that he will probably be best remembered for. He didn't just deliver a very emotional performance as Maximus but he also created one of the most powerful and coolest characters in cinema history. There was a lot of tears from his eyes and I could easily see the hatred and the rage from Maximus towards Commodus with nothing but vengeance on his mind. Maximus is an ordinary Roman general whose life is turned upside down when he is betrayed by the son of his great friend Marcus Aurelius when Commodus murders his father when he announces that he isn?t dependent enough to become Emperor and wants Maximus as his heir to the throne. Because of Commodus' jealousy he requests Maximus to be executed but Maximus escapes and rushes to his family and they are killed by Commodus' men. He then becomes a slave and a gladiator. A lot of things in Maximus' life changes when he becomes a gladiator. This is my favourite Russell Crowe film and I did love his powerful performance as Maximus but his performance is better and more emotional as John Nash in A Beautiful Mind even though I liked Gladiator more than A Beautiful Mind. Joaquin Phoenix delivers an even more emotional performance as Commodus. What I truly loved about Joaquin's performance in this one was that it was a character that seems very soft with a soft voice and looking like a nice man but when you cross him or when you do something that he doesn't like or approve of he becomes a very fearful and evil character. The evil and jealousy in Commodus came when his father Marcus Aurelius says that he isn't good enough to be Emperor of Rome. Hurt by this and wanting to become Emperor, he murders and suffocates his own father by rapping his arms around him so hard that he couldn't breath. After he finds out Maximus is still alive after requesting his execution, he starts to feel really reeled and feels betrayed by his sister and nephew. Despite of how good Russell Crowe's performance was, Joaquin's was better with a more believable and realistic character. The late Richard Harris's acting as Marcus Aurelius was absolutely brilliant because I could see a lot of emotion and a lot of deep meaning that Richard brought to the character especially coming out of this soft voice. He will be best remembered for Harry Potter and Gladiator. I loved Oliver Reed, Djimon Hounsou and Derek Jacobi were all awesome aswell. This film has an absolutely outstanding cast and is one of the rare films where all of the actors have delivered top-notch performances.

Ridley Scott directs this to almost complete perfection. He has always had a talent of making action films but with different genres. This is his best work to date and will probably always be his best film. He made this film totally unforgettable and a phenomenon for the ages. Scott shows he can make blockbusters as well as just ordinary not-so-highly grossing films. Gladiator is one of the very few blockbusters that have won Best Picture. Others are like Forrest Gump, The Silence Of The Lambs, Saving Private Ryan, Lord Of The Rings: The Return Of The King and particularly Titanic. This is a very different type of film as far as story is concerned that Ridley Scott has done. He has done a lot of cool unbelievable stories but this is one of the few that he did make believable. The script was very good with really amazing scenes. I love the scene where Maximus sees Commodus again after believing Maximus was dead. That was such a powerful scene with a lot of fantastic direction from Ridley.

This is Ridley Scott's best work to date and probably always will be. Alien, A Good Year, Thelma & Louise, American Gangster and Blade Runner are behind it on top Ridley Scott films. It is a damn shame that Joaquin Phoenix has quitted acting for music because he had such a great rare acting talent. Gladiator is probably his best film and he will be remembered for that just like he will for his other Oscar nominated performance in Walk The Line. Gladiator is my favourite film starring Russell Crowe and his performance was very much deserved but I thought his performance was better in A Beautiful Mind. Shame he didn't win Oscar for that otherwise he would have the third actor to have had back-to-back Oscars after Spencer Tracy and Tom Hanks. Gladiator made history by becoming 1 of the 2 blockbusters to win Best Picture in the 2000s decade along with The Lord Of The Rings: The Return Of The King. This is my favourite epic film, my favourite action film, it is my dad's favourite film which is a tie with Aliens which is another reason why I love it even more than I already do but most importantly Gladiator is definitely one of my favourite films of all time.

Over-rated? Sure, maybe a little, but how many great, iconic movies can you name that were released in the year 2000? Gladiator is a new millennium version of Spartacus' bloody Homeric heroism for the Star Wars/Matrix crowd. Despite the fact that Gladiator owes much of its shape to the sword and sandal epics of the 50's and 60's, its main man, Maximus (Russell Crowe, in the role he'll always be remembered for) is much more akin to Rambo than Ben-Hur. He's a decent man forced by circumstances to execute extraordinary things; a man who just wanted to go home to his wife and child, but must take up sword and armor to try and save the world

Ridley Scott's epic Gladiator charges into action almost immediately. We meet Maximus assembling his Roman soldiers for an assault on a horde of barbarians. 'At my signal--unleash hell!' orders the well-regarded leader. The sequence that follows is an exuberant display of flaming arrows and deadly mortal combat. It's Scott at his most viscerally exciting.
 
Emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) is pleased by the victory. He regards Maximus better than he does his own son, Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) or his own daughter, the shrewd Lucilla (Connie Nielson). The dying emperor wants Maximus, who is Spanish-born, to succeed him, and make Rome a republic again. Commodus of course will have none of that, and orchestrates the murders of everyone dear to Maxumus, including his wife and son. He nearly succeeds in having Maximus killed as well, but he is only wounded, and is captured by slave traders, sold into bondage and marked for death under the ownership of Proximo (the late Oliver Reed), who supplies gladiators.
 
With that Maximus is back in Rome, fighting in the Coliseum, in front of new emperor Commodus and rises to fame as the city's greatest warrior. With that are scenes of harrowing battles, with man and beasts, done with dazzling digital effects that would have had Cecil B. DeMille and William Wyler beaming. But action isn't the only selling point, this is after all the director of Alien, Blade Runner and Thelma and Louise we're talking about here, and characters are allowed to shine. Harris and Reed of course kick ass in their roles, but for me the scene-stealer is Phoenix. His Commodus is deliciously creepy, elegantly perverse, particularly when it comes to his comely sister. One of the best surprises of the casting is Derek Jacobi as the empire's most regarded senator, two decades after starring in the tv mini-series I, Claudius.
 
Still, it's Crowe's show all the way. He is colossal, an amazing follow-up to his role in The Insider, for which he was robbed of an Oscar. But it isn't his determination to win battles that makes him so memorable. It's his aching desire to be with his family again. It's that attention to character that made Gladiator a doozy, and still a powerful movie experience ten years later.

Phoenix is sufficiently malevolent and erratic as chief villain Commodus, though his prissy foaming at the mouth does go over-the-top on occasion. Nielsen redeems herself for "Mission to Mars" with her stunning portrayal of Lucilla, emanating both the poise and valor of her character, while supporting players Hounsou, Reed, and Jacobi acquit themselves nicely with their small but important roles. "Gladiator" is as exhilarating and memorable as blockbusters come. Ridley Scott has just about created a perfect film-- nary a fault can be found in the writing, performances, or the lensing. The release of Gladiator helped significantly in consolidating Ridley Scott's reputation as a master filmmaker. His best two works are still Alien, and Blade Runner made in the early 1980s. But Gladiator has been a cause of optimism for Scott, a box-office success, as well as being nominated for twelve Oscars, bagging five, including best picture. It's a confidence booster for the premier director whose works in the 1990s have been mediocre by his own towering standards.

A visual spectacle, Gladiator combines elements from Spartacus, and Ben-Hur, and is made in the tradition of classic epics, but enhanced with modern special effects technology. The result is a potent motion picture depicting loyalty, corruption, and slavery in the most brutal, uncompromising fashion, set in medieval Rome. The level of cinematography accomplished is of the highest standard, capturing Rome in astonishing detail, yet with a certain degree of credibility. The film is 2.5 hours long, but Scott keeps it tightly paced, without going overboard with fancy editing.

Russell Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix provide the two supporting pillars, carrying the bulk of the film on their shoulders, giving a powerhouse, and devilish display respectively. Gladiator would only be half as engaging without Hans Zimmer rousing, grandeur score. It's a perfect compliment to the visuals. Gladiator comes at a crucial time when the epic genre seems almost non-existent since Mel Gibson's Braveheart. It started a trend of similar films (Troy, King Arthur) but those are cheap offerings that makes us appreciate Gladiator even more.

SCORE: 9/10
