"Joey, do you like movies about gladiators?" Hey, who doesn't!?

The awe-inspiring trailers for Gladiator may have you dreaming of Spartacus and Ben-Hur, but you may be surprised to find this film in reality a less palatable mÃ©lange of Braveheart and Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome. This isn't altogether a bad thing, but those expecting a new Roman epic that will stand the test of time (like Spartacus and Ben-Hur) are in for some surprises.

The currently hot Russell Crowe stars as Maximus, "the general who became a slave" who begins the film as a commander so high in the echelons of the Roman army that the aging Caesar Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) hand-picks him to become the next Caesar... instead of his own son Commodus (not pronounced Commode-us, played by Joaquin Phoenix).

Joaquin Phoenix's appearance in a movie always means trouble, and sure enough, dad is soon dead, Commodus is Emperor, and Maximus is off to execution. It's a roundabout road (that lasts 150 minutes) to get from general to slave and slave to gladiator. From there, Maximus ends up in Rome at the Colosseum (you know: The Colosseum), threatening to overthrow the Emperor and return power to the Republic. And here we are, 1600 years before the American Revolution.

Gladiator's finest hour comes when the gladiating begins (though this is a good 60 minutes into the picture). And we are talking serious carnage. Bloodletting. Decapitations. People severed in two. Dirty fighting. Joey would like this movie.

Shot in an aggressive yet vaguely annoying chop-chop style, Gladiator borrows heavily from the camera style Spielberg used in Saving Private Ryan's battle scenes: Print every other frame of film twice, and run at regular speed. This casts everything in a dreamlike quality, which sometimes works in the film but gets old due to overuse and overall poor lighting.

Then there's the chit-chat of Gladiator's "plot," a threadbare bit of political intrigue, with Commodus worried sick about Maximus's rise to popularity via the mob crowds at the pit, Connie Nielsen's Lucilla (Commodus's sister), also worried sick in fear that her son will be killed... blah blah blah. I zoned out whenever one of these weepy people took the stage, waiting for the fighting to start again. You know, with the chariots! And the tigers!

There's something Jerry Springeresque about Gladiator, but Crowe lends a lot of legitimacy to the proceedings. Less effective is Phoenix, who invites you to believe he is an actual Emperor of Rome. This turns out to be impossible, as Phoenix comes across as, well, River Phoenix's little brother. There's also the little issue that Gladiator stretches the boundaries of "historical fiction" to new and impossible lengths, which almost goes without saying. Almost.

The new three-disc DVD set is exhaustive and exhausting, with a new, 17-minute-longer cut of the film anchoring the set that includes Russell Crowe's first ever commentary track. Oddly, director Ridley Scott all but disowns the cut -- saying the original theatrical cut is "the director's cut" (it's also included here). A 200-minute making-of documentary fills up one disc, and a third disc of various extras (storyboards, costume designs, more deleted scenes, and so on) round out the box set.

Whilst Crowe and Phoenix are well placed in their roles, its the supporting cast that are even more memorable - in the last great film both actors will be remembered for, watch out for superb performances from Richard Harris and Oliver Reed (his final movie), delivering a slice of Shakesperean majesty to this picture. 3.5: I absolutely adored this film when it was first released.  This is a picture I saw twice in one weekend when it was initially released and then twice more in German later that summer.  My enjoyment of it has been somewhat tempered over the years though.  The action sequences, sets, CGI, costumes, etc were all amazing then and still are.  It seemed as if Scott invented this style of battle.  All of the battle and gladiator scenes are absolutely riveting.  Most of the performances are top notch, in particular Harris, Phoenix, and Crowe.  The main issue I have with the picture involved a combination of the cast and the script.  Harris manages to make his speeches at the outset work, but whenever another character opens their mouth to discuss issues of a more philosophical bent (like Rome being the mob or Crowe being a man we should honor) it just smacks of the ludicrous.  Scott and company, instead of subtly making an argument through all the tools available to them in the cinematic medium, simply have the characters come right out and make overt statements.  A much lighter touch is required.  It doesn't ruin the picture for me, but it irks me every time.  The pictures strengths (the music being a big one) obviously outweigh these relatively minor flaws, but they are precisely what holds it back from the kind of greatness Scott achieved earlier in his career with Alien and Blade Runner.  In this sense, the picture is a failure.  It certainly does entertain though.  It's one of those films I fell in love with when I was falling in love with film.

There is much to appreciate about this picture but at the same time there is much to castigate as well. What could have been a thoroughly involving story turns out to be crippled by a lean script, some very indecisive direction and choppy editing. Not to mention some bad casting in the form of Richard Harris as Marcus Aurelius, a role that cries out to have been the last role played by Anthony Quinn. The film starts out well and looks bleakly authentic in its depiction of the pivotal battle in the wars between the barbarian tribes of Germania and the Roman Empire. But as the story gives way to 40 minutes of exposition following Commodus and Lucilla's introduction, Ridley Scott seems to tack things on whenever the script runs into weak spots. This leaves the film without a flowing narrative and it seems to want to please a mindless summer movie action market while at the same time aspiring to be something deeper. What it leaves us with is a schizophrenic, unequivocal story full of contradictions. There seems to be an epidemic in the past three or four years - films like this, Titanic, The Patriot, Pearl Harbor, Enemy at the Gates etc, try hard to be great epic films but at their core they are very slight and even trivial. The story in Gladiator holds promise but what little conflict there is set up and thrown at us in the first hour, leaving just a linear resolution to unfold for the remainder. A shame because so many elements could have been introduced in this story to make it truly an awesome and thoughtful epic. I guess complex stories like Spartacus and Ben-Hur will never be made again. This one falls somewhere short, though better than Demitrius and the Gladiators and the film it heavily borrows its narrative structure from - The fall of the Roman Empire. Technically the CGI is at times seamless and other times poor. When our troop of Gladiators run into the coliseum for the first time however the effect is absolutely jaw dropping and the scene that follows certainly delivers the action goods. The acting is very good throughout except for Tomas Arana as Quintus (about as bad as John Dall in Spartacus) and the aforementioned Richard Harris.

Ridley Scott has re-created the past perfectly in this action-packed epic.
Gladiator takes place in the late Roman Empire and follows Maximus, a roman general who loses everything he loves and vows for revenge, but what makes this film brilliant is its connection to the after life, Elysium which makes this story not just about death but about a reunion with our heroes loved ones.
But its not just the story that keeps me immersed into the film, its the brilliant way Ridley has directed it, we see high-budget scenery and landscape, the coliseum at its peak, great action sequences, superb imagery presenting an accurate atmosphere, the epic music, by Hans Zimmer and the outstanding acting by Russel Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix.
A lot of people have said that historical epics are finished, they were good back in the old days, but nowadays it cant be pulled off, but Gladiator has done it, kicking 'Spartacus' in the ass.
I recommend this film, and rate it in my top 3.

Enjoyable action flick that takes itself a bit too seriously. Gladiator is a one of the better "epic" movies. The action scenes are shot really well, and you get the sense that you are right there in the coliseum with Maximus. You don't think for a second that you are watching a movie, everything feels natural in the coliseum.
However, the movie tends to drag a bit in the speaking parts. There are no shades of gray whatsoever in this film. Maximus = Good, Commodus = Bad. This lack of moral complexity makes the talking scenes drag a bit. You think to yourself "I know the Commodus is really evil, can I go back to watching Russell Crowe fight a ax wielding giant guy?" All in all, one of the better action films in recent years.

(Spoilers ahead.) Pretty good entertainment, but the historical inaccuracies are disturbing. For example emperor Commodus certainly didn't die at the arena of the Colosseum, so why would you want to see this happen in a film that is not supposed to be fantasy or alternative history? This is like having JFK killed in the Vietnam war.

Also the political message about the Senate of Rome being a democracy and Marcus Aurelius being in favour of democracy is totally false. Rome had never been a democracy, and Marcus Aurelius didn't want it to become a democracy, but the filmmakers would have us believe that Marcus Aurelius was a closet democrat who didn't want his own son to become his successor, and who appointed a general as his successor instead, and told this general to make Rome a democracy. This is an anachronism. Apparently this political message about democracy is meant to appeal to the American audience because a lot of Americans believe in the utterly insane theory that the form of government of the United States of America has its roots in ancient Greece and Rome.

Also the story of Marcus Aurelius's son Commodus arriving in Germania only after the war has already been won by general Maximus is not consistent with historical reality. Commodus actually spent years in the war in Germania side by side with his father.

The token black guy in the film is an African slave who is forced to become a gladiator. For a reason never explained to the viewer, this black African slave, a former hunter from maybe Sudan or Senegal, is able to have a conversation with the former Roman general Maximus immediately after Maximus has been captured by slave traders, even though sub-Saharan Africans certainly did not speak Latin. This magic black man also immediately heals the wounds of this former Roman soldier using some mysterious herbal medicine. This black man himself was a slave, so how come had some magical herbs with which to cure other slaves, and why would he give a damn about the lives of some other slaves? The Roman man was totally unknown to him. Why would a sub-Saharan African slave spend time and resources to cure some unknown ill person? Psychologically and culturally implausible.

Gladiator is a 2000 epic film. It is directed by Ridley Scott and stars Russell Crowe, Joaquin Phoenix, Connie Nielsen, Djimon Hounsou and Richard Harris. Crowe portrays General Maximus Decimus Meridius, friend of Emperor Marcus Aurelius, who is betrayed and murdered by his ambitious son, Commodus (Phoenix). Captured and enslaved along the outer fringes of the Roman empire, Maximus rises through the ranks of the gladiatorial arena to avenge the murder of his family and his Emperor.

The film won five Academy Awards in the 73rd Academy Awards ceremony, including the Academy Award for Best Picture. The film's epic scope and intense battle scenes, as well as the emotional core of its performances, received much praise. The film's success may have helped to revive the historical epic genre, with subsequent films such as Troy, Alexander, 300 and Scott's own Kingdom of Heaven.

Gladiator" definitely is a classic film as it combines a simple, but moving, story with beautiful scenery, filming, direction and score â it is truly a "complete" movie.

I am mostly compelled with the beautiful script which in a way reminds me of poetry, though it is still everyday language. I love the acting portrayed by the late Oliver Reed and also Richard Harris. Russell Crowe, Djimon Housou and Joaquin Phoenix are also superb and the parts suit them perfectly. There are also a number of less "popular" artists who also deserve a big "bravo". Amongst them I have to mention ex-Mr Universe Ralph Moeller who is mostly used as the comic relief of the movie. In Gladiator we can also the beautiful and popular Maltese TV Star and actress Ruth Frendo, who although has a small part, she is totally brilliant and outstanding.

Actually I got to IMDb while I was looking for her name on the internet, in fact on IMDb she has some very stunning photos. I was lucky to meet Ruth Frendo whilst she was filming in another Maltese production. Ruth Frendo is not only a gorgeous and talented actress but she is also amazingly intelligent and very down-to-earth. We will definitely be seeing more of her work in the future... 

The scenery used for "Gladiator" is brilliant â and the opening battle scene is definitely one of my top favorite scenes. The modern camera technique contrasts sharply to the brutality of the gladiators actions and blood shed during the movie; and I love the light contrasts thanks to the lenses which most definitely have been used to create a surreal feel to the entire movie.

"Gladiator" deserves all the awards and great reviews it has received, and for those of you who still haven't gone and watched it â I can assure you that it will be well worth your time and money. So go on and rent it now!

Watching this and then 'The Patriot' at the cinema with Ian Pickup made me realise how much I love the movies. This is faultlessly produced, brilliantly directed, and totally engrossing. The most involving films need a good 3 hours or so and 'Gladiator' makes you feel like you were there, surrounded by some great characters such as the late Oliver Reed and Richard Harris. Russell Crowe is no Mel Gibson but does an adequate job as the lead - revenge and injustice is always the best basis for a story. However, the film's heartbeat is the incredible performance from the then virtually unknown Joaquin Phoenix. His character is the most interesting - turning from a sympathetic wimp to a cruel incestuous murderer. Things like Djimon Hounsou's back story are all very Pickup - add to this a score from Hans Zimmer that is both epic and touching.

Hot off filming The Insider, Russell Crowe lost 40 lbs. of weight and built up his muscles to play thinking women's sex object Maximus, the Roman general turned gladiator, in Hollywood's first true Roman epic for over three decades. Exiled when his mentor, Caesar Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) dies and is succeeded by his power-hungry son, Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix), Maximus, now in exile, trains as a gladiator and swears his revenge - understandable when you consider that Commodus not only kicked Maximus out of the bosom of Rome and tried to kill him, but also had his family murdered.
As you would expect from director Ridley Scott, the movie is epic not only in scale but also in imagery, as the majesty that was Rome is re-created superbly on screen (much praise is due here to Scott's cinematographer, John Mathieson). But Scott doesn't lose sight of the human side of the story amid the computer trickery, brilliantly staged battle sequences, and spectacular sets, delivering a fascinating, grisly, and heroic tale. With skilled actors, most notably Crowe, a wonderfully preening Phoenix and, in his final role, Oliver Reed who sadly died during filming - his remaining scenes were generated using stand-in and computer-enhanced filmwork.

I'm a big fan of Ridley Scott. Let's just get that out there. No one is better at creating atmosphere, in that he has an uncanny ability to transport us to another place or time in a convincing way. Whether it is the future (Alien, Blade Runner) or the past, as in Gladiator, he can create such compelling visions of the time that you actually feel like you're there. Such talent is rare in film because it is either overdone, or simply looks ridiculous (i.e., CGI).
The reason Gladiator is such a great movie is because it combines Scott's trademark vision with a good story. Everyone likes a revenge story, and this film delivers. Poor Maximus is screwed over so badly that you can't wait for him to get his vengeance. How he does so is a bloody and at times humorous adventure, which doesn't fail to satisfy.
Russell Crowe is perfectly cast as "Rome's greatest general" and Joaquin Phoenix plays the role of his life as Commodus, the depraved, evil Emperor. Phoenix was so convincing in this role that I can't help but think of him as this character even when I see him in other movies.
While not entirely accurate in pure historical terms, Gladiator is the sort of movie that can get people interested in real history because it is so visually compelling - it makes you want to hop on Wikipedia and start learning about Rome. That's a good thing.
Gladiator gives you everything you want, action, adventure, emotion and perhaps a glimpse of Rome as it truly was at the height of its power. When good story, amazing acting and Ridley Scott's vision all come together right, you get Gladiator. When they don't, you get Kingdom of Heaven.  8/10

For a film that was void of any originality whatsoever, it was grossly overrated in terms of critical acclaim.  This film did nothing more copy a standard formula for making an epic - rotating camera angles, panoramic views of battlefields prior to engagements, close-ups of the main characters while in battle, and a larger than life but over the top protagonist.  Even the soundtrack sounded as if it could've been imported from just about any other movie that Hans Zimmer scored.
I'll be the first to admit that the cinematography was impressive, but that alone should not be sufficient for designating a film Best Picture (but of course the Academy disagrees, hence explaining Titanic's win over LA Confidential). After all, were the shots in Gladiator really better than those in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (another Best Pic nominee that same year)?
As for the acting, I still don't understand how Russell Crowe won Best Picture over Geoffrey Rush's role in Quills. Russell has had better roles in other films - The Insider, LA Confidential, A Beautiful Mind.  In terms of the whole cast, Traffic (another Best Pic contender that year) definitely had a better ensemble (as well as a superior screenplay) than Gladiator.
At the end of the day, Gladiator is a good film, but not extraordinary.  Considering some other films that were out that same year - Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon; Traffic; QUILLS - Gladiator wasn't even the best of the bunch.

8.2/10

Germania, 150 AD, the setting of Gladiator's opening scene. Far from the blazing sun and dazzlingly beauty of ancient Rome, Ridley Scott shoots the opening sequence in a subdued light. The Roman legions are nonetheless impeccably turned out as they face the comparatively disorganised rabble that inhabits this miserable environment. Caesar's soldiers seem somewhat misplaced here. However, Russell Crowe is at home in this environment of knee-deep mud and merciless snow. He commands the screen with all the virtues of his motto: ?Strength and Honour.'

The plot, with its hero-to-zero-to-hero nature, runs through Gladiator's every vein. As General Maximus, Russell Crowe is welcomed by Marcus Aurelius Caesar (Richard Harris) to take the Roman throne as Emperor of a new Republic. All does not run smoothly however as mislead heir to the throne Commodus (Phoenix) takes over Rome with ill-gotten domination, having dispatched his own Father. Maximus is cast out to find his family murdered and his Spanish farm burnt to the ground. Taken in as a slave by Proximo (Reed), Maximus becomes a Gladiator and starts his journey to the Coliseum and revenge against Commodus.

Scott's cast is powerful and he is not left wanting as powerful performances are delivered by all. Due to his untimely mid-production death, Oliver Reed is created in some scenes by the grace of computer graphics, which are as convincing as they come; sometimes making it difficult to differentiate between Reed himself and his computerised counterpart.

It is, however, the supporting actors who create many of Gladiator's best dialogue-based scenes. In an accomplished demonstration of her acting ability as Lucilla, Connie Nielsen saves the occasional scene as Joaquim Phoenix shows us that he can ?do evil', but is less convincing when it comes to the more emotional qualities of his role.

As a vehicle for the plot, Scott's beautifully created and highly symbolic (there is an image of fire in nearly every shot of the film) dialogue scenes are of a certain merit with digitally created backgrounds that encompass the meticulous nature of the Roman Empire. However, dialogue alone does not an epic movie make, and it is in the film's spectacular action sequences that Gladiator come into its own. Shot on location in Malta, Scott's first arena was built by an army of locals and commanded some 5000 extras (a large majority of whom were of a cardboard variety). All of this pales in comparison as we arrive in a digitally created Rome which makes some scenes in Ben Hur some somewhat small scale. The Coliseum is immense, both inside and out, and the computerised provides the electric atmosphere in which Crowe and his feline companions (four sizeable, and real, Bengal tigers) perform.

The battle sequences are perfectly choreographed and shot as iconic masks and typically Roman chariots are abundant in their power and imagery. As swords clash and heads roll, Ridley Scott is triumphant in the application of special effects technology and his directorial prowess.

Always one to embrace technology, Scott's views over Rome's landscape are reminiscent of the beautifully created cityscape of Blade Runner. This is a film that fears so little and boasts so much, even a lady archer being sliced clean in half by a spiked chariot wheel!

All those involved with Gladiator should be delighted and confident with their creation, for indeed this is a convincing and enthralling display with epic proportions to take the wind from James Cameron's titanic sails.

Gladiator is a masterpiece. If nothing else at  all (which of course, is not true), it has an amazing soundtrack,  and hardly relegated for the battle sequences. Not since the Lion  King has Hans Zimmer created such mastery of score to be combined  with a motion picture. If you do decide to purchase the soundtrack  one day, you'll be pleasantly surprised by the vast variety and  masterful blend of musical themes, leitmotifs, vocals, and  orchestral arrangements. So, on that side note I highly recommend  it.

Right. On to the movie.

First off, let's start with the characters. We have the hero, an  honorable soldier with an impeccable reputation, cast aside and  betrayed by the country he loved and fought for after the greedy  and murderous usurper Commodus assumes the throne of imperial  Rome. Upon escape from his captors and a wild dash across the  wilderness, he soon discovers that his family is dead. He  collapses under exhaustion, only to find that he has been  overtaken as a slave and a witness to the barbarity and incivility  of his countrymen he once held with the highest esteem.  Overwhelmed by the loss of his family, mortally humiliated in his  fall from grace, and the utter betrayal of his nation, he shows  very human even anti-heroic traits. Utterly disappointed by the  immoral values of the vulgar crowd, he rebels against the custom  of fighting in the arena for sport. Inspired by a chance to win  his freedom in the Roman colusseum, he wins the spirit of the  crowd, which he uses to vie against the depraved emperor Commodus.  He regains strength to continue fighting through the memory of his  father and his family in the hope to overthrow Commodus and  restore the republic and, ultimately, the ideal of the "dream that  was Rome". Hope in the afterlife and the continuity of valor into  eternity restored after befriending Juba are also interesting  themes that emerge every now and then, but are ever present.  Watching Maximus's character develop through the movie is an epic  story enough.

Commodus is truly a villain above all others. After his father  privately names Maximus to be his successor due to a judgment of  valor and moral character, Commodus murders him and eschews  Maximus as a traitor for failing to owe loyalty unto him (AND  murders his family too). Obsessed by his autistic pipe-dreams,  taken by his greed, and sulking in his insecurity, he destroys  Rome and her ideals little by little, although these measures  become more and more extreme (as he even ends up lusting his  sister XC ). Nevertheless, his impulsiveness and lack of rationale  keeps the audience glued to their seat, ever wondering what kind  of bizarre or maniacal scheme he's got up his sleeve to maintain  power and popularity.

Then you have the others. Lucilla, a woman once pampered as a  princess enters the hellish nightmare of being unable to mourn for  her murdered father and Maximus's murdered family. Under Commodus,  she cannot reveal her true emotions, compassion, or thoughts for  fear of the safety and well-being of herself, her innocent son,  and for the honor of the plot she undertakes with Maximus and  senator Gracchus, another man whose ideals run high with his  country. Thus, subtle hints of feminism and womanly strength are  made considerable themes in the movie, perfectly interwoven with  patriotism, democracy, and a fight against political corruption.  Proximo, the gladiator handler, comes to a suprising revelation  that the value of the freedom of a country and her well-being is  more important than the money received from mortal combat and even  his own life, for he was once a gladiator himself, and thus, can  understand what that freedom is like. Juba, as I mentioned before,  plays a small role, but an important one in helping the main  protagonist find himself, restore his hope about valor and the  afterlife.

Wow. I've been talking a lot. Sorry. XD

The utter variety of sets, scenes, and backgrounds can be  breathtaking in their best moments, and the action sequences keep  you on the edge of your seat and ultimately contribute to the  development of the story. Highlighted by the aforementioned score,  Gladiator is a visual masterpiece, and its special effects are  AMAZING. Even being only a 2000 flick, the limited CGI that  Gladiator does employ artistically and creatively completes the  movie, unlike more recent films of the same genre.

Of course, like all films based on history, there is a  considerable amount of history that is distorted. However, this is  compromised by the fact that a masterpiece of a story is created  as a result. The story itself borrows considerably from  Shakespeare's master works, yet its pronounced themes, combined  with superior acting, special effects, and originality truly make  Gladiator a fantastic cinematic experience; it single-handedly  restored vitality to the sword-and-sandal genre. It is one of the  few films out there that can truly engage the audience in a  culture and inspire others to learn more about Ancient Rome.

In short, if you haven't seen Gladiator, SEE IT.

The first of my series of reviews for "War Movies" is the classic Roman Empire film, Gladiator.  If you need an example of a movie that does it right from the beginning, then use this one.
 
Opening with an epic battle, the movie immediately grabs your attention by the throat and ignores your pleas for air.  Throughout the rest of the movie, the gladiator battles are just as epic, fresh and nail-biting.  One of the movie's fortes are the battles, and it couldn't be anymore beautiful - as well as graphic.  Ridley Scott does an excellent job at capturing the historical aspects of the gladiator battles and makes you feel just as barbaric as the audience, cheering for and demanding death.
 
The acting in the movie is also extremely impressive.  Russel Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix create the perfect hero and villian combination.  I found myself silently cheering for Crowe (although not a personal fan for the most part) and cursing at the flamboyant Phoenix.  Djimon Hounsou and Ralf Moeller are also personal favorites, creating the perfect partners for Crowe during battles.
 
Continuing with the excellence, I should mention the storyline of the movie.  A perfect "revenge" type plot with so much meat you could sink your teeth into.  It does an excellent job at building individual characters and allowing you to bond with them, as well as keeps a perfect balance of action and plot that guides the story along without dragging it out.  I can't recall a moment that "I was not entertained" (my attempt at playing off of Crowe's lines).  Additionally, it plays into Crowe's family loss, and creates some very touching moments that you can play off as your "dry contacts".  To wrap it all up, the orchestrated scores are perfect and so fitting.
 
Overall, this movie is one of my favorites.  A classic war movie, and a must see.

This is a modern classic, directed by the great Ridley Scott(Alien,,Blade Runner, Crowes performance is outstanding and proves his Alist Standing, Phoenix is certanly proving to be as good as any young actor of his generation, and his performance here is spellbinding. The heart-wrenching plot was amazing, and served to move and thrill the audience. The cinematography is great, and even the score was perfect. This film was more than deserving of the Best Picture Oscar of 2000.

The story is inspiring, and the protagonist Maximus (Crowe) is someone everyone can idolize. The opening scene is one of the best of all time. The epic battle scenes are well shot, and still hold high merits even against today's technology. The fight scenes in the Coliseum were breath-taking as well.

This is one of the most moving, inspirational scenes/quotes in cinema. It was perfect.

The late Richard Harris and Oliver Reed provide a strong supporting ensemble-cast, the opening battle with the barbarian hordes is all blood and thunder, while some may find the violence a little harrowing.

All in all, a classic that will be watched again and again.

When a dying Caesar (Richard Harris) dashes the imperial ambitions of his temperamental son (Joaquin Phoenix) by naming a popular general (Russell Crowe) as protector of the Republic, by-passing the would-be successor, the offended heir kills his own father and orders the general executed, in order to usurp the throne. Unbeknownst to all, the veteran warrior (Crowe) kills his executioners and escapes, only to be captured by slave traders who sell him to a ring of gladiators -- men whose lot in life is to fight to the death for the depraved entertainment of the masses. Early in the film, a seemingly unattainable carrot is dangled before the slaved gladiators: if they're really good and they catch the emperor in a good mood, he might reward them with their freedom. For Maximus (Crowe), the real incentive is a trip to Rome, and to the Colosseum, to confront the emperor who ordered his death. Este es un filme que probó nuevamente que cuando un género o un tipo de película ha funcionado, pueden volver a hacerlo. Ya que esta cinta claramente retoma el tipo de películas épicas sobre Roma, que fueron muy populares antes con ejemplos como "Quo Vadis", aquí simplemente evitan tocar temas religiosos y mantienen la trama más neutral enfocada al conflicto entre los personajes principales interpretados por Russell Crowe y Joaquin Phoenix, donde ambos realizan un gran trabajo representando sus roles. El filme es también memorable al presentar el penúltimo trabajo del gran actor Richard Harris y el último filme del también gran actor Oliver Reed, quien murió precisamente durante la filmación de éste. Y aunque el filme no toque temas de Cristianismo, es sin duda una gran opción moderna para ver en Semana Santa, ya que los tópicos de la vida del Imperio Romano siempre han estado presentes por igual en esas épocas del año. Un excelente filme dirigido por Ridley Scott y una acertada colaboración en la parte musical de la mezzo-soprano y también compositora Lisa Gerrard y el sólido Hans Zimmer. Una impresionante producción que muestra como las avances tecnológicos logran resurgir el tema de las cintas épicas de la era dorada de Hollywood pero en un contexto moderno.

Captured, Maximus is forced into slavery, where he is sold to Proximo, a former gladiator who serves as both mentor and slavemaster. Maximus trains as a gladiator in the arena, where his fame grows. He goes to Rome, intent on avenging the murder of his wife and son by killing the new emperor Commodus. On his dying day Marcus Aurelius, the Emperor of Rome, names valiant General Maximus as his successor, rather than his immoral son Commodus. Out of spite, Commodus murders his father & orders the death of Maximus as well. Fortunately he survives, but only to discover his wife and child dead. He becomes a slave gladiator, eventually making his way to the Coliseum in Rome as part of Commodus' 150 days of games. In an attempt to have his revenge, Maximus battles Commodus for his own survival as well as the love of the spectators of Rome so that he may carry out Marcus Aurelius' wish for a republic.

Direction from Ridley Scott, acting from Russel Crowe & Joaquin Phoenix & a score from Hans Zimmer. What more could you want from a grand action film? Probably an explanation as to what that means. We see brilliant character development in both our hero & villain, both portrayed brilliantly by Crowe & Phoenix. And Scott's excellent directing combined with the fine script allows us to watch our characters progress perfectly while still working alongside the story. The story which mixes violent & thrilling action with political intrigue and emotional performances. And the beautiful score from Hans Zimmer sets the mood instantly for every scene, whether it be a grisly match in the arena or a pleasant walk through the wheat fields. The film has good flow as well; each scene easily breezes into the next seamlessly and keeps the plot defined at all times. The set pieces combined with the direction and the score create a brilliant image of ancient Rome, only improving the experience. But of course, a film cannot be this great without having a few skeletons in the closet. The runtime is an astounding two-and-a-half hours. As fine as the quality is, you really can feel how the film goes on and on. Also, the complete obliteration of the history books. In reality, Commodus was a great leader to Rome. And while he was killed by a gladiator, it was not Maximus, and it was in the bath. Granted, it doesn't sound like much of an ending, but painting a veritable hero of Rome to be an absolute monster is a bit discrediting. These basic things are the only potholes in the films road to a perfect score. So I am giving "Gladiator" 9 thumbs up from the Emperor out of 10.

Looking back on Gladiator, it's clear that the achievement here isn't in special effects or world building, as the film certainly shows its age, nearly 16 years from when it was first released. The real achievement here is a worthy call back to the epics of Ben-Hur and others combined with a modern analysis of Roman politics that probes at some of the uncomfortable oddities of our own society. Gladiator feels almost too big to be real, successfully capturing the majesty of the games while also featuring some truly fantastic one-on-one scenes between Crowe, Phoenix, Neilsen and Harris, where their characters manage some of the most passionate and moving dialogue is recent film history. One of the other aspects of the film that often gets overlooked is its exceptional fight sequences, with the fight in Germania standing out particularly as one of the most realistic fight sequences since Spielberg changed the game with Saving Private Ryan. In retrospect, it seems a bit odd that Scott didn't receive Best Director for this film, considering just how well everything comes together here. Absolutely a must watch and clearly a classic for the genre as well as a mile marker for one of the greatest living directors.

With state-of-the-art digital technology, the Roman epic of director Ridley Scott brings us the return of the glorious city that was Rome. It had never shone so densely opulent; so outlandishly declining. On the verge of dying, Emperor Marcus Aurelius makes the decision to name Maximus, general of his army, his successor, with the hope that he will protect Rome and give back the power to the people. But his ambitious son, decided not to fulfill his father's will, will untie a chain of events that will change the future of the Roman Empire. Maximus will have to survive the jealous wrath of Commodus, the murder of his family and the infamy of being enslaved. But as a gladiator he will find a way to serve Rome and to fulfill the promise done to the late Marcus Aurelius. The epic cinema returned big. Reliving all the pomp and ceremony of old civilizations, Gladiator will dazzle you with extraordinary battles, realistic scenes of fight and admirable views of England, Malta, Italy and Morocco. Russell Crowe is a magnificent gladiator; a combination of brain, muscles and a noble soul, that places him in the same rank of Kirk Douglas's Spartacus or Charlton Heston's Ben Hur. His Maximus is a hero in all the extension of the word, virtuous, genuine, charismatic and very, very human. The rest of the cast is magnificent, from the selection of Joaquim Phoenix as the despicable Commodus, whose resentments and jealousy are concrete, to Richard Harris in its small but impressive Marcus Aurelius. Under the skillful direction of Ridley Scott -  who brings out the best from the script supported by a range of technological tools -  Gladiator succeeds finding a perfect balance between action and emotion. Its main center is in the characters and in a history that captures the importance of our actions. Their protagonists emit vitality, in the battlefield, in the bloody sand and mainly, they convince us that it's worth to live or die by the values and ideals we have inside.

I could not believe that trash like Gladiator won an Academy Award for best picture. It sort of reminds me of Braveheart winning an Oscar for Best Picture (1995). The film is an obvious history according to Hollywood with a mixing of personalities, inaccuracy, and lots of action. The film opens up in Germania where Roman Legions under the command of Maximus are due to battle the Germanic soldiers in the middle of the woods, possibly in Vindobona. Maximus (Russell Crowe) demonstrates his skills and courage in the battle so much that dying Emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) decides to make Maximus into the Roman instead of his son Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix). However, things go wrong when Commodus murder his dad in a weeping rage and has Maximus arrested and his family executed. Maximus manages to escape execution and journey on home to find it razed. He collapses and is then taken to fight for his life and the entertainment of people. Meanwhile, Commodus is not getting along with the senate and decides to put some games that will involve fighting for life and death, blood and carnage for the entertainment of the people. He does as he pleases despite the indifference and resentment from his sister Lucilla (Connie Nielsen).  During one the many games, a reenactment is performed for the battle or massacre of Carthage where Roman fighters are to fight and destroy their next victims. However, I guess one of the characters did not care much about history because he and the small band of fighter manage to kill their Roman adversary. When Commodus asks for the identification of the leader, he quickly says I am Gladiator which turns out to be Maximus. Who knew? Yes, this plot sounds very silly and trash, but the film Gladiator is actually really entertaining and thrilling with its intense and fast pace action. The gladiator fights are really brutal especially with Maximus vs. the undefeated champion Tigris. I was stunned by the action, cinematography, direction, and the music from Gladiator. Still, it is kind of hard to see that this film won an Academy Award for Best Picture which I am guessing there were not a lot of good films or the judges could not look away Croweâ(TM)s manliness. I found Maximus rather interesting as I am guessing his character is actually based upon a number of real people including Spartacus and Narcissus. Filmmakers could not decide who the better guy to be based on, so why not bring the whole package? Joaquin Phoenix is fantastic as the cowardice and cruel Commodus who has this creepy method of approach his sister Lucilla. There are some things that do have to be cleared up. If you have seen the movie, you know what the fate beholds on Commodus as he confidently and cockily fights Maximus. I guess he should have not skipped out on those fighting lessons and the war with the Germanic tribe. In reality, Commodus was actually killed by his personal trainer Narcissus. I imagine that Narcissus, dressed in 80s workout outfit, rubbing and massaging Commodusâ(TM)s in the bathtub right before dunked him in the water and holding him the until the bubbles stopped flowing. Okay, that does it! Good, you got it.

An absolutely beautiful film.  It has a certain melodrama that really works in the setting and story and doesn't seem cheesy or fake.  To start off, I'll mention how great the acting was.  Russell Crowe did an outstanding job as Maximus, the general who becomes a gladiator when he is enslaved after losing his family.  Phoenix does a great job as Commadus (excuse spelling), who manages to pull of a very convincing spoiled brat emperor with an evil vision of Rome.  There are too many other great performances to list.  The battle scenes are done extraordinarily well, my only complaint being the shakiness of the camera in the first fight scene.  Other than that, amazing.  The music...wow.  Best music I've ever heard in a movie, except for maybe the score from The Last Samurai.  Hans Zimmer did them both anyway, so hats off to him.  The plot is great and progresses at a fairly average pace that doesn't seem too overwhelming but not too boring either.  The violence is brutal but not overbearing.  It gets the job done.  Ridley Scott pulls his usual magic by putting together a true epic that is sure to last for many years to come.

One of my all time favorite movies.

Germania, 150 AD, the setting of Gladiator's opening scene. Far from the blazing sun and dazzlingly beauty of ancient Rome, Ridley Scott shoots the opening sequence in a subdued light. The Roman legions are nonetheless impeccably turned out as they face the comparatively disorganised rabble that inhabits this miserable environment. Caesar's soldiers seem somewhat misplaced here. However, Russell Crowe is at home in this environment of knee-deep mud and merciless snow. He commands the screen with all the virtues of his motto: ?Strength and Honour.'

The plot, with its hero-to-zero-to-hero nature, runs through Gladiator's every vein. As General Maximus, Russell Crowe is welcomed by Marcus Aurelius Caesar (Richard Harris) to take the Roman throne as Emperor of a new Republic. All does not run smoothly however as mislead heir to the throne Commodus (Phoenix) takes over Rome with ill-gotten domination, having dispatched his own Father. Maximus is cast out to find his family murdered and his Spanish farm burnt to the ground. Taken in as a slave by Proximo (Reed), Maximus becomes a Gladiator and starts his journey to the Coliseum and revenge against Commodus.

Scott's cast is powerful and he is not left wanting as powerful performances are delivered by all. Due to his untimely mid-production death, Oliver Reed is created in some scenes by the grace of computer graphics, which are as convincing as they come; sometimes making it difficult to differentiate between Reed himself and his computerised counterpart.

It is, however, the supporting actors who create many of Gladiator's best dialogue-based scenes. In an accomplished demonstration of her acting ability as Lucilla, Connie Nielsen saves the occasional scene as Joaquim Phoenix shows us that he can ?do evil', but is less convincing when it comes to the more emotional qualities of his role.

As a vehicle for the plot, Scott's beautifully created and highly symbolic (there is an image of fire in nearly every shot of the film) dialogue scenes are of a certain merit with digitally created backgrounds that encompass the meticulous nature of the Roman Empire. However, dialogue alone does not an epic movie make, and it is in the film's spectacular action sequences that Gladiator come into its own. Shot on location in Malta, Scott's first arena was built by an army of locals and commanded some 5000 extras (a large majority of whom were of a cardboard variety). All of this pales in comparison as we arrive in a digitally created Rome which makes some scenes in Ben Hur some somewhat small scale. The Coliseum is immense, both inside and out, and the computerised provides the electric atmosphere in which Crowe and his feline companions (four sizeable, and real, Bengal tigers) perform.

The battle sequences are perfectly choreographed and shot as iconic masks and typically Roman chariots are abundant in their power and imagery. As swords clash and heads roll, Ridley Scott is triumphant in the application of special effects technology and his directorial prowess.

Always one to embrace technology, Scott's views over Rome's landscape are reminiscent of the beautifully created cityscape of Blade Runner. This is a film that fears so little and boasts so much, even a lady archer being sliced clean in half by a spiked chariot wheel!

All those involved with Gladiator should be delighted and confident with their creation, for indeed this is a convincing and enthralling display with epic proportions to take the wind from James Cameron's titanic sails.

Almost ten years later, "Gladiator" is still the rousing, exciting, and powerful historical epic it was.  The film is first and foremost a crowd-pleaser.  Although Ridley Scott pays respect to the traditions of the Hollywood sword-and-sandal epics of the 1950s and 60s, he dirties his vision of the past, and moves the story along at the terrific pace of an action movie.  The action scenes are certainly some of the most influential of recent memory (after "Saving Private Ryan," of course), displaying shaky camerawork, fast cuts, manipulated sound effects and music, and distorted visual speeds.  We don't sit back and admire the battles and fights like dances; instead, we are thrust into the chaos of them.  As a result, the editing is used less to explain tactics and show movements, and more to convey the kinetic force and thrill/fear of combat.  Yes, the manner has been copied and made conventional, but it has never been done better than in "Gladiator," even by Ridley Scott.  Some complain about the murkiness of the cinematography, but I think the film is wonderfully lighted.  The shots are so atmospheric they're almost chiaroscuro, with smoky blues, rusty reds, pale greys, and golden browns.  All this said, the most outstanding part of "Gladiator" is Russell Crowe's General Maximus, for with Maximus, Crowe created the great manly warrior-hero of the decade.

Nell'anno 180 d.C., durante la guerra contro i Barbari in Germania, l'anziano imperatore romano Marco Aurelio decide di scegliere come proprio successore il valente generale Massimo Decimo Meridio anziché il proprio figlio Commodo; considerato inadatto al ruolo. Marco Aurelio vuole che Roma torni ad essere una repubblica e che quindi Massimo ristabilisca di nuovo il potere del senato, ovvero al popolo romano, come era prima dell'avvento dell'età imperiale. Venuto a conoscenza della scelta, Commodo uccide il padre. Massimo capisce che l'imperatore non è morto per cause naturali, ma è stato ucciso dal figlio, dunque rifiuta di sottomettersi a Commodo, che allora dà ordine di uccidere Massimo e la sua famiglia, dopodiché rientra a Roma come imperatore.

Massimo è condannato ad essere ucciso da un gruppo di pretoriani, ma riesce a uccidere i suoi ex sottoposti, e si dirige ferito verso la propria abitazione, perché convinto che l'imperatore voglia sterminare anche i suoi eredi. Quando Massimo arriva nei dintorni della sua villa, dopo un estenuante viaggio della durata di numerosi giorni verso il suo podere in Spagna, trova i campi incendiati, i servi e gli schiavi carbonizzati e la moglie e il figlio crocefissi.

Catturato da un mercante di schiavi e venduto a Proximo, ex combattente che gestisce un gruppo di gladiatori, Massimo giunge in Africa ed è costretto a combattere nell'arena, dando presto prova delle sue eccellenti qualità di guerriero; diventa così il gladiatore favorito di Proximo, che ne fa una vera e propria attrazione.

Quando Commodo ordina un periodo di grandi feste (150 giorni) a Roma in memoria del padre (ma soprattutto per ingraziarsi il popolo), Proximo porta al Colosseo i suoi gladiatori, compreso Massimo, che comincia a pregustare la sua vendetta. Grazie alla sua esperienza guida i propri compagni alla vittoria in un combattimento disperato e viene acclamato dalla folla. Commodo, che intanto ha scoperto la reale identità dell'Ispanico (come è chiamato Massimo da gladiatore), teme che possa diventare troppo famoso e quindi troppo amato dal popolo e cerca di fare in modo che venga ucciso nell'arena. Tutti i suoi piani però falliscono e la celebrità di Massimo aumenta.

Nel frattempo Lucilla, sorella di Commodo ed ex amante di Massimo, sta cospirando alle spalle dell'imperatore con alcuni membri del senato per detronizzarlo. Tenta di liberare Massimo perché guidi una rivolta contro Commodo, ma questi scopre il suo progetto, allora cattura i gladiatori di Proximo e Massimo per poi affrontarlo e sconfiggerlo nell'arena davanti al popolo di Roma.

Per essere certo della vittoria Commodo infligge a Massimo, incatenato, una grave ferita con un pugnale prima di affrontarlo. Massimo tuttavia con un'ultima sovrumana prova di coraggio e di forza ha la meglio sul crudele tiranno che viene ucciso. Però Massimo non riesce a sopravvivere a causa delle ferite riportate e ha una visione dei suoi cari che ora può raggiungere nei Campi Elisi, mentre, morente, non può diventare direttamente imperatore ma viene acclamato dalla folla come un vero e proprio "Dio di Roma" ed il suo corpo viene sepolto tra la commozione di tutti i Romani.[it.wikipedia.org]

First off I want to say this movie, was an outstanding epic, of Roman times and a mans fight for freedom, and justice.  

I personally believe however, Rusell Crowe's performance is immensely overrated, and the best performance of this movie definitely belonged to Joaquin Phoenix.  

Despite this however, the elements that made this movie great was the fact that in Roman times you really did have to fight your way out of your trap.

Crowe's character of Maximus, is a good man, who at first is fighting just so he can get home to his family, but once everything is taken away from him, he fights not for himself, but for the people he fought for, for many years.  

His unselfishness, and his integrity are what make Maximus a good person.  

I loved Joaquin Phoenix, as the power hungry, young and jealous emperor.  

The inner battle between the two is even better than any physical spoken battle they may have. While the Emprorer has everything in terms of material, he doesen't have the respect that Maximus has had, or regains in the eyes of the bloodthirsty spectators at the Roman Colesium.

He wants it all, and until Maximus is dead, he won't have what he wants.  

This is an amazing story of good and evil, and pure jealousy and hatred.

In Gladiator, Ridley Scott showed his world-creating genius once again: his portrait of the Roman Empire at its frenzied height is every bit as visionary as the sci-fi worlds he previously created in Alien and Blade Runner. Russell Crowe is the strong centerpiece of this vision - but the rest of the cast is equally excellent; their characters are rich and multi-dimensional. The costumes, arms and armor look plausible, down to their tiny details. The battles are brutal and breathtaking. The city of Rome itself feels alive - dirty, chaotic, gaudy, beautiful, massive, sweltering. And yes, the plot is exciting and holds the viewer's interest. My one complaint (and I realize I'm nit-picking here) is that the writers butchered Roman history in order to have a stunning climax on the floor of the Colosseum: the actual emperor Commodus outlived his sister Lucilla by ten years (he killed her, not the other way around), and his murder brought the brutal Severan dynasty to power - a return of the Republic was never in the cards! It seemed a shame to me that with everything in this film feeling so authentic (down to the smallest details), that something so "big" would be so blatantly incorrect. That said, it's still a great film - and still five stars.

In Gladiator, Ridley Scott showed his world-creating genius once again: his portrait of the Roman Empire at its frenzied height is every bit as visionary as the sci-fi worlds he previously created in Alien and Blade Runner. Russell Crowe is the strong centerpiece of this vision - but the rest of the cast is equally excellent; their characters are rich and multi-dimensional. The costumes, arms and armor look plausible, down to their tiny details. The battles are brutal and breathtaking. The city of Rome itself feels alive - dirty, chaotic, gaudy, beautiful, massive, sweltering. And yes, the plot is exciting and holds the viewer's interest. My one complaint (and I realize I'm nit-picking here) is that the writers butchered Roman history in order to have a stunning climax on the floor of the Colosseum: the actual emperor Commodus outlived his sister Lucilla by ten years (he killed her, not the other way around), and his murder brought the brutal Severan dynasty to power - a return of the Republic was never in the cards! It seemed a shame to me that with everything in this film feeling so authentic (down to the smallest details), that something so "big" would be so blatantly incorrect. That said, it's still a great film - and still five stars.

Ridley Scott's 2000 sword and sandals masterpiece is a visual feast as is the rich engaging plot curtesy of Scotts masterful storytelling. Like Titanic, upon release this was hailed as one of the greatest films of modern times, however after the 'best picture' awards had sunk in and time passed the old audience favourite (seemed to be as popular as shawshank redemption) left the film forgotten about.
The extended version, which I am reviewing adds 17 minutes of extra detail in creating the best Roman experience possible. The cinematography is beautiful and has not aged a day in 8 years, but what really sets this apart from other epics like Scott's own Kingdom Of Heaven are the characters. The cast is impeccable, with Phoenix playing a corrupted murderous and possibly insane incapable emperor of Rome pitted against Crowe his nemesis who has had to endure the aftermath of errors resulting in his families murders and his capture as a slave. The films underlying topic of vengeance is suitably subtle and the redemption that follows Crowe to the end is heart-warming and spectacular to watch. Gladiator deserves a second chance from a long abandoned audience as its epic scale is so masterfully handled by Ridley Scott who oversees a level of emotions played out by some very well written characters which mould with the storyline. Gladiator is certainly a memorable experience, and what an experience it is. It does not suffer some snuff script parts like Titanic and it is able to flow so well with some great dialogue, award winning acting and some memorable sequences. Now under-rated. I suggest you return to this remarkable film.

It's laughable all the time and ruins scenes most of the time; how he was nominated for an Academy Award for this is beyond me. I just wished the dramatic stakes had been higher.

A Roman general seeks revenge on the greedy and jealous Roman Emperor that killed his family and made him a slave and gladiator. Ridley Scott's majestic epic takes elements of the great classics like Ben-Hur and Spartacus and updates them for the modern audience, in what became a great success which resurrected the genre's popularity. Aided by a wonderful Hans Zimmer soundtrack, breathtaking photography and amazing performances by Russell Crowe and Joaquin Phoenix, this film is a much loved entertaining film as well as a masterpiece of the epic genre.
Good dramatic flair, some unforgetable(or almost) moments.

Ridley Scott creates some wonderful films, and Gladiator is perhaps one of his best. This is the story of betrayal and honor, corruption and defiance. Gladiator delivers on every level. As a historical drama (it's very loosely based on a true story) it's engrossing and features a beautifully constructed Ancient Rome. As an action film, it is full of heat-stopping moments. Any time Maximus heads into the arena, you're in for a treat. Ridley Scott has had a magnificent career, and it's incredible how he was able to innovate with the action scenes at such an advanced age. Phoenix, Djimon Hounsou and Connie Nielson all put in nice supporting performances, but this is Crowe's movie. When he yells to the crowd ?Are you not entertained?!?? just try and not get chills down your spine. He carries an obscene amount of emotional weight throughout the whole film, and you can't blame him. Avenging the brutal death of you family is an easy motivation to give your lead character, but it never puts Maximus's direction in doubt. He is singular in his mission and you have no doubt throughout the film that he will either avenge his family or die trying.

If you are in to action movies that contain intense, vivid battle scenes, then this is the movie for you. If you want to see a movie that is an informative, historical account of the past, then look elsewhere.

The first 45 minutes or so of the movie set up the death and subsequent succesion of Emperor Marcus Aurelius. After his son, Commodus, hastens Marcus Aurelius' death by strangling him, he orders for the execution of the top military general, Maximus (Crowe). After a predicted escape from his executioners, Maximus is picked up by a group of slave traders. Here he becomes enlisted among the gladiators. Meanwhile the hated Commodus returns to Rome to begin his tyranny. As expected, Maximus and Commodus eventually meet at a huge gladiatorial spectacle in Rome. The crowd loves Maximus, so Commodus is unable to have him killed. The movie ends as Maximus fights in order to avenge the death of the former emperor. This all takes 2:45 min. Most of that time is filled with action-packed fighting scenes. While the plot seems to slow down.

The first scene of the movie, a startling depiction of the Roman war machine, made the movie worth the $7. Although the movie didn't invest much time in expanding or developing the plot (maybe because the producers were more interested in making a movie that would appeal to the mass), it did allow one to experience what the world would have looked like in 2nd century Rome. For this I gave the movie a good rating. If you are going to see it, see it in a theatre where the special effects pull you into the movie.

As with so many "historical" films, [i]Gladiator[/i] has only a passing similarity to Roman history.  The character relationships are all wrong--Maximus, of course, didn't even exist.  The weaponry is half right.  The costumes are often of the wrong period.  The reign of Commodus was much longer than the perhaps year that the film seems to imply.  (After all, those gladitorial games in which Maximus competes are to honour Marcus Aurelius, killed at the beginning of the movie.)  Lucilla was exiled to Capri and murdered/executed.  In fact, while Commodus was indeed crazy in that special way of Roman emperors, he was in fact beloved of his people and the army.  Of course, he probably wasn't a very good leader, but he wouldn't have been the only Roman leader to have been accused of that, either.  But [i]Gladiator[/i] is an entertaining movie, even if it isn't Roman history at all.

It is 180.  The Roman legions are fighting the Germanic tribes.  Emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) is there, and the commander of the legions is General Maximus Decimus Meridius (Russell Crowe).  The Romans are victorious.  Marcus Aurelius tells Maximus that he is dying, and he asks Maximus to ensure the transfer of power to the Senate.  Marcus Aurelius's son, Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix), feels cheated out of his inheritance, so he kills his father and sends soldiers to kill both Maximus and his family.  For reasons that kind of don't matter, Maximus survives the attack well enough to return to his home in Spain and weep over the crucified corpses of his wife and son--and then, for reasons that further don't matter, he ends up as a slave and gladiator, which somehow poises him to overthrow the evil Commodus.

Let us, for a moment, ignore Russell Crowe.  I think he gets too much credit for this movie anyway.  Let us instead discuss the glorious Joaquin Phoenix.  His older brother, River, was a great actor, and we can never truly know what he was capable of.  But Joaquin has come out from behind that shadow nicely; I'm sure there are fans of his who don't even remember River.  And here, Joaquin truly shines.  He makes Commodus into a more tragic figure than the script would suggest.  He really loved and felt betrayed by his father, and it makes him afraid of being betrayed by others.  He wants everyone, including all of Rome, to love him, and he doesn't know how to handle it when they don't.  Indeed, as Phoenix plays him, Commodus clearly doesn't understand what love is in the first place.  He is not cold, exactly, but he is distant.  He is unsure of himself yet must project the authority of Rome.  It is a challenging role, and I think Phoenix actually enhances it.  Russell Crowe is just running around being surly and killing people; that's not as great a performance.

The movie is visually striking.  I've always been impressed by the use of colour and light, the blending of CGI and real film.  Indeed, I don't know where Oliver Reed isn't really there!  The subtle, not-quite-slow-motion of the film has spawned quite a lot of imitators and will doubtless inspire more, but I think it is done to great effect here.  The plot's a little uneven, and not all of the acting is up to the standard set by Phoenix, but it is a lovely movie.  Okay, and I could frankly do without the slow, lingering shots of over-bright, spurting blood.  I don't need to see the closeups of gladiatorial death.  I suspect they're there to bring in the male audience, but surely the plot itself was enough to have ensured that!  I mean, even without the graphic details, there's still a lot of slaughter.  Also Russell Crowe fighting tigers.

To be perfectly honest, I fell asleep halfway through it this time.  Still, I've seen it several times, so I didn't really miss much.  Oh, I kind of wish I'd seen the "bees" bit, but I did get to see Commodus informing us that he's vexed, and that's my favourite line in the picture.  Oh, and of course there was plenty of Djimon Hounsou.  In the year Charlize Theron became the first African to win an Academy Award (really; she's from South Africa originally), Hounsou was nominated as well.  Actually, I saw this in the theatre, originally, and I've seen it every once in a while since then.  I don't, however, tend to watch it on TV, because a film like this deserves the scope of letterboxing.  I'm so glad that widescreen has become the DVD standard.

I probably would have appreciated this movie faster had I been able to watch it in one sitting. I've been a bit busy recently. But a second viewing helped me appreciate it more. While the story may not have always been as epic as you'd think, it's still good enough to hold up as a good movie when you put the main power of the movie into focus: the cinematography, action, and general look of the movie. It's spectacular what they did. Just like Ridley Scott impressed us with the art direction of Alien back in 1979, he really makes this look like a true Roman cinematic epic. They couldn't have gotten a better director. That isn't to say the movie isn't without it's minor, but standing flaws. I usually love and defend long movies, but if someone who is usually uncomfortable sitting through relatively long movies complains about this one, they do have an excuse. Sometimes the movie focuses too much on the character drama(especially that of Joaquin Phoenix's Commodus, another issue I'll get to), in that they drag out scenes longer than they need to showing us every emotion that the characters are feeling, even when we already know enough. Sometimes this slows down the film's pace, hence longer running time. But there isn't much more than 5 minutes or so that the movie might be able to do without. One other small problem I had was Joaquin Phoenix as Commodus. The performance he gave off was overall very effective, and I couldn't imagine anyone else cast as him. But sometimes, going into my previous issue, his dialogue scenes are fleshed out a bit too much, and it also feels at times that with all of the crying and yelling it seems as if he's overacting. But I think that might just be a side-effect from young ambitious power-hungry villains these days. Overall this is definitely a masterpiece in modern cinema. It is very seldom that we get a period epic of this caliber. Kudos to Ridley Scott, Russel Crowe(amazing performance as Maximus!), and all of the other cast and crew members! R.I.P Richard Harris(Marcus Aurelius, and highly a underrated Dumbledore), and Oliver Reed(to whom the film is dedicated, as he died during filming) as Proximo. Now We Are Free(a great song from a great score by Hans Zimmer, and Lisa Gerrard, to whom I must also praise).

Most films require that the viewer identifies with the character to truly be engrossed with the film. If you can't feel something for the character, than the audience is lost.

Luckily, in Ridley Scott's case, Russel Crowe is so captivating and convincing as a general loved by his troops and as a slave loved by the people that the movie really works. Possibly one of the greatest actors today, Crowe carries this epic film on his very capable shoulders.

Not to say that he is the only reason this works. The supporting cast, most notably Connie Neilsen, buoy the film to new perspectives.

Jacquin Phoenix definitely captures the egotisitcal persona he should display, stealing every scene he's in. Phoenix will surely be put on the map with Gladiator.

But the real shining star in this film are the incredible action sequences which jolt the viewer right in with the opening sequences, as Maximus' true worth to the Roman Empire is displayed. Scott's camera work within these completed sequences takes a modern twist that really works for the gruesome scenes.

Crowe will now get the respect he deserves for this collosal performance. Gladiator makes the most of its 2 and a half hours, marking a triumphant comeback for the long forgotten epics of the classic days of film. ALL HAIL MAXIMUS!

Most films require that the viewer identifies with the character to truly be engrossed with the film. If you can't feel something for the character, than the audience is lost.

Luckily, in Ridley Scott's case, Russel Crowe is so captivating and convincing as a general loved by his troops and as a slave loved by the people that the movie really works. Possibly one of the greatest actors today, Crowe carries this epic film on his very capable shoulders.

Not to say that he is the only reason this works. The supporting cast, most notably Connie Neilsen, buoy the film to new perspectives.

Jacquin Phoenix definitely captures the egotisitcal persona he should display, stealing every scene he's in. Phoenix will surely be put on the map with Gladiator.

But the real shining star in this film are the incredible action sequences which jolt the viewer right in with the opening sequences, as Maximus' true worth to the Roman Empire is displayed. Scott's camera work within these completed sequences takes a modern twist that really works for the gruesome scenes.

Crowe will now get the respect he deserves for this collosal performance. Gladiator makes the most of its 2 and a half hours, marking a triumphant comeback for the long forgotten epics of the classic days of film. ALL HAIL MAXIMUS!

Although this film has many great actors it was Crowe and Connie
Nielsen who give it heart. Crowe's presence fills the auditorium and
convinces the audience important events are taking place. Crowe pulls
you to his side and you root for him almost from the start of the film.

This work is his finest from his appearance as the fierce but reluctant
general who was a farmer at heart to his work as the brilliant,
unstoppable gladiator warrior to the final scenes when he finally faces
the man he has cursed and vowed to kill. 

He defies an emperor. 

The Emperor is a yellow-livered, depraved poor excuse for a human being
but he is no pushover. He is a determined worm of a man who knows what
he wants and how to get it. He is ruthless in attaining his goals,
always wrong-headed but unrelenting in his pursuit of satisfying his
twisted desires.

The movie culminates in a life and death contest between the Crowe and
the emperor and at times the outcome seems in doubt.

The film was lush and stunning representation of Imperial Rome and the
action, both on the battlefield and in the colosseum, is both beautiful
and compelling. 

This movie contains almost no historical truths but this quickly
becomes a matter of who cares? "Gladiator" is story telling at its best
and whether the naysayers, and there are many, like it or not,
"Gladiator" is destined be a classic.

Connie Nielsen brings a strong and pure feminine energy to the film and
her final scene, while is almost melodramatic, will remain firmly
established in my mind as one of my favorite movie memories.

Could anyone have played the emperor better than Joaquin Phoenix?
Possibly but could anyone else have given us greater insight into the
twisted soul of the emperor? Could anyone else have allowed us to
actually feel compassion for the tortured psyche of the emperor? I
don't know but Phoenix did all that and gave us a portrayal of the
complex and human side of a bad man

Single-handedly reviving a long-lost genre -- the "sword-and-sandals epic" -- this exciting action picture boasts top-notch production values, creative and engaged (if occasionally ill-considered) direction from Ridley Scott, and -- at long last -- a star-making performance from Australian actor Russell Crowe. The chief appeal of Gladiator is its retro vibe, but some of Scott's artistic choices smack of a shallow attempt to stay modern, such as the hand-held camera and hitching, as well as ultra-focused images in the film's battle sequences, both inspired by Steven Spielberg's Saving Private Ryan (1998). The script by David Franzoni, rewritten by John Logan and William Nicholson (some of it during filming), is sometimes scattershot, foregoing character development as it forages too widely in search of sweep, thus providing doses of everything under the Italian sun: revenge, political intrigue, romance, action, and historical background. Though never delivering the emotional power an audience might crave, Gladiator is rescued by sharp editing, marvelous design and effects, and superb performances from Crowe, the briefly seen Richard Harris, and the impressively slick, fey, high-camp posturing of the lizard-like Joaquin Phoenix. The mix of traditional costumes and set design with the new development of computer-generated imagery produces some eye-popping visuals, especially the lingering overhead shots of the coliseum in Rome, one of the best uses to date of high-tech special effects. As a summer popcorn picture, Gladiator succeeds on most levels and provides some unabashed, old-fashioned entertainment. Similarities were noted by many critics to the earlier epic The Fall of the Roman Empire (1964) from director Anthony Mann, which features many of the same characters.

This is wonderful storytelling. The opening Battle Scene simply mesmerizes, showing the brutal nature of combat for Roman conquests. I went back to see the film again. The first time I didn't hear anything Crowe said before the battle. I was just too visually caught-up. The second time I listened very closely and caught the wise yet succinct line from Maximus "what we do in life... echoes in eternity." Awesome. A simple man v. an emperor. I just loved the resilience Maximus showed throughout the movie. I find in most movies, there is an irritatingly slow process where the character has to "find himself," not so with Gladiator. Maximus does what is needed.

I liked how there were only two or three issues within this film. One was the afterlife. Aspects of the afterlife are opened, but not overdone. Love of family is given sizable focus. I liked the theme of love of country that we see as well, although it may not be justly deserved, it is never questioned. The visual effects were amazing. It actually had me wanting to believe that's the way Rome actually looked in all it's glory. The battle of Carthage reenactment was really great. The ending is just hypnotic. Intentionally or unintentionally it was simply emotional. The music is wonderfully beautiful as if Maximus' family are telling him...you have arrived. Bottom line: magnificent. Visually and emotionally satisfying.

This movie hasn't aged well. I still consider Gladiator a good movie but it is really overrated like most Ridley Scott films. 

What I disliked:

The story: is a pretty average run of the mill revenge flick. We have seen this 10000 times. Poetic justice. We saw this coming for miles and miles.

The rebellion near the end of the film is so paper thin. I know Scott was trying to avoid a three hour run time but Maximus was a fricking general in the Roman army, his little skirmish was smashed in seconds. Why were the gladiators all willing to join him so suddenly? So blindly? This part of the film seemed so rushed. 

I wanted more arena fights!!!!!!!!!!!

The theme song sounds a lot like Pirates of the Caribbean, it's so annoying.  

What I liked:

The characters: Russell Crowe plays a convincing general, Joaquin Phoenix plays a convincing baddie, and Oliver Reed gives his last hoorah. I love how Maximus is loved by the people than Commodus is. 

The first Battle scene is probably one of my favorite battle scenes in film history. So epic. Beautiful. 

Dialogue is pretty solid: some memorable quotes from Maximus and Richard Harris.  

This film is good but it's not epically good as it should have been.

I've seen parts of Gladiator before, but this is the first time I think I watched it from start to finish. I can see the inspiring story that so many people love, because it is a classic tale of one man against an evil empire. Also they do a superb job of creating serious emotional stakes in the film with the death of family members and also attempted murder. In fact there is a lot to love in this movie, especially the fight sequences which are bloody and exciting. They use some quick-cutting techniques that would ordinarily annoy me, but I felt the film did a good job of making it clear what exactly was happening at all times. There's really only 3 things that hold me back from completely embracing this film as a favorite, but they annoy me so much that I don't even feel the need to watch it again:

1. Certain scenes get quite repetitive. I feel they could have trimmed a decent amount of time out of the movie if they didn't include quite so many scenes of people meeting in secret multiple times, or Commodus being creepy with Lucilla again and again. I think you can frequently tell where things are going in Gladiator, and if it got there quickly it wouldn't be bad, but it drags at times so I find myself saying "Get on with it!"

2. The end of the film feels utterly contrived, as if it comes out of nowhere. **SPOILERS** Commodus suddenly choosing to step into the arena (even after weakening Maximus) is strictly there because they dug such a deep hole for Maximus that they had to invent a way for him to get at Commodus. The ending would have actually been more dramatic and effective if his escape plan and assault on Rome had worked. The ending is so completely out of step with the plot in the rest of the film I just start to laugh at its ridiculousness.

3. Last but not least, Russell Crowe is the lead. I don't have much experience with Crowe's movies, so I'll give him the benefit of the doubt and assume he actually can act, but I have yet to see it proven. He makes some dramatic facial expressions, but every single line delivery is completely without any emotion. I swear that the only difference between his lines when talking intimately with Lucilla, and his lines when shouting to his soldiers, is volume. I should be choked up at the end, and even more importantly every time he mentions his wife and son, but instead his cold emotionless performance rubs off on me.

Gladiator is not a terrible film, and I know why people are very passionate about it. I actually enjoyed it more than I expected, but because of these few flaws I wouldn't recommend it to others.

The slave who became a Gladiator.

The Gladiator who defied an Emperor.

A striking story ..."

So reads part of the script, with that particular line spoken by Joaquin Phoenix's Emperor Commodus towards the end of the film, and with (most of) it being used as part of the advertising for the film, with Russell Crowe as that General/Slave/Gladiator.  This was also Oliver Reed's last film, passing away during the shooting of it which led to some scenes being re-worked and others having him digitally inserted into the proceedings.
