"Strength and Honor"

#2 in my Top 13 list.  This movie starts off with a moment of peace before the storm.  The opening battle sequence was fantastic.  The massive pan across the broiling battle field full of Romans and the Germanic tribe they were pitted against, is breathtaking.

Then the depths of villany portrayed by Phoenix rose Commodus to brilliant levels of evil.  Subtle, and not so subtle.  Who did not cower when he shrieks "Am I not merciful!?"

With the Collesium as the backdrop for political power plays, slimey politicians, noble warriors and all the rest this is truely one of Scott's masterpieces.  Crowe brings equal passion to his deeply scarred Maximus as does Nielson to Lucilla.

The struggle of not one man, but many to bring this story to it's climax is well composed and executed.  From the wailing charioteers, the booming announcer, and the lumbering gladiators this movie doesn't lack anything.

Only complaint, again a small editorial glitch where there are arrows at the feet of the enemy in the opening battle, before the Romans ever fire.  A small mistake in an otherwise fantastic movie.  The dialog is well written from Maximus' speeches, Commodus' whingings, to Proximos rasp of "Shadows and dust..."

Well worth the 2.5 hours of viewing time.  Like Braveheart, this movie looks incredible on blu-ray.  Colors and sounds leap back to life like being in the theater again.

A sign of things to come for a very weak decade in movies.

Another film that benefits from all its academy glory due to a very weak year in film.  Of films in similar genres Crouching Tiger was a vastly superior and enjoyable film to this.  
As a film that is about a Roman gladiator you would think that the Coliseum battle sequences would get better as the movie progresses, however I found the exact opposite to happen, the first battle sequence is the best and at the end I really could care less.  The major reason for this and the problem throughout the whole film is because of the weak villain Commodus portrayed by Joaquin Phoenix.  Weather by direction or by his interpretation I found the Commodus role the pivot point that made me question the whole movie.  Granted I know of the questionable character of some of Romes inglorious leaders, like Nero, but they had qualities that made them likable, in Commodus their is no likable quality and the movie quickly fell apart once you realize this.
A film that started out strong, like a fire, but at the end was nothing more than a dying ember.

While I do not believe it should have won the Academy Award for Best Picture, per se, it did entertain me in the fact that it was one of the first historical epics to get some of the history right, even if that meant having to create an entirely new history in order to show the world the violence of the Roman Empire. The acting was decent (I'm confused about Joaquin Phoenix's Commodus - he's both hammy and delightfully sly), the scriptwriting isn't as bad as Roger Ebert wants us to believe (after all, some of his favorite films present depression as atmosphere), and I particularly liked the visuals near the end - it made the film seem like it was the ancient Blade Runner. Then again, that's just that: the film is sort of a re-hash of Blade Runner for history nuts.

It was a time unparalleled in human history. One of the great Empires of modern civilization ruled much of the globe, and despite a landscape littered with primitive technology and a knowledge base far less impressive than that of today, the same ideas, emotions, deceptions, loves, and hates influenced every decision, every waking hour, every breath, every moment of life and, ultimately, death. With such lesser knowledge and lesser understanding came heightened dangers for those less fortunate than others; it was a place where the well-to-do preyed on the weak and saw fit to buy and sell them not only for labor but for pleasure. Assembled from all corners of the Empire came the Gladiators -- often those of a "lesser" heritage, the poor, or even fallen heros -- men tasked with fighting to the death not for God, country, honor, or love, but for the enjoyment of others and the hope of seeing another day. It was a time when sport took on a life-and-death importance for the competitors. A time before contracts, memorabilia, product endorsements, and statistics on the back of trading cards, these athletes were bought and sold and fought and died unceremoniously, painfully, and with no remorse from those that would profit from their demise either financially or emotionally through the rush of the sport and the excitement of the kill. As witnessed in Ridley Scott's Oscar-winning epic Gladiator, it was brutal, bloody, unforgiving -- and the stuff of legend.

In the year 180 A.D., the Roman Empire is winding down a war with the stubborn Barbarian Tribes of Germania. Leading the final assault and capping another victory for the Empire was General Maximus Decimus Meridius (Russell Crowe, State of Play). He's proven his valor in battle yet again and is hailed as the Rome's finest general. His prowess on the battlefield and his humbleness off of it has earned him the respect of Rome's Emperor, Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris). In fact, an ailing Aurelius, who loves Maximus as a son, begs of him one final assignment before the hero returns home to live the simple life with his wife and son he so craves: to serve the Empire as the protector of Rome, rid her of the corruption that has begun even influencing his son, Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix, Signs), and prevent the Empire's inevitable decay. Maximus declines, his humble rejection sited by Aurelius as the reason why the General is exactly what the Empire needs to not only survive, but once again thrive. Commodus receives word of his father's decision to turn the Empire over to Maximus. In a jealous rage, the power-hungry Commodus murders his father and, before his father's wishes can be known, he declares himself heir to the throne and orders the execution of not only Maximus, but of his innocent wife and son. Sent to die a dishonorable death, Maximus barely escapes with his life but returns home to find his wife and son murdered. Giving up on life, Maximus collapses but later awakens as part of a slave caravan. He's sold to a former Gladiator named Proximo (Oliver Reed), and despite Maximus' initial refusal to demonstrate his skills as a fighter, his abilities become well-known once he's forced to defend himself from sharpened blades in the hands of determined foes inside the ring. Winning match after match, Maximus becomes a folk hero known as "The Spaniard," vanquishing his every foe with ease. When Commodus expresses a desire to meet the people's champion, he becomes visibly shaken as he learns the Gladiator's true identity and his ravenous thirst for revenge. 

Gladiator is a good old-fashioned tale of revenge framed in a hard-hitting and grisly Action picture that took the 2001 Academy Awards by storm, ending the evening with five wins, one each for Best Costume Design, Best Visual Effects, Best Sound, Best Actor (Russell Crowe), and Best Picture of the year. Certainly a worthy nominee, Gladiator found itself at the top of the heap in a year with minimal competition; certainly there was no movie in the same class as The Godfather or No Country for Old Men for it to contend with, though Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon did make for a formidable and deserving-of-the-award entrant. Gladiator hearkens back to several other sword-and-sandal pictures, chief among them Stanley Kubrick's Spartacus. Of course, the two films vary widely in style. Though both epics in terms of scope and runtime, Gladiator plays out with a frenetic visual pace that's more akin to Scott's Oscar-worthy follow-up Black Hawk Down than it is the masterpieces that defined the earlier part of his career, namely the slow and deliberate but nevertheless extremely effective Alien and Blade Runner. Gladiator's frenzied style sometimes hinders the film's innate beauty and storytelling abilities, and it often feels like the strong thematic elements are in competition with, rather than expertly integrated into, the action. Nevertheless, Gladiator works on several levels, chief among them as an epic Action piece with memorable characters and several top-notch performances that overcome the visual style and solidify the emotional core. 

Indeed, Gladiator's best attribute is Russell Crowe. Coming off a pair of strong performances in L.A. Confidential and The Insider (for which he earned his first of three Best Actor nominations), he shows another gear here, himself splendidly mixing action with emotion, even if the film as a whole seems to have a bit of trouble in doing so. His effort is sincere; the sense of loss is palpable, his humbleness at his accomplishments on the battlefield genuine, and his thirst for revenge driven by good intentions and a sense of honor that makes him easy to cheer for. Also delivering outstanding performances are actors Richard Harris and the late Oliver Reed, who passed away during the shoot. Harris' effort as Aurelius nearly matches Crowe's for depth and the palpable sense of honesty and goodwill that his character emotes with every line. The few scenes the two share together easily represent the best dramatic elements to be found in the picture, and there's a chemistry that's brought on by the well-scripted love for country and deeply-rooted respect for one another that the actors embrace wholeheartedly and capture effortlessly. Reed's effort, too, impresses, and his character represents perhaps the most interesting throughout the picture, providing him the opportunity to channel a broad range of emotion as he comes to be involved in Maximus' life. Also delivering solid efforts are Joaquin Phoenix, Connie Nielsen as Commodus' sister Lucilla, and Djimon Hounsou (Blood Diamond) as Maximus' fellow Gladiator, Juba. Director Ridley Scott certainly gets the most out of his actors, and while Gladiator's script isn't quite as deep, meaningful, and emotional as Braveheart's, it withstands the test of time and provides to its characters and, by extension, the actors that portray them, the opportunity to show some depth and range across a broad spectrum that proves to be the film's main attraction.

Another rare movie that I can watch over and over and never get tired of; Gladiator is an outstanding period piece and actioner.  It's not Russell Crowe's best performance, but he is very good nonetheless.  The movie ironically may belong to Joaquin Phoenix as the power-hungry Caesar Commodus.  There's a lot of emotion and anger behind his performance, and he makes a superb paranoid villain.  I also really liked Richard Harris' short stint as Marcus Aurelius.

The battle sequences are top-notch, production-wise, and quite bloody.  They really are companion pieces to the overarching story of Commodus' power-grab and attempts to tighten his grip on a population (and his sister) that detests him and finds a hero in the framed and disgraced Maximus (Crowe).  It was wise of Ridley Scott to place the battle scenes where he did, because most audiences would find it difficult to sit through the political machinations and side stories going on throughout the movie (I'm not one of those, but we all know the vast majority of movie-goers have the attention spans of hamsters).  

Gladiator has the same Oscar blueprints of Braveheart before it (bloody action and war, political maneuvering, loss of family, double-crosses, men desperately clinging to their power) but with better overall acting and more than a couple of compelling characters.  If Braveheart could win based on its own merits, Gladiator fully deserved to win so many Oscars.  You'd be hard-pressed to find much wrong with Gladiator as a near-perfect action movie because there's an actual plot to go along with the bloody-mayhem.

In all honesty, all "Gladiator" ever becomes is a story of revenge.  It's not making any grand statements.  Republics belong to the people.  Emperors are bad.  That's no brainer stuff.  But the film works because it doesn't bog itself down with messages or morality.

Maximus (Russell Crowe) is a natural leader who is unfairly persecuted.  It is his drive to right the wrongs that drives him and the film forward.  Since he lives in a world where entertainment is centered around bloodshed, the drama arises in his ability to really overturn an empire.  It sounds improbable and unbelievable and farfetched, but Ridley Scott tells the story so convincingly that you can't help but buy into it.

The film is not without flaws.  Joaquin Phoenix plays Commodus as a whiny and unthreatening ruler; someone who is bound to be murdered, if not by Maximus, then by the people of Rome.  Some of Maximus' heroics and speeches are hoaky, but overall I think "Gladiator" succeeds in telling this epic story of revenge.

'shadows and dust maximus; shadows and dust' that is what the late actor oliver reed tells russell crowe, who plays maximus, as he is about to enter the arena. this is the premise that the film 'gladiator' is trying to explain. it succeeds only mildly i suppose. the first impression i got after the 2.5 hours passed and the film was over was that i felt nothing dramatically. the spectacle of the film is convincing enough to carry you through the 2.5 hours but what else can you speak to. 

firstly let me start off the with the atmosphere of the film. films such as this, which are set thousands of years ago, depend hugely on how well they capture the essence of the time. well gladiator succeeds mildly and this is due to the visceral set pieces that take place within the rings where the gladiators compete. it is a place where little emotion is present and everyone is in the battle to stay alive; you are essentially a slave whose only legitimate means of freedom is to become a champion for once the people love you who can be against you. the helplessness of those not equipped to fight is conveyed in a early scene where a man wets his pants obviously thinking of what to expect when about to engage in a battle for his survival; he is mercifully the first to be murdered when he actually enters the ring. the colosseum itself which is the main attraction of the film is announced in true spectacle which sums up the film. this was the glory of rome; when the people were in fellowship it was to see bloodshed and watch men piss their pants. when you first see the colosseum it is announced in true fanfare: there is a strong headwind that keeps the flags alert, the sonorous notes of the trumpets are carried along that wind, the birds also make their ascent due to surprise at the clarion call of the trumpets. we are allowed to bask in the gladiators awe of this spectacle. that scene could have made or broke the film but it succeeds for even maximus is in awe because although he is a general of rome he is a spaniard and it does not seem that he has ever been at the centre of rome it self too often. the colosseum it self is presented as the centre of rome and therefore the film. this is essential because previous films (spartacus, Ben hur) that dealt on the subject of rome chose only t highlight  the city in all its splendour; they chose to highlight rome as the true centre of western civilization with all its bright lights and fanfare(much the same that america is doing). in 'gladiator' the filmamkers want to show that the brutality of the colosseum was the tru centre and the implications of this are that rome, whatever the period, is here represented as a nation built upon decadence and barbaric tendencies. one of the most poignant scenes of the film takes place at the beginning between marcus aurelius, the out going emperor, and maximus who has just won his campaign against the barbarians. marcus says, in my own summation, that rome is rotten whereas maxumus states that he has seen the cold and brutal world and rome is the light. this is still all imagery and maximus is to discover that marcus was right: rome is rotten. so his journey to the colosseum is highlighted by this imagery. certainly at the beginning there are a lot of dark shades to emphasise how the romans saw the world as being dark but by the time you reach the colosseum not even the bright splendour of rome can hide the darkness of its soul. this is the idea i am getting from the film. most scenes in the film seem to be taken straight from a painting for instance the scene where joaquin phoenix discovers that his sister has betrayed him. this is why the dialogue that highlight human interactions was not so convincing in the film because the film was trying to explain the civilization of rome as decadent and the best way to do it was through the eyes of a gladiator who once shared in its glories. this is why some people will not feel any emotional tug at their heart strings. you have to watch the film as a spectacle that was trying to convey, through imagery and dialogue,  the essence of rome. maximus is not the centre of the film, it is rome. that is the only way you will appreciate it.

the story itself basially goes through the motions. it is chanelled through abstracts. one man is evil the other is good; there is the supportive female and other friends that help the good man on his journey to exact revenge on the evil commodus. the duel between maximus and commodus takes place as if it were between two men trying to conquer each other in a bar fight. lets be honest which emperor is going to take the field in a colosseum so as to watch himself be murdered before his people. that is lame. most of the characters basically go through the motions. commodus is simply a spoilt child whose actions make him do evil things, his sister does not like his spoilt ways, maximus is a man who has to reclaim his dignity after he escapes an act of execution where he is the subject and his wife and son are murdered by commodus's praetorians. his tale is a simple one of revenge. he gets to see them when he dies and goes to heaven..boohoo. there are also the scheming senators who also want to bring down commodus and institute maximus as their ruler after all he defied the emperor as a simple gladiator why not have him rule. i am not sure they were aware of the plans of marcus aurelius and we are not sure if maximus would be a better ruler than commodus ( i dont think you could tell that he would be a great leader simply becaue the people chanted 'maximus, maximus' in one extended scene). i am not sure if the filmmakers were aware of this but he had to die because i hope for the love of god that they were not trying to promote that with maximus as emperor rome would suddenly be a great haven of prosperity. the only way to appreciate this part of the story is to see it as an extension of rome itself. try and see it as an extension of its politics. please dont try and sympathize with any of these schemers. why? well they were using maximus to achieve their goals. i am sure that only the girl knew maximus as the great general that he was i guess you can still care for maximus because he died a gladiator. you wil always be going back to that conversation between marcus aurelius and maximus in the beginning because it is the best and the most insightful in the filmwhen concerned with the machinations of rome. the rest of the film simply tries to flesh out that original conversation and it does not do that particularly well since most of the characters are not able to effectively translate the abstraction of roman politics disussed betweeen marcus and maximus at the beginning. that is what denied the film its greatness. 

the best interactions in the film take place between those not involved in the scheming but are nevertheless drawn into it because the film or hollywood dictates it. these interactions take place between maximus and djimon honsou and the late oliver reed. these interactions for me, apart from the discussions between maximus and the outgoing emperor which were dealing with all the abstractions that the film was trying to flesh out, were the most satisfying emotionally. when maximus and djimon honsou can speak of their lost families and if they will ever see them again it gives the film a certain gravitas that is not allowed to develop because of the schemers. the discussions between maximus and the late oliver reed are also poignant because reed is aware that he is a little man, although he is in charge of all these gladiators, when it comes to the affairs of rome (and the schemers). 'shadows and dust'. 

therefore the film was denied greatness because it never fleshed out effectively, through the characters, the abstraction that was ROME. however it does convey effectively through imagery  what ROME represented and that was what saved the film from falling flat. the imagery of rome that we were used to, prior, was shattered by this film and i recommend it for this only. in the end it is a poetic film; a film trying to come to terms with the empire that inspired it. try and see it as a spectacle, a fable and a dream. dont try and sympathize too much with the characters. 'shadows and dust' all that was left was the glory of ROME: the colosseum.

If there were to be any movie that took history and mixed it with some of the best action you can get in films, Gladiator would be the one. Directed by Ridley Scott, Gladiator is a simple tale stretched to a long and action-packed epic. The story seems simple and has been done before many times, but Gladiator is a payoff for that kind of story. What we, as the audience, see in this movie is the redemption and justice coming from a mile away. The film opens with an all-out war and for the first 10 minutes we can't even decifer what everyone is fighting about. Alas, that scene alone sets the mood of the movie. It lets us know its's not "going" for originality, or for something totally new. Revenge is a theme often used too many times in old mythological movies like this, but here it is an exception. Gladiator goes back to the old roots of movies such as Ben-Hur, or The Ten Commandments. A long story, famous actors, a wonderful score and an all-out battle of Good vs. Evil in the conslusion. Now, of course those movies were all Oscar-worthy and considered milestones for their time. I say this movie is just as good. By homage-ing and even taking after those old films it reinvents the genre in film known as, "epic." With dazling special effects, a good story and great actors, Gladiator is sure to be remembered and honored just as it's predesecors did. One of the common misconceptions I've heard about this picture, is it's accuracy. While it is a well made movie with splendid sets and cinematography, we all know it isn't entirely true to the old Rome civiilazion. But here's a thought: If this movie were TRYING to be so damn accurate, wouldn't they be speaking Latin? Or have foreign actors? Which is why Gladiator falls under the category of Big-budget blockbuster that just happened to be good enough to earn some Oscars. Of course, those 5 Oscars were all WELL deserved. Like I said before, the acting is great, even if Russell Crowe hardly speaks. But if you watch the movie, you'll find that that IS his character. A big, tough, sad, pissed of brute. The same goes for whiny Joaquin Phoenix's character. You hate him for being such a prissy snob of an Empero, but don't realize how much your becoming wrapped up in the movie. Oliver Reed I felt stole the show, even if most of his scenes were CGIâ(TM)d in, he still had one hell of an onscreen presence. The same goes for Richard Harris. As far as the pacing goes, I'd say pretty well. It feels more like an action movie then an epic which, again, is probably what those old movies(like Ben-Hur), were going for if only they had the right speical effects. Gladiator is a "patient" action film. Spewing out blood and gore left and right while still showing us a compelling story. A cliche one, but a compelling one at that. A film like this falls on par with such movies nowadays as "The Patriot," or "Pirates of the Carribean." It's great entertainment, but not the most original. But again, Gladiator is the exception becuase of it's shout-out to all those old epic classics that we all love.

"My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius, commander of the Armies of the North, General of the Felix Legions, loyal servant to the true emperor, Marcus Aurelius. Father to a murdered son, husband to a murdered wife. And I will have my vengeance, in this life or the next."



The general who became a slave. The slave who became a gladiator. The movie that is a masterpiece. In 180 A.D. General Maximus Decmimus Meridius has recently led the Roman Army to a victory over the barbarians of Germania. He is Emperor Marcus Aurelius' favourite soldier of the empire and he names the general 'Keeper of Rome' and will be given temporary leadership of the Roman Empire. Aurelius' believes his son, Commodus, will understand his decision but his son has other ideas. When Commodus learns Maximus will be made temporary leader of Rome, he suffocates his father to death as an act of revenge. Commodus then orders Maximus and his family to be executed. Maximus escapes execution but he does not make it back home in time to save the lives of his wife and son. After Maximus collapses at the sight of his dead loved ones, he is captured and taken to North Africa where he is enslaved and is forced to fight in gladiatorial games. His slavemaster, Antonius Proximo, sees how Maximus is able or organize fellow slaves into fighting as a cohesive unit and destroy any challenge. Maximus himself is undefeatable and Proximo decides to take the man to Rome to fight in the Roman Coliseum. Is in this gladiatorial arena where Maximus rises in rank, wins the favor of the crowds, and defies Emperor Commodus and inches each day closer to avenging his family as the gladiator. Just as how director Ridley Scott gave us gripping vision of the future in the science fiction classic Blade Runner, Scott here gives us an incredible story of a gladiator who became more powerful than the Emperor of Rome in ancient times. Gladiator is one of the most acclaimed epics of all time and is one of the many masterpieces of cinema Ridley Scott has delivered. Scott's aim with gladiator was both to craft a spectacular film and revive the swords and sandals epic; a genre which had not proved to be a decent crowd puller since Spartacus (1960) and The Fall and the Rise of the Roman Empire (1964). Gladiator deserves every amount of critical acclaim it has received over the years. It had a budget of $103 million and grossed $457,640,427 worldwide at the box office. It also won five Academy Awards which included Best Picture, Best Actor (Russell Crowe), Best Costume Design, Best Visual Effects, and Best Sound. It also received nominations for Best Supporting Actor for Joaquin Phoenix and Best Director for Ridley Scott. Delivering one of the best, if not the best performance of 2000 is Russell Crowe as the general turned slave turned gladiator, Maximus Decimus Meridius. He is of Hispano-Roman decent who is at the beginning of the film, unleashing hell in Germania. He is favored greatly by Emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris) who in a way wishes Maximus was the son he had. The son he does have is Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix), a vain and power hungry man who never proved to his father that he was fit for the throne. Commodus murders his own father, orders an assassination for Maximus and his family, and he also desires his own sister, Lucilla (Connie Nielson). Lucilla is a widow who seems to have had a desire for Maximus in the past and she has a son named Lucius Verus (Spencer Treat Clark). Maximus survives being executed and it is because of Antonius Proximo (Oliver Reed), a former gladiator himself, that Maximus joins the gladiatorial arena and makes his way to Rome to avenge his family. Each of the actors here really deliver their roles believably with each emotion. Phoenix plays his role excellently as the jealous, lazy, and sociopathic Commodus. Russell Crowe is without a doubt the highlight of the film and he completely makes a brutal gladiator a character for the audience to care for and believe in. The cinematography is excellent and you feel as if you have truly gone back in time to ancient Rome. The look of the Roman Coliseum is believable and people have finally got a true image of what the Coliseum must have looked like in its prime. The film uses both hand crafted sets and CGI for the landscape of Rome. Filming took place in four countries over a four month shoot. CGI was stealthily used to reanimate the late Oliver Reed (Proximo) who died during filming. The fight sequences are choreographed very well to deliver rousing actions scenes with a top notch score composed by Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrard. The costumes done on the gladiators are very striking and just as terrifying sometimes as the hungry tigers Maximus must defend himself against while he is battling Tigris of Gaul (Sven-Ole Thorsen), an undefeated gladiator called out of retirement. The crowds of the Coliseum are a sight to see themselves and the chants of Maximus ring through the walls of the Coliseum and in your mind once the credits have rolled. Gladiator has all of the ingredients of a classic epic masterpiece. The opening battle scene of Germania is cited as one of the best battle scenes of all time by CNN. Russell Crowe's portrayal of Maximus was named Entertainment Weekly's sixth favourite action hero and named Gladiator their third favourite revenge film. Gladiator has been responsible for an increased interest in Roman history, sometimes called the "Gladiator Effect." It assisted in the revival of the historical epic in the new millennium with films such as Tory, Kingdom of Heaven, and 300 being released. Gladiator isn't for everyone, as some may find the political jargle to drag the story down. It is still a film worth checking out if you can stand the long running time and have an interest in the story of a gladiator. "What we do in life echoes in eternity." - Maximus Decimus Meridius

A gargantuan, visually stunning and lavishly mounted old-fashioned sword and sandals epic spectacle, which is the first bona-fide one in four decades, this beloved often imitated critically acclaimed blockbuster started the modern renaissance of the sword and sandals cinema, it is full of intrigue and heroism, stylish, breathtaking with masterful direction by Ridley Scott and an intelligent screenplay that is filled with memorable dialogue by David Franzoni, John Logan and William Nicholson. The film opens in the forests of Germania circa 180 A.D., in a spectacular and bloody battle of unbridled brutality, General Maximus Decimus Meridus, played by Russell Crowe who is simply magnificent in a brilliant Oscar-winning performance of great physicality and emotional depth, he turns Maximus into a hero of mythic proportions, this is the film that propelled Crowe into the realm of international superstardom, he commands his legion of Roman soldiers to "unleash hell" on the barbarian hordes, with a deluge of arrows and catapults flinging flaming canisters that set their savage adversaries and their protective woods on fire, after Maximus has crushed Rome's enemies, he is summoned by the aging and dying emperor Marcus Aurelius, played with subtle and grace by the late Richard Harris, in a regal turn, who in private names Maximus "Protector of Rome," and tries to hand over his authority to Maximus, he does not want his son Commodes to inherit the throne because his son is not a moral man, and he recognizes Commodes for what he is, a weak, selfish, sniveling, immature tyrant, he is played by Joaquin Phoenix who delivers a superlative performance that is appropriately hateful and full of venom, Phoenix creates a genuinely treacherous and loathsome villain who hates Maximus and lusts after his own sister, Lucilla wonderfully played by the Danish beauty Connie Nielsen. Commodus murders his father assumes his power and orders Maximus executed, along with his wife and young son, escaping his execution and fleeing to his farm, Maximus discovers his family murdered, he is then captured by slave-traders and sold to Proximo, who is unforgettably played by the late Oliver Reed with such intense relish that he steals every scene he appears in, he is a pragmatic owner of gladiatorial slaves, who he routinely sends to their deaths in the province arena, so he could profit from their demise. After making his name as a gladiator with his ingenious fighting skill in the provinces, Maximus who is known only as "The Spaniard," is taken to Rome where he is forced to continue his enslaved life fighting to the death in the colosseum, there Maximus finally sees a chance to avenge the murders of his wife and son, he becomes a crowd favorite and threatens Commodus with his popularity, Commodus is shocked to see him still alive, and knows he cannot kill him right off because of the crowd, who now loves Maximus, he also knows that the only way to kill him is in the arena, the best part of this film takes place in the arena of the Colosseum with some extraordinary fight sequences, which includes deadly lady archers on chariots, ferocious man-eating Bengal tigers in the arena, and a jaw-dropping, suspenseful sword fight between Maximus and a massive, hulking gladiator named Tigris the Gaul, who is the only undefeated champion in Roman history, he is superbly played by character actor  Sven-Ole Thorsen, there are impeccable  supporting performances from Derek Jacobi, Djimon Hounsou, David Schofleid, John Sharpnel, and David Hemmings, Hans Zimmer and Lisa Gerrards deliver a lush, soulful musical score, gorgeous cinematography by John Mathieson, with a stupendous production design by Arthur Max, and a striking costume design by Janty Yates, the incredible Oscar-winning  CGI visual effects recreate ancient Rome in all of her majestic glory. A remarkable cinematic  achievement that is a total triumph for Ridley Scott and Russell Crowe.  Winner of 5 Academy Awards including Best Picture and Best Actor: Russell Crowe. Highly Recommended.

'Are you not entertained?'...I still most certainly am after watching this film countless times, it is now time for me to review the film the way it should be. Now in many cases, I believe the film is terribly underrated and I go against people and agree with this film winning best picture for many reasons. I cannot judge how historically accurate this all is, a lot of it does feel stylized and modernized and people believe that the bloodshed makes the film....but that is never the case. Sure Ridley Scott shoots the film with skill and experience and his battle scenes are great and bloody, but its his distant shots of war and Rome; and the close personal conflicts of characters where he is at his most powerful. 

The acting is a major highlight of the film, with Russell Crowe delivering a commanding and powerful performance, Joaquin Phoenix tapping into the depth of his character and being quite captivating and strong supporting roles by Connie Nielsen and Oliver Reed...and the always outstanding Richard Harris.

Another film I could go on and on about, many people are blinded by the violence and bloodshed that they don't see the true brilliance of this film. A masterpiece that will remain memorable for many years to come.

With this weekend's release of Ridley Scott's new film "Robin Hood", I wanted to reflect on an earlier collaboration he did with the film's star, Russell Crowe -- a little known film called "Gladiator". 

I know that I'm going to get a lot of comments disagreeing with me since I'm not a big fan of this film, and on how they feel how much of a "masterpiece" they think this film is.  But the fact of the matter is, I am still trying to figure out what makes this film so popular.

And if you disagree strongly, please don't just tell me you "disagree". Tell me, or better yet, "explain" to me why this film is so great and what I missed. Because I'm going to explain to you in detail why I think this film is the most overrated film of the decade.  

When I first saw this blockbuster film back in September of 2000, I can admit that I liked it....sort of. Yes, it was entertaining.  And at times, exciting. But I won't go as far as to say it was great.

Why? Well let's take it from the beginning:

The opening battle sequence where the Romans, led by Maximus Decimus Meridius, battle the Germanians for control of their land is so choppy and blurred, by filming this whole sequence in slow motion, it gets confusing and is hard to tell what's going on, and who's winning and who's losing. 

I figured veteran director Ridley Scott would have already known how to direct a battle sequence, considering Mel Gibson pretty much set the (then) new standard for battle sequences five years earlier in Braveheart -- it was Gibson's second directorial effort, and he won a Best Director Oscar for it.

But later on, there is one scene that I felt would redeem this film, and shows how this movie would have been great -- and it's a small scene that I don't mind watching over and over again -- it's the sequence where military guards take Maximus into the woods to execute him, and he asks to be given a soldier's honorable death. As soon as the soldier raises his sword on his victim, Maximus jumps up and head-butts the soldier, takes his sword and slays them all. 

THAT WAS A GREAT SCENE!

It was quick, to the point, without hesitation, without mercy....the way a scene like that should be filmed. But beyond that, the film begins to falter. The coliseum battle scenes once again become choppy and confusing; the performances are lackluster and without much feeling behind them (to me, Joaquin Phoenix was miscast and never should have been nominated for Best Supporting Actor), and if they're not that, they become shouting matches with too much overacting.

But I guess along with Scott's unusually amateurish direction, the other problem with Gladiator is Russell Crowe's performance. To me, it didn't feel like he was acting, but more like he was posing and going through the basic moves.

Crowe mumbled, grumbled, moped and sneered. Sometimes he yelled. But what's worse than that, he won an Oscar for Best Actor for this film!

I'm not picking on this talented actor. But the fact of the matter is that he is so much better than what he displays here. Some people call this his breakout film, but those are the people who have never seen all of his other, better roles. His performance as a neo-nazi skinhead in 1992's "Romper Stomper" is somewhat of an introduction to this future great actor. 

In 1997's "L.A. Confidential", his hot-headed, dim-witted police detective made critics notice his talent. And what I think is his best role, as tobacco industry informant Jeffrey Wigand in 1999's "The Insider" (a film I feel he should have won the best actor Academy Award for), showed that Crowe can play a victim as well as an aggressor.

But I guess the thing I disliked the most about this film is one of the last scenes -- where Maximus is laying in the center of an arena, bleeding to death. He mumbles, practically whispers his last words. It's something about "Quintus, release my men. Senator Gracchus is to be reinstated. There was a dream that was Rome...."

He's mumbling all of this out, just barely audible enough for one person to hear him. But it is suggested that the whole arena can hear him? I know it's supposed to be symbolic -- that although he's whispering, his voice is the voice of power, strength and rightousness, that he could not be easily silenced but....the whole arena can hear him?

Yes, "Gladiator" can be an exciting, entertaining, and at times, over-the-top piece of pop-culture.  But whenever I come across it on television, I tend to watch it again and try to figure out why this movie is held so close to so many's hearts.

Since Marcus Aurelius' has made no public announcement of his intentions yet, Commodus seizes the moment when he's told of it and strangles the old man, taking the succession for himself. There conflict goes on. From about to be emperor Maximus turns slave, this is really a twist in the story. His wife and his son are killed by the soldiers sent by Commodus.

Undeniably Russell Crowe's greatest performance ever, Gladiator simply took my breath away. It has become one of my all-time favorites, and none of my friends have ever found faults in it (except perhaps my grumpy old dad, but even he liked it which says quite a lot). 

Set in the year A.D. 180, this is an epic tale of war, politics and love. Crowe stars as the succesfull Roman general, Maximus Decimus Meridius, a leader of Rome's Northern Armies and a veteran of the just-completed campaign against the Germanic barbarians at the time where the Roman Empire was the height of its power. Deeply loyal to his old friend the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, he is shocked when he hears that the dying Ceazar wants him to take over as Roman Emperor instead of nominating Commodus, the true heir to the throne. 

Upon being told, Commodus murders his father in a fit of rage and jealousy, and then orders the execution of Maximus. Narrowly escaping death, Maximus travels back to his homestead in Hispania only to find his son and daughter already dead, hanging above the rubble of his old farm. Succumbing to grief and exhaustion, he faints.

After waking up, he finds that he has been captured by slave traders and is taken to an outpost in a Roman province in North Africa. From there onwards, sold as a Gladiator he finds that he must use his fighting skills not only for mere survival, but also to get a chance at revenge against the man who destroyed his life.

This tragic yet beautiful story of one man's epic struggle against a tyrant broke new ways in CGI effects: The crowd, the complete Colosseum (where a third had been rebuilt in plaster and plywood) and large parts of Rome where all shown with advanced CGI techniques. For example, a small crowd was first shot, and then digitally multiplied 6 times over to make it look larger. This step was in fact repeated when they had to fill the whole of the Colosseum, whioch has room for 50.OOO people. That set aside, the quality of the acting (Crowe won the Best Actor award at the 73rd Academy Awards), script, filming and over-all ploit and setting is extremely compelling. Nobody can watchthis movie and call it a waste of time, let alone be disappointed. I clearly recommend this movie for people of all ages, although some of the gore may not be for kids. Two thumbs up, it totally deserves my vote of 100%!

Oscar Sunday 2010.
G is for Gladiator, which won Best Picture at the awards 10 years ago.
In the barren wilderness of Germania, General Maximus  Decimus Meridius (Russell Crowe) is fighting for the dream that is Rome. The aging emperor, Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris), watches his victory and decides that this man should be the one to restore hope and prosperity to Rome. This does not go over well with the emperor's son and presumed heir Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix), who learns of his father's decision and opts to kill both him and Maximus before those plans come to fruition. The emperor succumbs, but Maximus survives, to see his family and home destroyed, to be taken captive and sold as a gladiator, to return in glory to Rome. There he fights in the Coliseum in the games that Commodus has commanded in order to win the hearts of the mob. There, in the gladiatorial ring, he reveals himself to the Emperor and continues to defy him and plot his revenge, until at last the opportunity arises.
This is a gripping film, a near-perfect blend of top-notch action, plot, character, and acting, a beautiful production that seamlessly transports its audience to the world of ancient Rome. The story is classic - there are heroes to love and villains to despise, and there is drama and tension and conspiracy. There are triumphs and there are losses; I would be the first to admit that this film reliably makes me cry (though "Gladiator" is certainly not alone in this regard). Unfortunately, it also has a bit more gore and testosterone than I care for, which puts that final tomato just out of reach.
Overall, an excellent historical epic drama and worthy Best Picture winner that still enthralls a decade later.
An exceptionally strong cast, headed by Crowe and Phoenix, turn this action spectacle into a masterpiece.

Most directors would kill to have one masterpiece in their body of work. Most would crawl across broken glass to have two. But with Gladiator, Ridley Scott joins the hallowed ranks of Stanley Kubrick, David Lynch and Francis Ford Coppola, with his third complete and utter triumph. After a long period in the critical wilderness, few could have believed that this prodigious talent, who peaked so early in his career, could ever recapture his past form. But disregarding his subsequent efforts, there can be no doubt from watching Gladiator that Scott is one of the greatest directors of the last twenty years.

Ten years after its release, it's easy to blame Gladiator for any number of films which have followed close on its heels. Aside from Scott's slightly underwhelming Kingdom of Heaven, we've had to deal the hagiographic hyperbole of Troy and Alexander. And then there is 300, which combined the looks of Gladiator and Sin City before stripping out all the substance of both to create something truly silly. One could further argue that without Gladiator, there would be no Pirates of the Caribbean; Scott's success, both critical and commercial, seemed to suggest that long-dead genres were not so long-dead.

If we ignore its legacy for the moment, we are left with a powerful film which, like Batman Begins, is a perfect marriage of substance and spectacle. Like Christopher Nolan, Scott is a commercially-minded auteur, someone who marries a pure artistic vision with a no-nonsense approach to filmmaking. Scott knows what will sell, but he doesn't let the box office dictate his shooting style. Gladiator is a very accessible film, but it is also emotionally intense and visually striking, containing any number of images which wouldn't look out of place in an art film. These range from the poppies falling in the arena before the final showdown, to the shadows on the bust as Marcus Aurelius is killed: one eye is seen in light, the other in shadow, representing the empire slipping into darkness.

Being a swords-and-sandals epic, the film does have to conform to some extent to the conventions of Spartacus and Ben-Hur. Despite coming from all over the Roman Empire, our main characters all speak English in vaguely British accents. We know that our main character will not die before the end of the film. Much blood will be spilt, there'll be plenty of crowd shots, and there definitely won't be a happy ending. On that basis, you'd think you could sketch out the plot of the film on the back of a serviette. But Scott is cleverer than that, and knows that we're cleverer too.

What Scott manages to do in Gladiator is to inject these conventions with new life, not by subverting them so much as bending them and adding his personal touch. Scott gives us a central battle between good and evil, but he twists it by making Maximus either the most reluctant of heroes or the most enticing of anti-heroes. He is not a killing machine on a spiritual warpath; he kills because he has to, only when he has to, and he does not enjoy it. The film avoids falling into the trap of justifying his killings, either by belittling the people he kills, or by suggesting that the reward of seeing his family in Elysium was worth all the bloodshed. It's ultimately tragic, since the central character is essentially broken and slowly dies over the course of the film.

Russell Crowe's performance in the central role is incredible, but equally incredible is that of Joaquin Phoenix as Commodus. In the emperor Scott gives us a villain who is sinister and creepy, and yet strangely vulnerable. His incestuous love for Lucilla is writ large, but this can equally be read as his means to express an overall desire to be loved. Commodus is also a tragic figure, insofar as he causes his own downfall, craving to be loved whether by his sister or the people of Rome. In the end, both turn against him; his sister realises her love for Maximus, and the crowd look on in silence as Maximus pushes a knife slowly into his throat. We do not warm to Commodus but we completely understand his pain and anguish at being neglected by his father and lied to by his own soldiers. We feel sorry for him as he dies, rather than just cheering Maximus on.

Credit must also go to Scott, as well as the writers, for giving this story a compelling female presence, something which previous historical epics have lacked. Scott has a good track record with strong female characters; think of Ripley in Alien, Rachael in Blade Runner, or both leads in Thelma and Louise. Unlike James Cameron, however, he never feels the need to gloss over their more 'feminine', sensitive qualities. Where Cameron in Aliens gave Ripley a gun and called it feminist, Scott allows Connie Nielsen's character to work to her own strengths. She is a loving mother with genuine feelings, who is also intelligent and wise in matters of the state, and exerts influence by choosing who she trusts.

At its heart, Gladiator is not really a film about revenge, redemption, or weaponry. It's a film about love, whether for one's family or the people one serves. What starts off as a film about duty and honour slowly transforms into a battle between the hardship of the mortal world and the forgiving arms of the next. After the death of his family, Maximus spends the rest of the film in a deep quandary. He knows he must fight the injustice of Commodus' rule, but the longer he resists, the longer he stays away from his family, and the further he must go in stopping his foe.

What Scott manages is to give us all these interesting and arresting ideas within a well-told story beset with enough breathtaking spectacle to stop us losing interest. Unlike The Dark Knight, the set-pieces are kept to a minimum and make sense in the order in which they come. More impressively, the themes of the story are never put on hold as the crowd-pleasing action unfolds. Even in its most blockbuster moments, like Maximus and Commodus having a punch-up in the arena, the film still carries immense weight and depth. They are not just men in shorts hitting each other, they are symbols, locking horns for the future of Rome in a way which neither really wants.

All of Scott's films are visually arresting, but in this one he really excels himself. John Mathieson's cinematography is brilliant, capturing Scott's 2nd century through a wonderful range of metallic greys, woody browns and olive greens. By opening with a battle scene, we are thrust straight into this world. Five minutes in, before a single word has been spoken, we feel right in the centre of that battlefield, in a world with its own culture in all dimensions. The battle scenes themselves are gripping; before the arrival of The Lord of the Rings, this was one of the best on-screen battles around.

Gladiator is a monumental triumph of a film, an epic with a great sense of heart and purpose which never fails to enthral and entertain. Although on a par with Alien and Blade Runner, the film is perhaps most similar to Apocalypse Now: for all its tiny flaws and little meanderings, the film holds an intense hypnotic pull on your senses, so that in the end you just can't help but love it. If you want realism or historical accuracy, you won't find it here. But what you will find is a powerful story which echoes through the ages, brought to us through riveting performances and helmed by a director at the top of his game. If Robin Hood even faintly resembles this, it could be the film of the year.

Director Ridley Scott brings back the good old days of epic films and Roman era movies with a look into the history and corruption of the Roman empire and the sick brutality that was the gladiator games.

An old Caesar reflects on his life and the fate of Rome. After victory in Germania to bring peace in the Empire, Marcus Aurelius chooses the General to his army, Maximus, to be the next ruler of Rome and not his own son, Commodus. In an act of emotional passion, Commodus kills his father to become Caesar and orders Maximus and his family to be killed. Maximus survives his execution, but finds his family dead. Now with nothing he becomes a gladiator. But the fates would have it that Maximus will once again see Commodus and have his vengence. It's a classic revenge tale that though that the most of the characters are pretty basic. A strong willed and likeable hero that defies the empire by being liked by everyone. But the whole movie souly rides on Commodus and Joaqin Phoenix's brilliant acting. Truely my favourite performance of his. Commodus is a man who is never respected, not even by his own father, and that tears him up in so many different ways. And he has a perverted fondness to his sister as well. Commodus really is the best character in the movie. If only the rest of the characters had that kind of complexity. But the whole movie seems to theme around one old Emperor and his influence on people's fate.

Nothing short of amazing when it comes to this movie in almost every direction. The Roman Colosseum is brought to life with this movie's amazing achievements in CGI. A breathtaking and highly detailed look around every corner. The shooting areas, the costumes, the props and fucking everything. EVERYTHING is perfection in this movie. The cinematography is no exception either. Through Ridley Scott's incredable talent, there are many scenes with beautiful lighting and mise-en-scene. It's a visual feast for the eyes that adds so much flavour to the movie. And to top it all, the powerful music composed by Hanz Zimmer makes every scene epic.

With powerful preformances from the cast, great directing and perfect production detail, Gladiator influences Hollywood to bring back the classic Roman epics in a BIG way. The story is just short of being absolutely perfect, but that's not to say that this movie isn't a strong character based story with lots to analyze and feel. But this movie is made in such a way that it is always entertaining to watch anytime.

What a great movie. Gladiator is the perfect mix between big mainstream spectacle and moviemaking at its best. The story is about roman general Maximus Meridius (Russell Crowe), fighting for his freedom and justice ( The plot is not that thin, but I don't want to reveal any spoilers). No with a setting like that, in 99% of the cases, the director would go on the easy way and just crazy swort and sandal action, but because this movie's directed by Sir Ridley Scott, it doesn't follow the mass.

Scott takes us on a journey, from the first frame up to the last. He spends more time developping characters, than showing great action scenes and because he does that, when the action hits, it's way more effective and in a strange way we fund ourselves in the arena rooting for our hero. I'm praising a lot of Scott's great direction, but I should also praise the magnificent cast.

Russell Crowe is fantastic as Maximus. He's one of those actors who completely dissapear in his role. Besides Joaquin Phoenix, I thought the supporting cast was top-notch. My problem with Joaquin Phoneix was that he delivered a very awkward performance. First of all he cries too much for a roman emperor, that seemed a bit out of range. There are scenes where you could hand him over the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor right away, and there are scenes where he plays a bad villain stereotype. So as a whole I thought his performance could've been a better.

This movie has a great director, a fantastic cast and a beautiful soundtrack. Yes the soundtrack in this movie is fantastic. The composer is Hans Zimmer and this ranks among his best work. There is a track in the soundtrack called "Now we are free" that captures both happiness and sadness at the same time and it conducts perfectly the end of the movie.

I strongly recommend Gladiator, Ridley Scott has created another masterpiece after ALIEN and Blade Runner.

Don't get me wrong because I think Gladiator is one of the best Roman Empire epics I have ever seen. The sword and sandal epic had been dead for years until Ridley Scott and Russell Crowe decided to reboot it and they made a spectacle for the ages out of it. The story centers on General Maximus Decimus Meridius (Russell Crowe),who's army wins a war against the Germanic barbarians and is offered the throne in Rome from the current dying Emperor (Richard Harris). However,the power hungry son of the Emperor Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix),murders his father and kills Maximus' wife and son. And if that couldn't get any worse,Maximus is put in slavery but goes on a vengeance once he's sold to the gladiator teacher Proximo (Oliver Reed). This is when Maximus must fight his way through the gladiatorial games in Rome in order to ultimately achieve his revenge against Commodus.

Russell Crowe is absolutely fantastic as Maximus. His character is very strong-willed and completely unphased in his determination for vengeance. His performance is very intense but inspiring for anyone who watches it. Joaquin Phoenix is the epitome of a slimy,evil son. He makes you feel completely scornful of what his character does and he is completely unrelenting in his control over Rome. Other standout performances include Connie Nielsen as Commodus' sister and Djimon Hounsou as Maximus' closest friend Juba.

Once again,Ridley Scott is the standout in masterminding every aspect of this film. He uses a lot of CGI for the backdrops of ancient Rome but it looks pretty damn close to the way it looked back then. He stages the battle sequences in a perfectly choreographed way and has you on the edge of your seat for most of the action that takes place. He creates a very epic scale of the setting and turns it into an environment that just grabs you from the very beginning and never lets go of you until the end of the film.

Gladiator is a complete revival of a once dead genre but what a way to reboot it! I know that some people say it isn't Best Picture material but I don't care because I think Gladiator is one of the most entertaining,engrossing epic films I have ever seen in my life.

Win the crowd, and you will win your freedom. Russell Crowe stars as Maximus Decimus Meridius, a warrior whose family is murdered, and vows revenge against the ruler of Rome. That new leader of Rome is Commodus played by Joaquin Pheonix. This historical epic puts accuracy and history to the side in favour of action, spectacle and story. Director Ridley Scott definitely made the best choice by doing this. Scott focuses on the fact that power comes from trust. Maximus is a slave gladiator who fights only for the entertainment of others. Eventually, that entertainment becomes Commodus' worst enemy. Gladiator is an epic in every which way and combines style and substance creating a sweeping journey that is hair-raising. Sometimes Gladiator tries to makes its point too much when we already get the general idea. But, the over dramatization is quickly forgotten as you cheer for Maximus in the Roman colosseum. With a lot of violence and great battle sequences, the adrenaline flows fast and hard. What takes this epic to another level is the highly compelling story of revenge. Yes, revenge is nothing new to a plot scheme, but the story is crafted and built up so well, you really want Maximus to get his revenge. The emotions are true, and that is all you can really ask for.  Gladiator is a massively entertaining epic that proves revenge isn't getting old in Hollywood just yet.

What really helps this movie succeed is the wave of emotions that come from the Roman crowd. It is not the fact that they are displeased with Commodus running the country, they are just content. They need to be more than just content. Commodus gives them the entertainment they deserve. But, that entertainment that he has created turns out to be his downfall. Maximus is a warrior picked up by the slave trade and forced to fight for his freedom. Maximus knows that Commodus has killed his own father, as well as his wife and daughter. All I can say is look out, because this man is gunning for blood. Even when Maximus isn't in front of the Roman crowd, he is vengeful and furious. He bursts into the ring against four opponents, kills them easily, and finishes the last one off with a double-sword decapitation. "Are you not entertained?", he screams to the onlookers. Maximus is losing focus. His anger shouldn't be one winning the fight, but gathering a following of fans. After all, what can one Caesar do against thousands of Roman citizens? Not much. Ridley Scott gets inside what Maximus is feeling and it makes the motivation for revenge essential to the story and not just for a reason to root for Maximus. When Maximus reaches Rome, he plans to over throw Commodus by winning the crowd over. Strangely, this manages to work. Commodus is doomed from the start. He throws free food and gifts into the audience in an attempt to win them over. Commodus doesn't realize that trust trumps bribery. The people of Rome come back to see Maximus defeat whatever the Caesar throws at him. Commodus is an unfit leader who cuts corners and cannot be noble and true to his people. This even comes in the final battle where desperation has forced Commodus to fight Maximus. "Do you think I'm afraid of you?", asks Commodus to Maximus, to which Maximus replies "I think you have been afraid all your life." Commodus then stabs Maximus in the side to handicap him for the match. But, these matches that we watch throughout the movie are what make us, the audience, feel like one of the crowd.

With spectacular editing and rousing choreography, Gladiator delivers the entertainment along with the motivation. What I like most about Gladiator, is that is only gory when it needs to be. Scott's choices are similar to those of Scorsese in Gangs of New York. In the opening brawl in New York, the cleavers fly and people get slashed left and right. There are only flashes of red and a hint of blood, yet we are entranced. The idea of violence in our heads is enough. Gore isn't that scary because audiences today are desensitized to it. Overkill with the gore is what has kept many horror franchises (Saw, Hostel) from being frightening and many other movies from being nothing more than entertainment. The movies that stick with you have staged violence that doesn't dwell on the bloodbath part of that violence. They dwell on the action and the idea that what you don't see is the scariest part of all. The fact that Gladiator shows a stab, and then quickly cuts away makes us feel like we are watching this fight. Someone gets hurt, we turn away in shock and then look back again. Scott sweeps across the arena with animals, trap doors, chariots and swords. Scott also shows the unification of survivors when all of the gladiatorial slaves band together. They all raise their shields and then move forward and under to knock down a chariot. The crowd cheers and so do we. The actions not only entertains, but resonates. 

As for the performances in this movie, for the most part, they are great. Russell Crowe nails this role on the head. He has the right attitude of a broken and noble man. He doesn't deserve what has happened to him, but he goes with it anyway. He is a born leader and uses that to his advantage in the fight. Joaquin Pheonix is a scene stealer. His eyes always look like he is on the edge of losing control. That is the most disturbing aspect of all. He is like a ticking time-bomb just waiting to go off. All you can do is wait. Connie Nielsen plays Lucilla, Commodus' sister. She was good, but highly underused. I felt like they put her in just so they could have a kiss in the preview for Gladiator. She is a very tiny role and I felt her importance could have been amplified a lot bigger. The rest of the supporting cast is in classic epic fashion. They al contribute to the story nicely. Scott doesn't spend too much time with build up, which I liked, but sometimes he over dramatizes his characters. For instance, Commodus (Pheonix) looks at a statue of his father that he murdered and starts slashing at it with a sword and crying. The entire movie is built around Commodus hating his father, murdering him, taking his throne and changing Rome into an entertainment center. I think we get that he doesn't like his father. This is just too much.

However, there never is enough blood in Gladiator. The battle scenes were so well shot, I wish I could have seen some more of that. You feel like one of the Roman's. As you anticipate the next fight, and you can't wait to see what the Caesar has in store for Maximus next. Screw historical accuracy, this movie is an example of Hollywood conventions used to their full potential. We have seen countless revenge stories over the years, but Gladiator is highly compelling. The acting, the nice pace of the story and the gargantuan arena battles makes you care. Even when Gladiator starts pounding the messages home, Crowe stands tall. This isn't Ridley Scott's best film, but it is definitely one of the more entertaining and high caliber epics out there. Am I entertained Maximus? The answer to that is a big yes.

Before I get tons of messages and e-mails of people telling me how much an idiot I am for not giving this a brilliant score, I want to make this clear: THIS IS MY REVIEW!! My Opinion, and my thoughts on the film. If I were to agree with everyone else I might as well not have an opinion. Gladiator isn't even a bad film, it's just ok in my opinion, and I'll explain why. The action scenes were amazing, the acting was great and the cinematography was beautiful. All of this was down to the fantastic direction by Ridley Scott. The score also fit the moods perfectly. My problems with the film are that the scenes without action for the first hour and a half were really dull. The dialogue could have been better, and the scenes were uninteresting. It was only towards the end where we got to see how the Political Aspect worked that they became interesting to me. Also, the length bugged me. Much could have been cut to easily make this a two hour film. The pace as well is quite slow. But despite my criticisms, Gladiator is an ok film and shows that Scott knows how to deliver a great feel of different time periods.

When I went to see Gladiator on it's release in 2000, I walked out the cinema bitterly disappointed. It went on to win 5 Oscars (including Best Picture) and received a further 7 nominations. This only added to my feelings of resentment towards it.
As a result, I chose to avoid seeing it again and didn't mince my words on my dislike for it. However, plenty of people - who's opinions I respect - seemed to love it. For that reason, I chose to have a reappraisal.
 During the days of the Roman Empire, dedicated soldier Maximus (Russell Crowe) loyally serves the emperor Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris). When the emperor is killed, Maximus refuses to transfer his loyalty to his son and new emperor, Commodus (Joaquin Phoenix) and suffers the consequences. He is ordered to be killed but manages to escape, ending up in the hands of slave trader Proximo (Oliver Reed), who pits him into the Roman Colosseum as a gladiator. It's here that Maximus realises he can still use the arena and the crowd to his benefit and plan his revenge on Commodus.
 On only my second viewing of this film, my opinion has changed and changed for the better. I still have issues with it but it's granduer is undeniably impressive and as a slice of entertainment it can't be faulted. I can honestly admit now, that my scornful opinion of this film was slightly unjust. It was much better than I remember but still not the classic it's proclaimed to be. For a start, it has a high tendency for melodrama. This is acceptable in some cases but with the acclimations that Gladiator has recieved over the years, I find it needs to be scrutinised a little further. One of the main causes for it's melodramatic approach is some ridiculous dialogue. Reportedly, during production Russell Crowe himself had complaints with screenwriter William Nicholson's dialogue, apparently telling him it was "garbage". I found that to be the case in several scenes and when delivering it, the uncomfortableness in the actors looked apparent. However, they manage to carry it well enough; Crowe is a commanding presence in his Oscar winning role but it's by no means his best performance. I think his abilities were better tested the year before in "The Insider", where he was absolutely superb and deserved the Oscar then. Phoenix is another actor I admire and he also delivers a good performance but unfortunately suffers with a poorly written and stereotypical character. He's no more than a cartoon villain - complete with dark eye shadow - and he couldn't really get any more nasty. Old hands, Harris and Reed phone their performances in and it looks as if Reed is just there for the beer tokens. Jacobi, however brief, shows his thespian abilities and the always excellent Djimon Hounsou is wasted in another poorly written role. There's not a lot going on for the character's as ultimately, this is all about the spectacle. And a fine, grandiose one it is. With "Blade Runner" and most recently "Prometheus", Scott has never been known to scrimp on the visual front and this is no different. It is 
exquisitely detailed (kudos to cinematographer John Mathieson) and filmed in the grandest of scales. The director can't be faulted in his ability to capture the hearts and minds of an audience and this is no more apparent than the impressively choreographed battle scenes and wonderfully ethereal afterlife sequences - shot with a highly artistic eye. Such scenes are afforded a greater power by a superb score from Hans Zimmer and the amazing vocal talents of Lisa Gerrard (for those unaware, check out her beautiful work with Australian outfit "Dead Can Dance"). On a visual and audio front, this film can't be reckoned with but unfortunately, I found it to succumb to formula. Despite the fact that the real life Commodus did actually fight in the the gladiatorial arena, the ending stretched credulity for me but I suppose dramatic license is commonplace in film's of this type.
 I enjoyed this a far-sight more than I used to, as it's undeniably epic and visually arresting. Essentially though, this is an action movie. A good one but not much more than an action movie dressed in the Emperor's clothes.

Gladiator, the 2000 Best Picture winner, is the culmination of Ridley Scott's career, the absolute pinnacle of his filmmaking craft. And though it may somewhat pale in comparison to his more thoughtful early films, a la Alien or Blade Runner (incomparable though they may be), it's not very easy to deny that Gladiator is one hell of a movie. A historical epic made with an all-star cast and the budget of a summer action blockbuster, Gladiator benefits from an ensemble cast at the top of their game, expert direction by Scott, a focused and driven script by David Franzoni and John Logan, and, of course, good old fashioned balls-to-the-wall gladiatorial action. More violent than most films of its kind, only made more epic by the beautiful fight choreography. Of course, this film would still be little more than another historical epic if it were not for the outstanding, career-defining effort from Russell Crowe. Crowe throws himself completely and utterly into the role of Maximus, and takes his acting to new heights, establishing himself as one of the go-to guys of Hollywood's best and brightest. Maximus is one of film's greatest modern heroes, tough and resolute yet so vulnerable and charismatic, that you can't help but root for him at every misfortune that comes his way. However, the rest of the cast must also be applauded. Joaquin Phoenix completes the good vs. evil dynamic as the despicable Commodus, a very easily hated villain. Simple, yes, but effective in his role in the story, and Phoenix makes him as creepy and deplorable as humanly possible. Djimon Hounsou, Richard Harris, Derek Jacobi, and Oliver Reed (in his final film role) also give memorable character to their roles. Connie Nielsen may be the only misstep in terms of acting ability, as she occasionally comes off as a tad wooden. This is a film with few flaws, and plenty of memorable scenes. Overall, if you're a fan of movies in general, Gladiator may be just the spectacle you crave.

I really thoroughly enjoyed the action sequences in Gladiator, but in retrospect, I find that that was about the only part of the film that I *did* thoroughly enjoy.
I do often get tired of overabundant use of CGI effects, and Gladiators CGI effects are a prime example of what happens when a film is overly reliant on effects that quickly become dated. Rather than tell the story, the effects were more of the flashy parts of the picture that started to take me out of the film rather than draw me in. I did really like the colors and the art direction. The cinematography was even fairly impressive at times. The problem was that I got sick of seeing all the CGI, which looks monumentally corny by any other standards outside of the year 2000.
I was also quite unimpressed with the dialogue. A little overly reliant on melodrama, the dialogue pales in comparison to the dialogue I heard in such pictures as Ben-Hur and Spartacus. Now, I am not saying that the dialogue was bad. I am just saying that I was unimpressed with it, and enough unimpressive dialogue has a tendency to produce a rather unimpressive movie.
I did like Russell Crowes performance and I also liked Joaquin Phoenixs performance. A lot of the actors were acting a little too melodramatic for my taste, though. Too many of these characters were just too uninteresting, especially when compared to the new emperor, who was easily the best written character in the film. Yes, even more so than Maximus Decimus Meridius.
Now, I do want to praise the action sequences. They made the film worthy of watching the one time. However, I have never seen a film that held up so poorly in my life. The over reliance on effects over screenplay might be a part of that, but it still doesnt make up for the fact that I cannot bring myself to like the film beyond my first encounter.

In his time, Ridley Scott has directed and produced some of the most interesting, and successful films that mark upon violence and emotion in human nature. Amongst these are films like Black Hawk Down, Alien, and Blade Runner. However, out of all these outstanding additions to the Hollywood library, there is only one that had the emotional aspect and tone of violence to singe-handedly bring back interest to an overused genre, and stands as one of my favorite films of all time. This is Gladiator, a tale of betrayal, violence, revenge, and redemption.

Maximus Decimus Meridius is an honorable Roman general, in the time of the Roman conquering of Germania. He is looked up to by not only thousands of his soldiers that he fights with, but the Emperor of Rome himself, the head of the Caesar family. After an intense final battle with the reluctant Germanic people, and successfully managing to secure a valiant victory over the territory, Maximus is visited by the head of the Caesar family himself, in order for congratulation. Also, however, something far more urgent and important: Caesar does not trust his own son to helm the Roman people after he steps down. In order to retain popularity and servitude to the Caesar family after he has passed on, Caesar wants to pass on the honor of ruling the empire to Maximus.

Reluctantly, Maximus agrees to it. However, when Caesar explains his feelings to his son, Commodus, he is unable to understand the circumstances, and kills his father in protest. Then, to avoid the blame and turn the tables on the real heir to the throne, Commodus blames the murder on Maximus. Before the Roman general knows it, his wife and son are murdered, and even after he escapes execution, he becomes a slave.

However, the life of a slave is no burden to Maximus. As a Roman gladiator, he works his way up in popularity and eventually makes his way back to the heart of Rome, to fight at the Coliseum and eventually confront the man who ruined his life, and may eventually be the end of the Roman Empire. 

Striking not only at the intense violence that the Roman Era was famous for, Ridley Scott also manages to successfully show the political tension that runs beneath the lives of the rulers. In spectacular fashion, mixed in with gritty tones, and a phenomenal cast of beautiful actors (including Russel Crow and the always-fascinating Joaquin Phoenix) Gladiator is a near-perfect film, that goes in with immediate interest, and comes out with a lasting, emotional impact.

In short, a remarkable film that not only re-imagines several swords-and-sandals epics, but manages to present the political tension and brutal violence with surprising flare. A wave of applause goes out to Ridley Scott, as well as the entire cast of this incredible film.

Bravo, bravo.
